Now, let me ask you something. Have you ever been in a room full of people and still felt completely alone?
Have you ever watched everyone around you celebrate answered prayers, new opportunities, and exciting milestones... While you were quietly wondering when your own circumstances would change?
Maybe you've been praying for something for months. Maybe even years.
And at first, you were hopeful. You prayed faithfully. You trusted. And you believed you could remain patient.
But then the waiting continued.
And eventually, you began asking questions you never expected to ask.
Lord, do You see me?
Do You hear my prayers?
Have You forgotten what I'm going through?
Now, I want you to understand something. Those questions don't automatically mean you've abandoned your faith.
Sometimes they reveal how deeply you're hurting.
And Scripture gives us examples of faithful people who brought those kinds of questions before God.
Today, we're going to study one of the most comforting passages in the book of Isaiah.
We're going to look at David's honest prayers. We're going to revisit the story of a woman named Hagar. And we're going to talk about what it means to remember God's faithfulness when our emotions tell us we've been forgotten.
Our lesson is called... When You Feel Forgotten — Remembering God's Faithfulness in the Waiting.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Lord, today we're talking about something that can be difficult to admit. Feeling forgotten. Feeling overlooked. And wondering whether anyone truly sees what we're carrying. Father, You know every person listening. You know the prayers they've prayed. The disappointments they've experienced. And the situations that have left them feeling alone. Lord, help us approach Your Word with honesty and humility. Remind us of Your character. Help us understand Your promises in their proper context. And draw our hearts closer to Jesus Christ. May this time of study bring encouragement to those who are weary. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — ISAIAH 49:14–16 Now, let's turn to Isaiah chapter 49.
We're going to begin with verses 14 through 16. But before we read them, I want to explain what's happening in this passage.
The prophet Isaiah speaks about God's relationship with His people. And in this section, Zion is pictured as a woman who believes the Lord has abandoned her.
God's people had experienced suffering, displacement, and deep uncertainty.
And the language of the passage expresses their fear that God had forgotten them.
Now, let's read Isaiah chapter 49, verses 14 through 16, from the King James Version. "But Zion said, The LORD hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me. Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee. Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me."
Now, I want you to think about those words.
Zion says... "The LORD hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me."
Now, doesn't that sound like something a hurting person might say?
Lord, where are You?
Why hasn't anything changed?
Why does it feel like You've forgotten about me?
But then God responds.
And His response is filled with reassurance.
He uses the picture of a mother's compassion for her child.
Now, think about that. The bond between a mother and her nursing child is one of the strongest examples of human care.
And yet, God says that even if a mother were to forget, He would not forget His people.
Now, that's a powerful image.
Then He says... "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands."
Now, in the original context, God is reassuring Zion that He has not abandoned His covenant people.
We should be careful not to turn this passage into a promise that every personal circumstance will change according to our wishes.
But it does reveal something beautiful about God's character.
He is not careless toward His people.
And His faithfulness is greater than their present feelings of abandonment.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH Feeling forgotten doesn't mean God has forgotten you. Our feelings are real, but they don't always tell us the whole truth about God's faithfulness.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes our circumstances can make us feel invisible.
Sometimes silence can feel like rejection.
And sometimes waiting can make us question whether God is paying attention.
But Scripture encourages us to remember His character.
Not simply what our emotions are telling us in a difficult moment.
WHEN SILENCE FEELS LIKE ABANDONMENT Now, let's talk about something that can happen during long waiting seasons.
Silence begins feeling like abandonment.
Maybe you've prayed about something repeatedly.
You've asked God for wisdom. You've asked Him for help. And you've asked Him to change a difficult situation.
But nothing seems different.
And eventually, you begin wondering whether your prayers matter.
Now, I want to be careful here.
We shouldn't pretend to know why a particular prayer hasn't been answered the way someone hoped.
Sometimes we don't know.
And we shouldn't tell someone that God is delaying an answer because they haven't learned a particular lesson.
We simply don't have that kind of knowledge.
But we can encourage one another to keep turning toward the Lord.
We can continue praying honestly.
And we can remember that God's faithfulness isn't measured only by how quickly our circumstances change.
Now, here's something I want you to think about. Have you ever confused a lack of immediate answers with a lack of care?
Sometimes we do that in our human relationships.
Someone doesn't respond to a message as quickly as we hoped. And we begin imagining that they don't care.
Now, sometimes there really is a problem that needs to be addressed.
But other times, we're making assumptions without enough information.
And something similar can happen in our spiritual lives.
We don't understand what's happening. And we begin drawing conclusions about God's character.
But Scripture gives us a better foundation.
It reminds us who God has revealed Himself to be.
PSALM 13 — DAVID'S HONEST QUESTION Now, let's turn to Psalm chapter 13.
This is one of my favorite passages to study when we're talking about difficult emotions.
Because David doesn't hide what he's feeling.
Let's read Psalm 13, verses 1 and 2. "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me? How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?"
Now, I want you to hear those words again. "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD?"
David is speaking to God.
And he's asking whether God has forgotten him.
Now, think about that. David was a man who knew the Lord.
He had experienced God's faithfulness. He had worshiped Him. And he had trusted Him through difficult circumstances.
Yet here he is, asking... "How long?"
Now, I think that's important. Because sometimes we believe that strong faith means never asking difficult questions.
But Scripture shows us something different.
David brings his pain directly before the Lord.
He doesn't pretend everything is fine.
He doesn't hide his sorrow.
He prays honestly.
And I want you to understand something. Honest prayer is not the enemy of faith.
Sometimes honest prayer is how we continue turning toward God when life is difficult.
WHEN YOUR HEART IS TIRED OF WAITING Now, let's stay with Psalm 13 for a moment.
David says... "Having sorrow in my heart daily."
Now, that phrase is powerful.
Because sometimes sorrow isn't something we experience for a few minutes and then move beyond.
Sometimes it follows us through ordinary days.
We wake up carrying it. We go to work carrying it. We sit down for dinner carrying it. And we go to bed carrying it.
Now, maybe someone listening today understands exactly what that feels like.
Maybe you're carrying grief. Maybe you're worried about someone you love. Maybe you're facing a situation that hasn't been resolved. Or maybe you're simply exhausted from trying to remain hopeful.
Now, I want you to hear something important. You don't have to pretend that your sorrow isn't real.
And you don't have to feel ashamed for needing support.
Sometimes we need someone to pray with us.
Sometimes we need a trusted friend to listen.
And sometimes we need professional support to help us navigate overwhelming emotions.
Those things aren't failures of faith.
They can be important parts of caring for ourselves wisely.
DAVID'S RESPONSE — REMEMBERING GOD'S MERCY Now, let's continue reading Psalm 13.
We're going to read verses 5 and 6. "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation. I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me."
Now, notice something beautiful.
David began the psalm by asking whether God had forgotten him.
But he ends by remembering God's mercy.
Now, the passage doesn't tell us that every circumstance changed between verse 1 and verse 6.
It doesn't say that David suddenly received all the answers he wanted.
Instead, we see a movement in his prayer.
He begins with sorrow.
He brings his concerns before God.
And he remembers the Lord's mercy and salvation.
Now, that's something we can learn from.
Sometimes prayer doesn't immediately change our circumstances.
But prayer gives us an opportunity to bring our hearts before the Lord.
To remember His Word.
And to renew our attention toward His faithfulness.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You can acknowledge your pain and remember God's goodness at the same time.
Those things aren't opposites.
You can be grieving and still pray.
You can be disappointed and still worship.
And you can be uncertain while continuing to trust the Lord.
HAGAR — THE GOD WHO SEES Now, let's turn to Genesis chapter 16.
We're going to look at the story of Hagar.
And I want us to approach her story carefully.
Because Hagar wasn't simply someone who was impatient.
She was an Egyptian servant in Abraham and Sarah's household.
And she was placed in a difficult and unequal situation.
Sarah had not been able to have a child.
And she gave Hagar to Abraham in an attempt to obtain children through her.
Now, that arrangement involved serious power imbalances.
And after Hagar became pregnant, conflict developed.
Sarah treated Hagar harshly.
And Hagar fled.
Now, think about that. Hagar was vulnerable. She was pregnant. And she was away from the household where she'd been living.
Now, let's read Genesis chapter 16, verses 7 and 8. "And the angel of the LORD found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain in the way to Shur. And he said, Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go? And she said, I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai."
Now, notice something. The angel of the Lord found Hagar.
She was in the wilderness.
She had fled from mistreatment.
And the Lord was not unaware of her circumstances.
Now, later in the chapter, Hagar gives a name expressing what she has learned about God.
Let's read Genesis chapter 16, verse 13. "And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?"
Now, I love those words. "Thou God seest me."
Now, think about what that meant for Hagar.
She had experienced mistreatment.
She had fled into the wilderness.
And yet, her story reminds us that God was aware of her suffering.
Now, here's something important. The account includes instructions given to Hagar within her particular historical circumstances.
We should not use that narrative to tell someone today that they must return to an abusive or unsafe situation.
If someone is in danger, seeking safety and appropriate support is important.
But Hagar's story does show us something meaningful about God's awareness of the vulnerable.
She was not invisible to Him.
WHEN PEOPLE OVERLOOK YOU Now, let's talk about something that can be painful.
Being overlooked by people.
Maybe you've worked hard on something.
You've given your time. You've helped others. You've shown up when people needed you.
But when recognition comes, your name isn't mentioned.
Maybe you've supported someone through a difficult season.
But when you're the one struggling, you feel alone.
Or maybe you've simply felt invisible in a room full of people.
Now, those experiences can hurt.
And it's okay to acknowledge that.
But here's something I want you to remember. Your value isn't determined by how much attention other people give you.
And your worth isn't measured by public recognition.
As Christians, our identity is rooted in our relationship with Jesus Christ.
Now, that doesn't mean we should ignore unhealthy relationships.
Sometimes we need to communicate our needs.
Sometimes we need healthier boundaries.
And sometimes we need to seek relationships where mutual care and respect are present.
But we don't have to measure our entire worth by whether someone notices everything we do.
HEBREWS 6 — GOD IS NOT UNRIGHTEOUS TO FORGET Now, let's turn to Hebrews chapter 6, verse 10. The King James Version says: "For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister."
Now, let's think about that. The writer of Hebrews is encouraging believers who have demonstrated love through service to God's people.
And he reminds them that God is not unjust.
Their labor of love isn't meaningless.
Now, here's something important. This passage isn't promising that every act of service will bring public recognition.
It doesn't mean we'll always receive thanks.
And it doesn't mean every effort will produce the outcome we hoped for.
But it reminds us that faithful service matters to God.
Now, maybe someone listening today has been serving quietly.
Maybe you've been helping someone who cannot repay you.
Maybe you've been volunteering.
Maybe you've been caring for a loved one.
Or maybe you've been doing the right thing without anyone noticing.
Now, I want you to remember something. Faithful service doesn't become meaningless simply because it isn't celebrated publicly.
And you don't have to turn every act of kindness into an accomplishment that others can see.
Sometimes loving others faithfully happens in quiet places.
And those moments matter.
PAUSE AND PRAY — LORD, DO YOU SEE ME? Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about an area of your life where you've been feeling overlooked.
Maybe it's a relationship.
Maybe it's a responsibility.
Maybe it's a prayer you've been carrying.
Or maybe it's a difficult season that nobody else seems to understand.
Now, bring that before the Lord. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, You know the places where we've been feeling forgotten. You know the situations that have left us discouraged. And You know the burdens we've been carrying quietly. Lord, help us remember Your faithfulness. Give us wisdom to recognize when we need support. Help us communicate honestly with the people around us. And remind us that our worth isn't determined by public recognition. Father, draw us closer to Jesus Christ. And help us continue seeking You through every season. In His precious name, Amen.
HAGAR'S SECOND WILDERNESS EXPERIENCE Now, I want us to return to Hagar's story.
Because her experience in Genesis chapter 16 wasn't the last time she faced uncertainty.
In Genesis chapter 21, Hagar and her son Ishmael were sent away from Abraham's household.
They traveled into the wilderness.
And eventually, their water ran out.
Now, think about how frightening that situation must have been.
Hagar was a mother.
And her child was in danger.
Let's read Genesis chapter 21, verses 17 through 19. "And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is. Arise, lift up the lad, and hold him in thine hand; for I will make him a great nation. And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water; and she went, and filled the bottle with water, and gave the lad drink."
Now, notice something important. God heard.
And God provided for Hagar and Ishmael in that particular moment.
Now, we shouldn't turn this story into a guarantee that every crisis will end with an immediate miraculous provision.
But the narrative does reveal God's concern for people who were vulnerable and afraid.
And it reminds us that Hagar and Ishmael were not forgotten in the wilderness.
Now, I want you to think about that. Sometimes people feel forgotten because they're in a place they never expected to be.
Maybe life changed suddenly.
Maybe a relationship ended.
Maybe an opportunity disappeared.
Or maybe circumstances forced them into a season they never planned.
Now, those experiences can be frightening.
But we can continue turning toward the Lord.
And we can seek the practical help and support we need.
WHEN YOUR PRAYERS FEEL UNANSWERED Now, let's talk about something that connects directly with this week's theme.
Sometimes we begin feeling forgotten because our prayers haven't been answered the way we hoped.
Maybe you've prayed for healing.
Maybe you've prayed for a relationship.
Maybe you've prayed for an opportunity.
Or maybe you've prayed for a difficult situation to change.
And you're still waiting.
Now, here's something important. We don't always know why a particular outcome hasn't happened.
And we shouldn't assume that waiting always means a better version of our original request is coming.
Sometimes the outcome may be different.
Sometimes we may need to make new plans.
And sometimes we may continue carrying questions for a long time.
But we can still pray honestly.
We can continue seeking wisdom.
And we can remember that our relationship with God isn't based on receiving every answer according to our preferred timeline.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. God's faithfulness is greater than our ability to understand every circumstance.
ROMANS 8 — NOTHING CAN SEPARATE US FROM CHRIST'S LOVE Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 8.
I want us to look at one of the most encouraging passages in the New Testament.
Paul is writing about the believer's security in God's love through Jesus Christ.
And he asks a powerful question.
Let's read Romans chapter 8, verse 35. "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?"
Now, notice what Paul includes.
Tribulation. Distress. Persecution. Famine. Danger.
These are serious hardships.
And Paul doesn't pretend that believers will never experience them.
Instead, he reminds us that hardship doesn't have the power to separate those who belong to Christ from His love.
Now, let's read Romans chapter 8, verses 38 and 39. "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."
Now, I want you to think about those words.
"Nor things present, nor things to come."
That includes the uncertainty of the future.
Now, here's something important. Paul isn't promising that Christians will never suffer.
He's reminding believers of the security of God's love in Christ.
And that's the foundation of our hope.
Not that every situation will turn out exactly as we hoped.
But that our Savior is faithful.
WHEN YOU FEEL INVISIBLE IN YOUR OWN LIFE Now, I want to talk about something personal.
Sometimes we become so busy caring for everyone else that we begin feeling invisible in our own lives.
We make sure everyone has what they need.
We keep up with responsibilities.
We answer messages.
We show up for appointments.
And we try to make sure everything keeps moving.
But somewhere along the way, we stop paying attention to our own needs.
Now, I want you to hear something. Caring for others is important.
But you also have responsibilities toward your own well-being.
You need rest.
You need healthy relationships.
And sometimes you need support.
Now, that's not selfish.
It's part of living wisely.
And here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to earn your worth by being needed every moment of every day.
Your identity in Christ is deeper than the number of responsibilities you carry.
LAMENTATIONS — REMEMBERING WHAT IS TRUE Now, let's turn to Lamentations chapter 3.
We're going to read verses 21 through 23. The King James Version says: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."
Now, notice how the passage begins. "This I recall to my mind..."
The writer is intentionally remembering something.
And what does he remember?
The Lord's mercy.
His compassion.
And His faithfulness.
Now, let's remember the context.
Lamentations is filled with grief.
These words weren't written in a season where everything was easy.
They were spoken in the midst of sorrow.
And that's what makes them so meaningful.
Sometimes remembering God's faithfulness is a deliberate choice.
Not because our feelings aren't real.
But because our feelings aren't the only source of truth.
We can acknowledge what hurts.
And still remember what Scripture teaches about God.
PRACTICAL WAYS TO REMEMBER GOD'S FAITHFULNESS Now, let's talk about a few practical ways we can apply today's lesson.
First, be honest about what you're feeling.
If you feel forgotten, acknowledge it.
Bring it before the Lord.
And don't feel that you have to hide your emotions behind religious language.
Second, return to Scripture.
Read passages that reveal God's character.
Study them in context.
And allow God's Word to shape your understanding.
Third, remember examples of God's faithfulness.
Maybe you've experienced His provision in the past.
Maybe you've seen how Scripture has guided you.
Or maybe you've witnessed His grace through the support of other believers.
Now, those memories can encourage you.
Fourth, seek healthy relationships.
Sometimes feeling forgotten is made worse by isolation.
And we need people who will listen, pray, and offer practical support.
And fifth, continue living faithfully.
Even while you're waiting.
Your life still matters.
And there are still opportunities to honor Christ today.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... Where have I been feeling forgotten or overlooked?
Maybe it's a relationship.
Maybe it's a responsibility.
Or maybe it's a prayer you've been carrying. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... What emotions have I been experiencing during this waiting season?
Maybe it's sadness.
Frustration.
Loneliness.
Or discouragement.
Now, take a moment to acknowledge those feelings honestly. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... What does Scripture teach me about God's character when I feel forgotten?
Think about Isaiah 49.
Psalm 13.
And Romans 8. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... What practical step can I take to seek support or encouragement during this season?
Maybe it's reaching out to someone you trust.
Maybe it's asking for prayer.
Maybe it's setting aside time for Scripture.
Or maybe it's seeking help with a responsibility that's become overwhelming. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — THE GREATEST EVIDENCE OF GOD'S LOVE Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because the greatest evidence of God's love isn't found in whether every prayer is answered according to our plans.
It's found in Jesus Christ.
Romans chapter 5, verse 8, says: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
Now, think about that.
God demonstrated His love through Christ's sacrifice.
Jesus lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, that's the foundation of Christian hope.
And when we feel forgotten, we can return to that truth.
We can remember that God's love has been revealed through Jesus Christ.
And that our ultimate hope rests in Him.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. You may feel overlooked by the world, but your worth is not determined by who notices you. In Christ, your life has meaning, and God's faithfulness remains.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we become so focused on whether people recognize us that we forget where our identity belongs.
Our worth isn't measured by attention.
It's not measured by accomplishments.
And it's not measured by how quickly our circumstances change.
Our hope is rooted in Jesus Christ.
LIVING IT OUT — REMEMBERING GOD'S FAITHFULNESS Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a few minutes and write down three things.
First... One area where you've been feeling overlooked.
Second... One truth from Scripture that reminds you of God's character.
And third... One practical step you can take to seek encouragement or support.
Now, after you've written those down, take a moment to pray.
Bring your feelings before the Lord.
And ask Him for wisdom about what to do next.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, the area where I've been feeling forgotten is...
Our second prompt is... One truth about Your faithfulness that I need to remember is...
And our third prompt is... Help me respond to this season with faith by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. When I feel forgotten, I will remember God's faithfulness, seek His wisdom, and keep my hope rooted in Jesus Christ.
Now, say that again. When I feel forgotten, I will remember God's faithfulness, seek His wisdom, and keep my hope rooted in Jesus Christ.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize Psalm 13, verse 5. "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation."
Now, throughout the day, return to that verse.
And whenever you begin feeling overlooked or forgotten, take a moment to pray.
Remember God's mercy.
And ask Him to help you respond with wisdom.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHEN YOU FEEL UNSEEN Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
And I ask you this question. Have you ever experienced a season when you felt invisible?
Maybe you were doing your best to remain faithful.
Maybe you were carrying responsibilities that nobody else recognized.
Or maybe you were struggling through something that others didn't understand.
Now, think about what helped you during that season.
Was it prayer?
Was it encouragement from someone you trusted?
Was it studying Scripture?
Or was it simply having someone listen without trying to fix everything? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. What could you do this week to help someone else feel seen?
Maybe you could send an encouraging message.
Call someone who's been struggling.
Offer practical help.
Or simply take time to listen.
Because sometimes one of the most meaningful ways we can reflect Christ's love is by noticing people who feel overlooked.
CLOSING REFLECTION — GOD HAS NOT FORGOTTEN HIS PEOPLE Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Maybe you're in a season where you feel forgotten.
Maybe you've prayed for something for a long time.
Maybe you've watched other people move forward while your circumstances remain unchanged.
Or maybe you're simply tired of feeling as though nobody understands what you're carrying.
Now, I can't promise that every situation will change tomorrow.
I can't promise that every prayer will be answered according to your preferred timeline.
And I can't explain why every difficult season happens.
But I can encourage you to remember what Scripture teaches about God's character.
He is faithful.
He is merciful.
And His love has been revealed through Jesus Christ.
Now, remember David.
He asked whether God had forgotten him.
But he also remembered the Lord's mercy.
Remember Hagar.
She experienced hardship and vulnerability.
But her story reminds us of God's awareness of her circumstances.
And remember the words of Romans chapter 8.
Nothing can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Him.
Now, that's where our hope belongs.
Not in receiving every answer according to our preferred timeline.
But in the faithful Savior who gave Himself for us.
So if you're feeling forgotten today...
Bring that feeling before the Lord.
Open your Bible.
Seek encouragement.
And remember that your story isn't measured only by what hasn't happened yet.
Your life still matters.
And you can continue walking faithfully with Christ.
Even while you wait.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for reminding us of Your mercy and faithfulness. Lord, You know every person listening. You know the ones who feel forgotten. The ones who feel overlooked. The ones who are carrying disappointment. And the ones who are struggling to remain hopeful. Father, help us remember Your character. Help us bring our concerns before You honestly. And help us recognize when we need encouragement or support. Lord, I pray for the person who's waiting for an important answer. Give them wisdom and patience. I pray for the person who's carrying grief. Surround them with compassion and care. I pray for the person who feels invisible in their relationships. Help them find healthy connections and mutual support. And I pray for the person who's beginning to question their worth. Remind them of the love You've revealed through Jesus Christ. Father, help us become people who notice others. People who listen. People who encourage. And people who reflect Your love through practical acts of kindness. Thank You for Jesus. Thank You for His sacrifice. His resurrection. And the promise of eternal life through Him. May our hope remain firmly rooted in our Savior. And may we continue following Him faithfully. Even while we wait. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Eight, Day Three. And I hope today's lesson has encouraged you to remember that feeling forgotten doesn't mean God has forgotten you.
Your emotions matter. Your struggles are real. And you can bring them before the Lord honestly.
Tomorrow, we're going to continue our study of trusting God's timing. And we're going to talk about something that can happen when we become frustrated with waiting. When You Want to Take Control — Surrendering Your Timeline to God.
We'll explore how the desire to control outcomes can affect our decisions and what Scripture teaches about trusting God's wisdom.
Until then, remember... You don't have to measure God's faithfulness by how quickly your circumstances change.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: When You Want to Take Control: Surrendering Your Timeline to God
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — WHEN WAITING MAKES US WANT CONTROL Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today. Whether you're listening while getting ready for your day, driving down the road, working around the house, or sitting quietly with your Bible, I'm glad you're here.
Today is Week Eight, Day Four. And we're continuing our study called Trusting God's Timing in the Waiting.
This week, we've been talking about what it means to remain faithful when life doesn't move according to our preferred timeline.
On Day One, we talked about finding faith in the in-between.
On Day Two, we talked about patience.
And yesterday, we talked about those seasons when waiting makes us feel forgotten.
But today, I want to talk about something that can happen when we're tired of waiting.
We start trying to control everything.
Now, let me ask you something. Have you ever been waiting for an answer... And finally thought... "Well, if nobody else is going to do something about this, I guess I'll handle it myself!"
Now, maybe you said that out loud. Or maybe you simply thought it.
But either way, you were tired of waiting.
You wanted answers. You wanted progress. And you wanted to know that something was finally going to change.
Now, here's something important. Taking responsibility isn't wrong.
Making plans isn't wrong.
And sometimes we absolutely need to take action.
But there's a difference between responsible action and trying to control outcomes that aren't ours to control.
Sometimes we make decisions because they're wise.
Other times, we make decisions because we're afraid.
Sometimes we act because something genuinely needs our attention.
Other times, we act because we can't tolerate the uncertainty any longer.
And that's where we need to be careful.
Because the desire for control can lead us into decisions we haven't thought through.
It can affect our relationships.
It can influence the way we pray.
And sometimes it can make us feel as though everything depends entirely on us.
Now, I want you to hear something. God hasn't called us to control every outcome. He's called us to trust Him and live faithfully.
And that's what we're going to study today. Our lesson is called... When You Want to Take Control — Surrendering Your Timeline to God.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Lord, You know how difficult waiting can be. You know the situations we want to change. The answers we're hoping to receive. And the moments when uncertainty makes us uncomfortable. Father, help us understand the difference between faithful responsibility and the desire to control everything. Give us wisdom when decisions need to be made. Patience when we need to wait. And humility when our plans don't unfold the way we expected. Lord, teach us to trust Your character. And help us keep our hope rooted in Jesus Christ. In His precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — PROVERBS 16:9 Now, let's turn to Proverbs chapter 16.
We're going to read verse 9. The King James Version says: "A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps."
Now, let's read that again. "A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps."
Now, I want us to slow down and think about those words.
Because this verse teaches us something important about planning and God's sovereignty.
A person makes plans.
We think about the future. We consider possibilities. And we make decisions.
But ultimately, we don't control every circumstance that affects the outcome.
The Lord remains sovereign.
Now, that doesn't mean planning is useless.
And it doesn't mean we should avoid making responsible decisions.
But it reminds us that our plans are limited.
We don't know everything.
We can't predict every change.
And we can't guarantee every outcome.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Faithful planning acknowledges God's sovereignty without abandoning personal responsibility.
WHEN OUR TIMELINE BECOMES AN EXPECTATION Now, let's talk about something that happens when we make plans.
We begin imagining how everything should unfold.
Maybe we set a goal.
We decide when we'd like to reach it.
And we begin working toward that timeline.
Now, there's nothing wrong with setting goals.
But sometimes, without realizing it, our preferred timeline becomes an expectation.
And then, when something doesn't happen when we planned, we begin feeling frustrated.
Maybe you thought you'd have a particular job by now.
Maybe you expected a relationship to be different.
Maybe you thought a financial situation would have improved.
Or maybe you expected an important opportunity to arrive sooner.
Now, those disappointments can be real.
But here's something important. Our expectations aren't always the same as God's promises.
We can hope for something.
We can pray about it.
And we can work toward it.
But that doesn't mean God has promised the outcome will happen according to our schedule.
Now, that's where humility becomes important.
We can make plans.
But we also need to acknowledge that our understanding is limited.
ABRAHAM, SARAH, AND HAGAR — WHEN PEOPLE TRY TO FORCE AN OUTCOME Now, let's return to the book of Genesis.
Yesterday, we talked about Hagar.
And earlier this week, we talked about Abraham and Sarah waiting for God's promise.
Today, I want us to look at the decisions that led to Hagar becoming part of their story.
Let's turn to Genesis chapter 16.
God had promised Abraham descendants.
But Abraham and Sarah had not yet had a child together.
And as time passed, Sarah became concerned about how the promise would be fulfilled.
Now, let's read Genesis chapter 16, verses 1 through 3. "Now Sarai Abram's wife bare him no children: and she had an handmaid, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar. And Sarai said unto Abram, Behold now, the LORD hath restrained me from bearing: I pray thee, go in unto my maid; it may be that I may obtain children by her. And Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai. And Sarai Abram's wife took Hagar her maid the Egyptian, after Abram had dwelt ten years in the land of Canaan, and gave her to her husband Abram to be his wife."
Now, let's think carefully about what's happening.
Sarah wanted a child.
And she proposed using Hagar, an enslaved woman in their household, as a means of obtaining one.
Now, that decision involved a serious imbalance of power.
Hagar wasn't an equal participant in the household.
And the consequences of the arrangement affected her deeply.
Now, this is important. Because sometimes people tell this story only as an example of Sarah being impatient.
But we shouldn't overlook the harm that resulted.
Real people were affected by the decisions Abraham and Sarah made.
And Hagar experienced mistreatment.
Now, let's continue reading Genesis chapter 16, verses 4 through 6. "And he went in unto Hagar, and she conceived: and when she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes. And Sarai said unto Abram, My wrong be upon thee: I have given my maid into thy bosom; and when she saw that she had conceived, I was despised in her eyes: the LORD judge between me and thee. But Abram said unto Sarai, Behold, thy maid is in thy hand; do to her as it pleaseth thee. And when Sarai dealt hardly with her, she fled from her face."
Now, think about what happened.
Sarah wanted an outcome.
She proposed a plan.
Abraham agreed.
And the situation led to conflict and mistreatment.
Now, here's something important. We should not use this story to suggest that every decision made during a waiting season is wrong.
And we shouldn't assume that taking initiative means someone lacks faith.
But the narrative does show us how attempts to secure an outcome can involve harmful choices.
And that's something we need to consider.
When we're desperate for an answer, we still have a responsibility to act with wisdom, justice, and compassion.
Our frustration doesn't excuse harming others.
And our desire for progress doesn't justify ignoring what is right.
WHEN WE TRY TO MAKE SOMETHING HAPPEN Now, let's bring that lesson into our everyday lives.
Sometimes we become so focused on making something happen that we stop asking whether our actions are wise.
Maybe we're trying to repair a relationship.
And we begin pushing someone to respond before they're ready.
Maybe we're pursuing an opportunity.
And we begin ignoring warning signs because we don't want to miss our chance.
Maybe we're trying to solve a financial problem.
And we consider a risky decision simply because we're desperate for immediate relief.
Now, here's something important. Urgent circumstances sometimes require urgent action.
But urgency doesn't eliminate the need for wisdom.
And when we feel pressured, it can be especially important to seek reliable information and appropriate support.
Now, I want you to ask yourself something. Am I pursuing this because it's right?
Or because I'm afraid of what will happen if I wait?
Am I considering how my decision will affect other people?
And am I willing to change my plan if I recognize that it isn't wise?
Now, those are important questions.
Because surrendering our timeline to God isn't simply about becoming more patient.
It's also about allowing His Word to shape the way we make decisions.
PROVERBS 3 — TRUSTING BEYOND OUR UNDERSTANDING Now, let's turn to Proverbs chapter 3.
We're going to read verses 5 and 6. The King James Version says: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths."
Now, we've returned to these verses several times throughout our Bible studies.
And I think they connect beautifully with today's lesson.
Because we often want to understand everything before we're willing to release control.
We want to know why something hasn't happened.
We want to know when the answer will arrive.
And we want to know exactly how everything will turn out.
But Scripture reminds us that our understanding is limited.
Now, here's something important. Trusting God doesn't mean refusing to think carefully.
It doesn't mean ignoring evidence.
And it doesn't mean assuming that every personal feeling is a direct message from the Lord.
Instead, trusting God means approaching life with humility.
We seek His wisdom.
We study His Word.
And we recognize that our own perspective isn't complete.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Surrender isn't the absence of responsibility. It's the willingness to honor God even when our plans must change.
JAMES 4 — IF THE LORD WILL Now, let's turn to James chapter 4.
We're going to read verses 13 through 15. The King James Version says: "Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain: Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that."
Now, let's think about that.
James describes people making business plans.
They intend to travel.
Spend a year in a city.
Buy and sell.
And make a profit.
Now, the problem isn't simply that they're planning.
The problem is their confidence that they control the future.
They speak as though tomorrow is guaranteed.
But James reminds them that human life is uncertain.
Now, I want you to notice the phrase... "If the Lord will..."
That isn't simply a religious expression to add to the end of every sentence.
It's an attitude of humility.
It's recognizing that our plans are subject to God's will.
Now, that doesn't mean we stop setting goals.
But it does mean we hold our plans with humility.
We prepare.
We work.
And we acknowledge that circumstances may change.
Now, here's something practical. The next time you're making an important plan, ask yourself... Am I willing to adjust this plan if circumstances change?
Am I making this decision with wisdom?
And am I placing my ultimate confidence in God rather than in my ability to control the outcome?
THE BURDEN OF TRYING TO CONTROL EVERYTHING Now, let's talk about something that can become exhausting.
Trying to control everything.
Maybe you're the person everyone depends on.
You're the one who keeps track of appointments.
The one who handles problems.
The one who makes sure things get done.
And over time, you begin feeling as though everything depends on you.
Now, responsibility can be a good thing.
But sometimes we begin carrying responsibilities that aren't entirely ours.
We try to manage other people's decisions.
We try to predict every possible problem.
And we try to prevent anything from going wrong.
Now, here's something important. We cannot control other people's choices.
We cannot guarantee every outcome.
And we cannot eliminate every uncertainty.
But we can act responsibly.
We can communicate clearly.
We can establish healthy boundaries.
And we can ask for help when responsibilities become overwhelming.
Now, I want you to hear something. You are responsible for your faithfulness, not for controlling every result.
And sometimes recognizing that difference can help us approach life with greater wisdom.
PSALM 37 — COMMIT YOUR WAY TO THE LORD Now, let's turn to Psalm 37.
We're going to read verses 3 through 5. The King James Version says: "Trust in the LORD, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed. Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart. Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass."
Now, this is a beautiful passage.
But we need to understand it carefully.
Psalm 37 contrasts the way of the righteous with the way of the wicked.
It encourages God's people not to become consumed by the apparent success of those who do evil.
Instead, they're called to trust the Lord and continue doing good.
Now, I want you to notice something. "Trust in the LORD, and do good."
Those two ideas belong together.
Trusting God doesn't mean abandoning faithful action.
We continue doing what is right.
We continue living according to His Word.
And we commit our way to Him.
Now, here's something important. Verse 4 isn't a guarantee that God will give us every personal desire exactly as we imagine it.
The psalm calls us to delight in the Lord and align our lives with Him.
And that is very different from treating prayer as a way to control outcomes.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. We can commit our plans to God without demanding that He fulfill them according to our preferred timeline.
PAUSE AND PRAY — RELEASING THE NEED FOR CONTROL Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about one situation where you've been trying to control the outcome.
Maybe it's a relationship.
Maybe it's a financial concern.
Maybe it's an opportunity.
Or maybe it's a decision someone else needs to make.
Now, ask yourself... What part of this situation is actually my responsibility?
And what part remains outside my control? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, You know the situations where we've been trying to control everything. You know the fears beneath our need for certainty. And You know the responsibilities we've been carrying. Lord, help us recognize what is ours to do. Give us wisdom to make responsible decisions. Humility when our plans need to change. And patience when outcomes remain uncertain. Father, help us trust Your character. And keep our hope firmly rooted in Jesus Christ. In His precious name, Amen.
JESUS IN GETHSEMANE — SURRENDERING TO THE FATHER Now, let's turn to Luke chapter 22.
We're going to look at Jesus praying in the garden of Gethsemane.
This is a deeply significant moment in the Gospels.
Jesus is approaching His suffering and crucifixion.
And He prays to the Father.
Let's read Luke chapter 22, verses 41 and 42. "And he was withdrawn from them about a stone's cast, and kneeled down, and prayed, Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done."
Now, we need to approach this passage with reverence.
Jesus wasn't simply facing an ordinary disappointment.
He was approaching the suffering through which He would accomplish our redemption.
And His prayer reveals His submission to the Father's will.
Now, here's something important. We shouldn't compare every personal inconvenience to the suffering of Christ.
But we can learn from His example of prayerful submission.
Jesus brought His request before the Father.
And He submitted to the Father's will.
Now, sometimes we pray with a particular outcome in mind.
We ask for healing.
We ask for provision.
We ask for reconciliation.
Or we ask for an opportunity.
And it's appropriate to bring those requests before God.
But we also need humility.
We acknowledge that our understanding is limited.
And we entrust ourselves to His wisdom.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Surrender doesn't mean you stop praying for what matters to you. It means you bring those desires before God while trusting His wisdom above your own.
WHEN SURRENDER FEELS LIKE LOSING Now, let's talk about something that can make surrender difficult.
Sometimes surrender feels like losing.
Maybe you've worked hard toward a goal.
You've invested time.
You've made sacrifices.
And you've imagined how everything would turn out.
But now circumstances are changing.
And you may need to reconsider your plans.
Now, that can be disappointing.
Sometimes it involves grief.
Sometimes it requires difficult conversations.
And sometimes it means acknowledging that something isn't going to happen the way we hoped.
Now, here's something important. Changing a plan isn't always failure.
Sometimes it's wisdom.
Sometimes it's a response to new information.
And sometimes it's simply recognizing that circumstances have changed.
Now, surrendering our timeline to God doesn't mean we pretend disappointment doesn't hurt.
We can grieve.
We can ask questions.
And we can seek support.
But we don't have to allow disappointment to lead us away from faithful living.
PHILIPPIANS 4 — BRINGING OUR CONCERNS TO GOD Now, let's turn to Philippians chapter 4.
We're going to read verses 6 and 7. The King James Version says: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus."
Now, let's think about that.
Paul encourages believers to bring their concerns before God through prayer.
And he speaks about the peace of God guarding their hearts and minds in Christ.
Now, here's something important. This passage isn't promising that every difficult emotion will disappear immediately.
And it doesn't mean that someone who experiences anxiety has failed spiritually.
But it does invite us to bring our concerns before the Lord.
Now, think about how that connects with our desire for control.
Sometimes we become overwhelmed because we're trying to carry every possible outcome.
We're imagining what might happen.
We're trying to prevent every problem.
And we're exhausting ourselves with uncertainty.
But prayer gives us an opportunity to bring those concerns before God.
We can ask for wisdom.
We can ask for help.
And we can continue trusting Him while taking responsible action.
THREE QUESTIONS FOR SURRENDERING CONTROL Now, I want to give you three practical questions to use when you feel the need to control everything.
The first question is... What am I afraid will happen if I don't control this situation?
Now, sometimes our desire for control is rooted in fear.
We're afraid of disappointment.
We're afraid of failure.
Or we're afraid that someone else won't make the decision we want.
Now, identifying that fear can help us understand what's happening.
The second question is... What can I responsibly do right now?
Maybe you need to gather information.
Maybe you need to make a decision.
Maybe you need to communicate clearly.
Or maybe you need to ask for help.
Now, those are actions within your responsibility.
And the third question is... What outcome do I need to acknowledge is outside my control?
Now, that may be the hardest question.
Because sometimes we want certainty.
But we can't always have it.
And recognizing that limitation can help us approach life with humility.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... What situation have I been trying to control?
Maybe it's a relationship.
Maybe it's a decision.
Maybe it's a financial concern.
Or maybe it's an opportunity. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... What fear or expectation is influencing my desire for control?
Are you afraid of failure?
Afraid of disappointment?
Or afraid that things won't happen according to your timeline? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... What would a wise and faithful response look like?
Maybe you need to act.
Maybe you need to wait.
Maybe you need to seek advice.
Or maybe you need to change your plan. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... How can I acknowledge God's sovereignty while remaining responsible for my own decisions?
Think about what you can do.
And what you need to entrust to Him. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — TRUSTING THE FATHER THROUGH JESUS Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because surrender isn't simply a strategy for feeling less stressed.
It's part of our response to the God who has revealed Himself through Jesus Christ.
Jesus lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, that's the foundation of Christian hope.
And as we follow Him, we're called to grow in humility.
To seek God's wisdom.
And to submit our lives to His will.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn salvation by surrendering perfectly.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And our obedience grows out of that relationship.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. You can make wise plans, take responsible steps, and still trust God with the outcome. Surrender means remembering that your timeline isn't the foundation of your hope.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we become so attached to our plans that we forget to consider whether they're still wise.
But we can hold our plans with humility.
We can remain open to new information.
And we can continue seeking the Lord.
LIVING IT OUT — RELEASING YOUR TIMELINE Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a few minutes and write down one situation where you've been trying to control the outcome.
Then draw two columns on your page.
In the first column, write... What I Can Responsibly Do.
And in the second column, write... What I Cannot Control.
Now, begin filling in those columns.
Maybe you can make a phone call.
Gather information.
Prepare for an appointment.
Or have a conversation.
Those are things you can do.
But you may not be able to control another person's response.
You may not be able to control the timing of a decision.
And you may not be able to guarantee a particular outcome.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Ask God for wisdom about your responsibilities.
And entrust the uncertain outcome to Him.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, the situation I've been trying to control is...
Our second prompt is... The fear beneath my desire for control is...
And our third prompt is... Help me surrender my timeline while remaining faithful by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. I will make wise decisions, remain faithful to God's Word, and trust Him with outcomes I cannot control.
Now, say that again. I will make wise decisions, remain faithful to God's Word, and trust Him with outcomes I cannot control.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize Proverbs chapter 16, verse 9. "A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps."
Now, throughout the day, return to that verse.
And whenever you begin feeling the need to control everything, take a moment to pause.
Ask yourself... What is mine to do?
And what do I need to entrust to God?
Then choose one responsible action.
AROUND THE FIRE — LETTING GO OF CONTROL Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
And I ask you this question. Have you ever made a decision simply because you were tired of waiting?
Maybe you rushed into something.
Maybe you tried to force a conversation.
Or maybe you ignored warning signs because you wanted an answer.
Now, think about what you learned. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] And here's another question. Can you remember a time when changing your plans turned out to be a wise decision?
Maybe you received new information.
Maybe you recognized that something wasn't right.
Or maybe you realized that a different approach was needed. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's something I want you to remember. Surrender isn't always about doing less.
Sometimes it's about doing what is right without trying to control everything else.
CLOSING REFLECTION — GOD'S WISDOM ABOVE OUR TIMELINE Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Sometimes we become so focused on when something will happen that we forget to consider how we're living while we wait.
We want answers.
We want progress.
And we want circumstances to change.
But Scripture reminds us that our plans are limited.
We don't know everything.
And we cannot control every outcome.
Now, that doesn't mean we stop taking responsibility.
It means we approach our responsibilities with humility.
We seek wisdom.
We act with integrity.
And we remain willing to adjust our plans.
Now, remember Proverbs chapter 16, verse 9. "A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps."
We can make plans.
But our hope doesn't have to rest entirely on those plans.
Our hope can remain firmly rooted in Jesus Christ.
So if you're struggling with the desire to control everything today...
Take a moment to pause.
Ask God for wisdom.
Identify what is yours to do.
And acknowledge what remains outside your control.
You don't have to predict every outcome.
You don't have to manage every decision someone else makes.
And you don't have to force every situation to fit your timeline.
You can continue living faithfully.
One step at a time.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for reminding us that You are sovereign. Lord, You know every person listening. You know the plans they're making. The answers they're waiting for. And the situations they're trying to control. Father, help us approach our decisions with wisdom. Give us patience when circumstances remain uncertain. Humility when our plans need to change. And courage when we need to take responsible action. Lord, I pray for the person who's overwhelmed by trying to manage everything. Help them recognize what is truly their responsibility. I pray for the person who's afraid of losing control. Give them wisdom and support. I pray for the person who's disappointed because life hasn't followed their timeline. Help them process that disappointment honestly. And I pray for the person who's facing an important decision. Guide them through Your Word, wise counsel, and careful consideration. Father, help us remember that our ultimate hope isn't found in controlling every outcome. It's found in Jesus Christ. Thank You for His sacrifice. His resurrection. And the promise of eternal life through Him. May we continue growing in faithfulness. And may we learn to trust You through every season. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Eight, Day Four. And I hope today's lesson has encouraged you to remember that surrendering control doesn't mean abandoning responsibility.
It means making wise decisions while trusting God with outcomes we cannot control.
Tomorrow, we're going to continue our study of trusting God's timing. And we're going to talk about something beautiful. Growing While You Wait — Letting God Shape Your Heart in the In-Between.
We'll explore how we can continue growing spiritually, serving others, and living faithfully even when we're waiting for an answer.
Until then, remember... You can make plans. You can take responsible steps. And you can trust God with the outcome.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: Growing While You Wait: Letting God Shape Your Heart in the In-Between
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — WHAT IF YOU'RE GROWING WHILE YOU WAIT? Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today. Whether you're listening while getting ready for work, driving down the road, sitting at home with your Bible, or taking a quiet moment with the Lord, I'm glad you're here.
Today is Week Eight, Day Five. And we're continuing our study called Trusting God's Timing in the Waiting.
This week, we've talked about finding faith in the in-between. We've talked about patience. We've talked about feeling forgotten. And yesterday, we talked about surrendering our desire to control everything.
But today, I want to ask you a question. What if something meaningful can happen in your life even while you're waiting for something else?
Now, think about that. Maybe you've been waiting for an answer.
Maybe you've been waiting for an opportunity.
Maybe you've been waiting for a difficult situation to change.
And because that particular thing hasn't happened yet, you've begun feeling as though your life isn't moving forward.
But what if progress doesn't always look the way we expected?
What if spiritual growth can take place even when our circumstances remain uncertain?
Now, I want to be careful here. Not every difficult circumstance has been arranged to teach us a particular lesson.
And we shouldn't assume that every delay has a hidden purpose we can identify.
Sometimes things happen because we live in a world affected by sin, suffering, and human limitations.
Sometimes we simply don't know why something is taking longer than expected.
But even when we don't understand our circumstances, we can continue growing in our relationship with God.
We can continue studying Scripture. We can continue learning patience. We can continue practicing kindness. And we can continue serving others.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Your spiritual growth doesn't have to stop simply because your circumstances haven't changed.
And that's what we're going to study today. Our lesson is called... Growing While You Wait — Letting God Shape Your Heart in the In-Between.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Lord, You know the seasons of waiting we're experiencing. You know the prayers we've prayed. The answers we're hoping for. And the circumstances that haven't changed. Father, help us understand what Your Word teaches about spiritual growth. Help us recognize opportunities to grow in faith, patience, wisdom, and love. Give us humility when we need correction. Strength when we're weary. And wisdom when we need to make decisions. Lord, may this time of study draw us closer to Jesus Christ. And may Your Word continue shaping the way we live. In His precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — JAMES 1:2–4 Now, let's turn to James chapter 1.
We're going to read verses 2 through 4. But before we read them, I want to explain the context.
James was writing to believers who were experiencing various trials.
And he encouraged them to understand that the testing of their faith could produce patience, or steadfast endurance.
Now, this doesn't mean suffering is pleasant.
And it doesn't mean Christians should pretend to enjoy painful experiences.
But James teaches that trials can become occasions for spiritual endurance and maturity.
Now, let's read James chapter 1, verses 2 through 4, from the King James Version. "My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience. But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing."
Now, let's slow down and think about those words.
James says... "Count it all joy..."
Now, that can sound surprising.
Because when we're going through something difficult, joy may be the last thing we're feeling.
But James isn't telling believers to pretend that hardship is enjoyable.
He's encouraging them to recognize that God can work in their spiritual lives even through trials.
Now, notice what he says next. "The trying of your faith worketh patience."
Now, the patience James is describing is more than simply waiting without complaining.
It involves steadfastness.
The ability to continue trusting and following God through difficulty.
And then James says... "Let patience have her perfect work..."
Now, the word translated "perfect" here points toward maturity or completeness.
James is encouraging believers to grow toward spiritual maturity.
And that's where today's lesson begins.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH God can continue shaping our character while we wait, even when the outcome we're hoping for remains uncertain.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we become so focused on what hasn't happened that we overlook the ways we're growing.
Maybe you're learning to respond with greater patience.
Maybe you're becoming more thoughtful in your decisions.
Maybe you're learning to pray more honestly.
Or maybe you're beginning to recognize the importance of healthy boundaries and wise counsel.
Now, those things matter.
They may not be the outcome you originally hoped for.
But they can still be meaningful parts of your spiritual growth.
THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN WAITING AND STANDING STILL Now, let's talk about something important.
Waiting and standing still aren't always the same thing.
Sometimes we wait for an answer while continuing to fulfill our responsibilities.
Sometimes we wait for an opportunity while developing our skills.
Sometimes we wait for a decision while gathering information.
And sometimes we wait for circumstances to change while continuing to care for the people around us.
Now, think about a student preparing for an exam.
The exam date may be weeks away.
But the student doesn't have to stop learning until the day arrives.
They can study. Practice. And prepare.
Now, the same principle can apply to many areas of life.
We can continue growing while we're waiting for a particular outcome.
And spiritually, we can continue seeking the Lord.
We can study Scripture.
We can pray.
We can serve others.
And we can practice living according to God's Word.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Waiting for one part of your life to change doesn't mean every other part of your life has to stop.
ROMANS 5 — SUFFERING, ENDURANCE, AND HOPE Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 5.
We're going to read verses 3 through 5. The King James Version says: "And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us."
Now, let's think about that.
Paul connects tribulation with endurance.
Endurance with proven character.
And proven character with hope.
Now, that doesn't mean suffering automatically makes everyone spiritually mature.
People can respond to hardship in many different ways.
And sometimes suffering leaves wounds that require care and support.
But Paul is describing the hope believers have through God's grace and the work of the Holy Spirit.
Now, here's something important. Christian hope isn't simply optimism.
It's not the belief that every personal plan will succeed.
It's confidence rooted in God's love revealed through Jesus Christ.
And that's what gives us a foundation for endurance.
Now, think about your own life.
Have you ever experienced a difficult season that changed the way you approached life?
Maybe you became more compassionate.
Maybe you learned the importance of asking for help.
Maybe you developed greater patience.
Or maybe you began taking your relationship with God more seriously.
Now, those changes don't make the suffering itself good.
But they can reflect meaningful growth.
GROWTH ISN'T ALWAYS VISIBLE Now, let's talk about something that can be discouraging.
Sometimes growth isn't immediately visible.
Think about planting a seed.
You prepare the soil.
You plant the seed.
You water it.
And then you wait.
Now, at first, you may not see anything happening above the ground.
But that doesn't necessarily mean nothing is happening.
Roots may be developing beneath the surface.
And eventually, if the conditions are right, growth becomes visible.
Now, that's a helpful illustration.
Because spiritual growth doesn't always happen in dramatic moments.
Sometimes it happens through ordinary faithfulness.
Choosing to pray when you're discouraged.
Choosing to speak kindly when you're frustrated.
Choosing to apologize when you've been wrong.
Choosing to seek wisdom before making an important decision.
Now, those may seem like small things.
But they're meaningful.
And over time, those choices can reflect spiritual maturity.
JOHN 15 — ABIDING IN CHRIST Now, let's turn to John chapter 15.
We're going to look at Jesus' teaching about the vine and the branches.
This is a beautiful passage about the believer's dependence on Christ.
Let's read John chapter 15, verses 4 and 5. "Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me. I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing."
Now, I want us to think about that picture.
Jesus describes Himself as the vine.
And His followers as the branches.
Now, a branch doesn't produce fruit independently of the vine.
Its life and nourishment depend on its connection to the vine.
And Jesus uses that image to teach His disciples about abiding in Him.
Now, here's something important. Spiritual growth isn't simply about becoming more disciplined.
It's about remaining connected to Jesus Christ.
We study His Word.
We pray.
We seek to obey His teachings.
And we depend on His grace.
Now, I want you to notice something. Jesus doesn't say that His followers can produce lasting spiritual fruit entirely through their own strength.
He teaches that they must abide in Him.
Now, that changes the way we think about growth.
Because spiritual maturity isn't simply another achievement to add to our list.
It's part of our ongoing relationship with Christ.
WHEN WE BECOME OBSESSED WITH RESULTS Now, let's talk about something that can happen when we're waiting.
We become obsessed with results.
We keep asking... Has anything changed?
Have I made progress?
Am I closer to the outcome I want?
Now, there's nothing wrong with evaluating progress.
Sometimes it's necessary.
But if we measure our entire lives by one particular outcome, we may overlook other meaningful things.
Maybe you're waiting for a job opportunity.
And while you're waiting, you're learning new skills.
Maybe you're waiting for a relationship to improve.
And during that time, you're learning to communicate more clearly and establish healthier boundaries.
Maybe you're waiting for an important decision.
And you're learning how to prepare carefully and respond with patience.
Now, those things don't guarantee the outcome you're hoping for.
But they still matter.
And spiritually, we can continue growing in our understanding of God's Word.
PHILIPPIANS 1 — GOD'S WORK IN BELIEVERS Now, let's turn to Philippians chapter 1, verse 6. The King James Version says: "Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:"
Now, let's understand the context.
Paul is expressing his confidence concerning God's work among the Philippian believers.
He is thankful for their partnership in the gospel.
And he looks toward the day of Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something important. This verse isn't promising that every personal project we begin will succeed.
It's speaking about God's work in His people.
And it reminds us that our spiritual growth is connected to His faithfulness.
Now, that should encourage us.
Because sometimes we become discouraged by our imperfections.
We recognize areas where we still need to grow.
We make mistakes.
And we realize that we haven't become the people we want to be.
But spiritual growth is a process.
We continue learning.
We continue repenting when we sin.
And we continue depending on God's grace.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to become spiritually mature overnight. You can continue growing faithfully through your relationship with Christ.
WHEN GROWTH REQUIRES CHANGE Now, let's talk about something that isn't always comfortable.
Sometimes growth requires change.
Maybe you've developed a habit that isn't helping you.
Maybe you've been responding to frustration in ways that hurt your relationships.
Maybe you've been neglecting time in Scripture.
Or maybe you've been carrying responsibilities that require healthier boundaries.
Now, recognizing those things can be uncomfortable.
But spiritual growth often involves honest reflection.
We ask God to reveal areas where we need wisdom.
We examine our choices in light of Scripture.
And we seek to make changes that reflect Christ's teachings.
Now, here's something important. Change doesn't always happen immediately.
Sometimes we need practice.
Sometimes we need accountability.
And sometimes we need support from others.
But we can continue taking faithful steps.
COLOSSIANS 1 — GROWING IN THE KNOWLEDGE OF GOD Now, let's turn to Colossians chapter 1.
We're going to read verses 9 through 11. The King James Version says: "For this cause we also, since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray for you, and to desire that ye might be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding; That ye might walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing, being fruitful in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God; Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness;"
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul prays for believers to grow in the knowledge of God's will.
In wisdom.
In spiritual understanding.
And in fruitful living.
Now, that's a beautiful picture of spiritual growth.
It isn't simply about knowing more information.
It's about allowing God's truth to shape the way we live.
We grow in understanding.
And we seek to apply that understanding through faithful action.
Now, notice something else. Paul includes patience and longsuffering.
Those qualities connect directly with our theme this week.
Because waiting can provide opportunities to practice patience.
To seek wisdom.
And to continue walking faithfully with Christ.
PAUSE AND PRAY — LORD, HELP ME GROW Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about one area of your spiritual life where you'd like to grow.
Maybe it's patience.
Maybe it's prayer.
Maybe it's understanding Scripture.
Maybe it's learning to forgive.
Or maybe it's practicing healthier boundaries and wise decisions.
Now, bring that before the Lord. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for the opportunity to continue growing in our relationship with You. Lord, You know the areas where we need wisdom. You know the habits we need to change. And You know the responsibilities we're carrying. Father, help us remain connected to Jesus Christ. Teach us through Your Word. Give us humility when we need correction. And patience as we continue learning. Lord, help us recognize opportunities for faithful living, even while we're waiting for circumstances to change. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
GALATIANS 6 — DON'T GROW WEARY IN DOING GOOD Now, let's turn to Galatians chapter 6, verse 9. The King James Version says: "And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not."
Now, let's understand the context.
Paul is encouraging believers to continue doing good.
Especially in their relationships with one another.
And he reminds them that faithful living matters.
Now, here's something important. This verse isn't a promise that every personal project will produce financial success or public recognition.
It's an encouragement to persevere in doing good.
And that's something we can apply during seasons of waiting.
Maybe you're waiting for an answer.
But you can still show kindness.
Maybe you're waiting for an opportunity.
But you can still serve others.
Maybe you're waiting for a difficult situation to improve.
But you can still seek wisdom and live with integrity.
Now, that doesn't mean you should ignore exhaustion.
Rest is important.
And sometimes we need to ask for help.
But we can continue seeking opportunities to do good as we're able.
PSALM 92 — STILL BEARING FRUIT Now, let's turn to Psalm 92.
We're going to read verses 12 through 15. The King James Version says: "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon. Those that be planted in the house of the LORD shall flourish in the courts of our God. They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing; To shew that the LORD is upright: he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him."
Now, I love the picture this psalm gives us.
It describes the righteous flourishing like trees.
And continuing to bear fruit even in old age.
Now, the psalm uses poetic imagery.
It isn't promising that believers will never experience physical decline or hardship.
But it celebrates the enduring faithfulness of God and the fruitful lives of those who belong to Him.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Spiritual growth isn't limited to one stage of life.
We can continue learning.
We can continue serving.
And we can continue growing in our relationship with Christ.
Whether we're young. Middle-aged. Or older.
And whether we're experiencing a season of excitement or a season of waiting.
GROWTH DOESN'T HAVE TO BE DRAMATIC Now, I want to talk about something that can be encouraging.
Sometimes we expect spiritual growth to happen through dramatic experiences.
We imagine a powerful moment.
A sudden change.
Or an experience that transforms everything overnight.
Now, God can certainly work through significant moments.
But much of Christian growth happens through ordinary faithfulness.
Opening your Bible.
Taking time to pray.
Choosing kindness.
Practicing self-control.
Asking forgiveness when you've been wrong.
And continuing to seek the Lord.
Now, those things may not seem dramatic.
But they matter.
And over time, they can reflect meaningful spiritual maturity.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... What area of my life has felt like it's standing still?
Maybe you're waiting for an answer.
An opportunity.
Or a change in circumstances. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... What areas of my spiritual life can continue growing while I wait?
Maybe it's patience.
Prayer.
Understanding Scripture.
Or serving others. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... What small habit could help me grow in my relationship with Christ?
Maybe it's setting aside time for Scripture.
Keeping a prayer journal.
