We're going to read verse 18. The King James Version says: "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit."
Now, I love that verse.
Because it reminds us of God's concern for those who are hurting.
Now, this doesn't mean every brokenhearted person will immediately feel comforted.
And it doesn't mean every difficult circumstance will suddenly change.
But it does remind us of the Lord's character.
He is not indifferent to suffering.
And Scripture repeatedly encourages His people to bring their burdens before Him.
Now, maybe you're listening today with a broken heart.
Maybe you're missing someone.
Maybe you're grieving a relationship.
Maybe you're facing a disappointment that has changed the way you imagined your future.
Now, I want you to remember something. You can bring that sorrow before the Lord.
You don't have to pretend.
You don't have to find the perfect words.
And you don't have to explain every emotion.
You can simply pray.
"Lord, I'm hurting."
"Lord, I miss them."
"Lord, I don't understand."
And sometimes those honest prayers are all we can manage.
ECCLESIASTES — A TIME TO WEEP AND A TIME TO LAUGH Now, let's turn to Ecclesiastes chapter 3.
We're going to read verses 1 through 4. The King James Version says: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted; A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up; A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;"
Now, I want you to notice those last words. "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance."
Now, Scripture acknowledges the variety of human experiences.
There are times of celebration.
And times of sorrow.
Times of building.
And times of loss.
Now, here's something important. Life doesn't always separate those experiences neatly.
Sometimes joy and sorrow overlap.
Maybe you're celebrating a new baby while missing someone who isn't there to meet them.
Maybe you're enjoying a family gathering while remembering someone whose chair is empty.
Maybe you're proud of an accomplishment while grieving the person you wish could have witnessed it.
Now, those feelings can exist together.
You can celebrate what is happening.
And still grieve what is missing.
You can laugh.
And still miss someone.
And you can experience a beautiful moment without forgetting the people you've lost.
WHEN JOY MAKES YOU FEEL GUILTY Now, let's talk about something that people don't always discuss.
Sometimes grief can make us feel guilty for experiencing joy.
Maybe you laugh at something funny.
And then suddenly you remember the person you've lost.
And you feel guilty.
You wonder whether it's too soon to laugh.
Or whether enjoying life means you're moving on without them.
Now, I want you to hear something. Experiencing joy doesn't erase love.
And it doesn't erase memory.
You can remember someone deeply.
You can honor their life.
And you can still experience moments of happiness.
Now, grief may change the way those moments feel.
And sometimes a happy memory can bring both laughter and tears.
But those experiences aren't necessarily contradictions.
They're part of being human.
And as Christians, we can bring all of those emotions before the Lord.
ROMANS 12 — WEEP WITH THOSE WHO WEEP Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 12.
We're going to read verse 15. The King James Version says: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep."
Now, that's a short verse.
But it's incredibly meaningful.
Paul calls believers to enter into the experiences of others with compassion.
When someone is celebrating, we can celebrate with them.
And when someone is grieving, we can grieve with them.
Now, notice something. Paul doesn't say... Tell everyone who is grieving to stop crying.
He says... "Weep with them that weep."
Now, I think that's something we need to remember.
Because sometimes we feel pressure to fix someone's grief.
We want to say the perfect thing.
We want to make the pain disappear.
And we want to offer an explanation.
But sometimes there isn't an explanation we can give.
Sometimes what someone needs most is our presence.
Someone who will listen.
Someone who will sit beside them.
Someone who will remember the person they lost.
And someone who won't rush them through their grief.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to have all the answers to offer meaningful comfort.
Sometimes compassion is more important than explanation.
AROUND THE FIRE — THE EMPTY CHAIR Now, I want you to imagine something with me.
Imagine a family gathered around the dinner table.
There's conversation.
There's laughter.
And there's food being passed around.
But there's also an empty chair.
A chair where someone used to sit.
Someone whose voice was familiar.
Someone whose laughter filled the room.
And now, they're missing.
Now, that family may still laugh.
They may still celebrate.
And they may still enjoy being together.
But the empty chair matters.
The absence is real.
And sometimes the most loving thing we can do is acknowledge it.
Maybe we share a memory.
Maybe we say their name.
Maybe we laugh about something they used to do.
Or maybe we simply sit quietly together.
Now, here's something important. Not everyone wants to remember in the same way.
Some people want to talk.
Others need space.
And we can respect those differences.
But we don't have to pretend the empty chair isn't there.
And we don't have to pretend that joy and sorrow can't share the same room.
PAUSE AND PRAY — LORD, COMFORT THE BROKENHEARTED Now, let's take a moment to pause.
If you're grieving someone today, I want you to think about them.
Maybe there's a memory that brings you comfort.
Maybe there's something you wish you could tell them.
Or maybe you simply miss their presence.
Now, take a moment.
You don't have to rush. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, You know the people we're missing. You know the memories we carry. And You know the grief that sometimes feels difficult to explain. Lord, comfort those who are brokenhearted. Help us remember that we can bring our sorrow before You. Give us compassion for one another. And help us offer meaningful support to those who are grieving. Father, remind us of the hope we have through Jesus Christ. And help us continue walking faithfully through difficult seasons. In His precious name, Amen.
2 CORINTHIANS 6 — SORROWFUL, YET REJOICING Now, let's turn to 2 Corinthians chapter 6.
We're going to read verse 10. The King James Version says: "As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things."
Now, I want you to hear those first words again. "As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing."
Now, that's a powerful statement.
Paul is describing the paradoxes of his ministry.
He experienced genuine hardship.
And yet, his hope in Christ remained.
Now, I think that helps us understand something important.
Sorrow and Christian joy aren't always mutually exclusive.
We can experience grief.
And still find hope in Christ.
We can acknowledge disappointment.
And still recognize God's faithfulness.
We can have difficult days.
And still remember the promises of the gospel.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Christian joy isn't the absence of sorrow. It's a deeper hope that can remain meaningful even in sorrow.
WHEN COMFORT COMES THROUGH OTHER PEOPLE Now, let's return to 2 Corinthians chapter 1.
Remember what Paul said. God comforts us in our affliction so that we may be able to comfort others.
Now, I want you to think about that. Sometimes comfort comes through Scripture.
Sometimes through prayer.
And sometimes through the people God has placed in our lives.
Maybe someone sends a message when you're having a difficult day.
Maybe someone brings you a meal.
Maybe someone remembers an important anniversary.
Or maybe someone simply asks... "How are you really doing?"
Now, those moments matter.
Because grief can feel isolating.
And sometimes being remembered can bring meaningful encouragement.
Now, here's something important. We shouldn't assume that every person who has experienced suffering is automatically ready to comfort others.
Sometimes people need time and support themselves.
And that's okay.
But when we're able, we can use the compassion we've received to care for someone else.
REVELATION 21 — THE PROMISE OF A FUTURE WITHOUT TEARS Now, let's turn to Revelation chapter 21.
We're going to read verse 4. The King James Version says: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away."
Now, this is a beautiful promise.
But let's understand its context.
Revelation 21 describes the new heaven and new earth.
It points toward the future fulfillment of God's purposes.
And it describes a reality in which death, mourning, and pain are no more.
Now, that's the Christian hope.
It doesn't mean believers will never grieve in this present life.
And it doesn't mean every loss will be reversed according to our preferred timeline.
But it points us toward the ultimate hope we have through Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Our hope in Christ extends beyond the difficulties of this present life.
And that hope can bring comfort even when we still have questions.
JOHN 16 — JESUS ACKNOWLEDGES TROUBLE Now, let's turn to John chapter 16.
We're going to read verse 33. The King James Version says: "These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world."
Now, I want you to notice something. Jesus doesn't tell His disciples that they will never experience trouble.
He tells them that tribulation is part of life in this world.
But He also directs them toward the peace found in Him.
Now, that's important.
Because sometimes we think faith should prevent hardship.
But Jesus Himself prepared His followers for difficulty.
And He encouraged them to remain rooted in Him.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The presence of hardship doesn't mean the promises of Jesus have failed.
Our hope is rooted in His victory.
And that hope remains meaningful even while we grieve.
WHEN YOU DON'T FEEL COMFORTED Now, let's talk about something important.
Sometimes we pray for comfort.
We read Scripture.
We attend church.
And we still feel deeply sad.
Now, if that's where you are today, I don't want you to feel ashamed.
Grief can be complicated.
And sometimes it affects our sleep.
Our concentration.
Our energy.
And our relationships.
Now, seeking additional support can be an important part of caring for ourselves.
Maybe that means talking with a trusted friend.
A pastor.
A grief support group.
Or a qualified mental health professional.
Now, those steps aren't evidence that prayer has failed.
And they aren't evidence that your faith is weak.
Sometimes we need people to walk beside us.
And as Christians, we should be willing to offer that support.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... What sorrow or disappointment have I been carrying lately?
Maybe it's the loss of someone you love.
Maybe it's a relationship.
Maybe it's a difficult change.
Or maybe it's a dream that hasn't unfolded the way you hoped. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... Have I been putting pressure on myself to feel better before I'm ready?
Think about whether you've been judging yourself for still grieving.
And remember that grief doesn't follow a single timetable. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... Who has offered me meaningful comfort during a difficult season?
Maybe it's a family member.
A friend.
A pastor.
Or someone who simply listened. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... How can I offer compassion to someone who is hurting?
Maybe it's checking on them.
Listening without judgment.
Remembering an important date.
Or offering practical help. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — OUR HOPE IN THE RISEN SAVIOR Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because the deepest foundation of Christian hope is found in Him.
Jesus lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, that's the foundation of our hope.
And that hope remains meaningful even when our hearts are hurting.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn God's love by grieving correctly.
We don't earn salvation by being strong enough.
And we don't have to pretend that we're never discouraged.
Our salvation rests in God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And our hope is rooted in Him.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. You can miss someone deeply and still experience joy. You can cry and still have faith. And you can grieve while remaining rooted in the hope of Jesus Christ.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we think joy means moving on without looking back.
But joy doesn't require forgetting.
And faith doesn't require pretending.
LIVING IT OUT — COMFORT IN ACTION Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... Comfort in Action.
Now, beneath that heading, write down three things.
First... One emotion you've been carrying.
Maybe it's sadness.
Disappointment.
Loneliness.
Or grief.
Second... One source of meaningful support.
Maybe it's someone you trust.
A support group.
A pastor.
Or a professional who can help.
And third... One way you can offer compassion to someone else.
Maybe it's sending a message.
Making a phone call.
Offering help.
Or simply listening.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Bring your emotions honestly before God.
And ask Him to help you recognize meaningful ways to receive and share comfort.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, the sorrow I've been carrying is...
Our second prompt is... One truth from Your Word that brings me hope is...
And our third prompt is... Help me receive and offer comfort by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. I can acknowledge my sorrow while remaining rooted in the hope and comfort I have through Jesus Christ.
Now, say that again. I can acknowledge my sorrow while remaining rooted in the hope and comfort I have through Jesus Christ.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize 2 Corinthians chapter 1, verse 3. "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort;"
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about one meaningful way you can offer comfort to someone else.
Maybe it's a message.
A phone call.
A meal.
Or simply taking time to listen.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHEN LAUGHTER AND TEARS SHARE THE SAME ROOM Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
And I ask you this question. Have you ever been laughing about a memory of someone you love... And suddenly found yourself crying?
Maybe the memory was funny.
Maybe it reminded you of something they used to say.
Or maybe it brought back a moment you wish you could experience again. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. What did that moment mean to you?
Did it remind you of the love you shared?
Did it bring comfort?
Or did it remind you that grief and gratitude can exist together? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to remember something. You don't have to choose between laughter and tears.
You can experience both.
And both can be honest expressions of love.
CLOSING REFLECTION — YOU DON'T HAVE TO HIDE YOUR TEARS Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Maybe you're listening today with tears in your eyes.
Maybe you're missing someone.
Maybe you're carrying a disappointment.
Or maybe you're grieving a season of life that has ended.
Now, I can't promise that your grief will disappear tomorrow.
I can't tell you exactly how long healing will take.
And I can't explain why every painful experience happens.
But I can encourage you to remember what Scripture teaches about God.
He is the Father of mercies.
And the God of all comfort.
Now, remember Jesus at the tomb of Lazarus.
He wept.
And remember Paul's words.
"As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing."
Now, those passages remind us that sorrow and Christian hope can exist together.
So today, I want to encourage you.
Don't feel ashamed of your tears.
Don't feel guilty when you laugh.
And don't feel pressured to pretend that everything is fine.
You can grieve.
You can seek comfort.
And you can continue walking with Jesus Christ.
One day at a time.
Because sometimes joy and sorrow meet in the same moment.
And both can be part of a life lived faithfully before God.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for reminding us that You are the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort. Lord, You know every person listening. You know the people they're missing. The memories they're carrying. And the grief that sometimes feels difficult to explain. Father, comfort those who are brokenhearted. Help us remember that tears aren't a failure of faith. And help us become people who offer compassion rather than judgment. Lord, I pray for the person who's grieving someone they love. Surround them with care and support. I pray for the person who's facing disappointment. Give them wisdom and encouragement. I pray for the person who's feeling alone. Help them find meaningful connection. And I pray for the person who's struggling emotionally. Help them receive appropriate support. Father, teach us to rejoice with those who rejoice. And to weep with those who weep. Help us become people who listen. Who encourage. And who love others well. Thank You for Jesus Christ. Thank You for His sacrifice. His resurrection. And the promise of eternal life through Him. May our hope remain rooted in our Savior. And may we continue following Him faithfully through every season. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY FIVE Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Nine, Day Four.
And I hope today's lesson has reminded you that you don't have to hide your sorrow to have faith.
You can cry.
You can grieve.
And you can still remain rooted in the hope we have through Jesus Christ.
Tomorrow, we're continuing our study of Finding Joy in Every Season. And we're going to talk about something that can help us recognize joy even when circumstances are challenging. The Joy of Giving — Finding Blessing in Serving Others.
We'll explore what Scripture teaches about generosity, kindness, and the joy that can come from serving others in love.
Until then, remember... Your tears don't mean your faith has failed.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: The Joy of Giving: Finding Blessing in Serving Others
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — THE BLESSING OF BEING A BLESSING Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Whether you're listening while enjoying your morning coffee, driving down the road, getting ready for work, or sitting somewhere quiet with your Bible, I'm glad you're here.
Today is Week Nine, Day Five. And we're continuing our study called... Finding Joy in Every Season.
Now, this week we've talked about finding joy in the Lord, choosing gratitude, appreciating the little things, and recognizing that joy and sorrow can exist together.
But today, we're going to talk about something a little different. We're going to talk about giving.
And before you start thinking this is going to be a lesson about money... I want you to know something. Giving is about so much more than what's in your wallet.
Sometimes giving looks like preparing a meal for someone who's struggling. Sometimes it looks like spending an afternoon helping a neighbor. Sometimes it looks like offering someone a ride. Sometimes it looks like sitting beside a grieving friend. And sometimes it looks like giving someone your full attention when they need to be heard.
Now, let me ask you something. Have you ever helped someone and walked away feeling encouraged yourself?
Maybe you volunteered somewhere. Maybe you surprised someone with a small gift. Maybe you offered encouragement to someone who was having a difficult day.
And when it was over, you realized that the experience had meant something to you, too.
Now, that's something I want us to explore today. Because Scripture teaches us that generosity and service are important parts of Christian living.
But I also want us to understand something. Serving others doesn't mean neglecting ourselves.
It doesn't mean giving beyond our ability. And it doesn't mean allowing people to take advantage of us.
Biblical generosity is rooted in love, wisdom, and a willingness to care for others.
And when we serve with the right heart, those experiences can become meaningful expressions of our faith.
Now, here's the question I want us to consider today. What if some of the most meaningful moments of joy come not from what we receive, but from the love we're able to share?
Our lesson today is called... The Joy of Giving — Finding Blessing in Serving Others.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for the opportunity to learn more about living faithfully. Lord, today we're talking about generosity and serving others. Help us understand what genuine Christian service looks like. Teach us to recognize the needs of those around us. Give us wisdom to know when and how we can help. And help us serve with love rather than a desire for recognition. Father, remind us that even small acts of kindness can be meaningful. Help us become more compassionate. More generous. And more attentive to the people around us. May everything we learn today draw us closer to Jesus Christ. In His precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — ACTS 20:35 Now, let's turn to Acts chapter 20.
We're going to focus on verse 35. But before we read it, let's understand what's happening.
In Acts chapter 20, the apostle Paul is speaking to the elders of the church in Ephesus.
He's preparing to leave them. And he knows they may not see him again.
So he reminds them of his example. His work. His faithfulness. And his concern for others.
Paul explains that he worked diligently and sought to help those who were weak.
Then he reminds them of something Jesus taught.
Now, let's read Acts chapter 20, verse 35, from the King James Version. "I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive."
Now, I want you to hear those last words again. "It is more blessed to give than to receive."
Now, that's a powerful statement.
But I want us to understand something important. Jesus isn't saying that receiving help is wrong.
And He isn't saying that people who need assistance should feel ashamed.
Instead, this teaching reminds us of the blessing connected to generosity.
Now, think about that. When we have the opportunity to help someone, we're participating in something meaningful.
We're recognizing another person's needs. We're responding with compassion. And we're reflecting the love of Christ through our actions.
Now, that doesn't mean every act of service will make us feel happy.
Sometimes helping others requires sacrifice. Sometimes it's tiring. And sometimes the circumstances are difficult.
But Christian service isn't measured only by how it makes us feel.
It's rooted in love and faithfulness.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH The joy of giving isn't found in how much we give, but in the love and faithfulness with which we serve.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we think generosity has to be something big.
We think we need a lot of money. A lot of free time. Or a special position.
But Scripture reminds us that service can take many forms.
And sometimes the smallest acts of kindness are deeply meaningful.
GIVING IS MORE THAN MONEY Now, let's talk about something important.
When we hear the word giving, we often think about money.
We think about donations. Offerings. Fundraisers. And financial support.
Now, those things can be important.
Financial generosity can help meet real needs.
It can support ministries.
Provide food.
Assist families.
And make meaningful services possible.
But giving isn't limited to money.
Sometimes the most valuable thing we can offer someone is our time.
Think about a person who's lonely.
Maybe they don't need another material gift.
Maybe they need someone to sit and talk with them.
Think about a parent who's overwhelmed.
Maybe what they need is someone to help with a practical responsibility.
Think about someone who's grieving.
Maybe what they need is a friend who will listen without trying to explain away their pain.
Now, those acts of service matter.
And they can reflect the love of Christ.
MARK 10 — JESUS CAME TO SERVE Now, let's turn to Mark chapter 10.
We're going to read verses 42 through 45.
In this passage, Jesus is teaching His disciples about greatness and service.
They had been discussing positions of honor.
And Jesus challenges their understanding of what greatness means.
Let's read. "But Jesus called them to him, and saith unto them, Ye know that they which are accounted to rule over the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and their great ones exercise authority upon them. But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all. For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."
Now, I want you to think about those words. Jesus tells His disciples that greatness in His kingdom looks different from worldly greatness.
It's not simply about power.
Position.
Or recognition.
It's about service.
And then Jesus points to His own example.
He came not to be served, but to serve.
Now, that's powerful.
Because Jesus didn't simply teach about serving others.
He demonstrated it.
Through His compassion.
His ministry.
And ultimately, through His sacrificial death.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Christian service isn't about proving how important we are. It's about reflecting the love of the One who served us first.
THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SERVING AND SEEKING RECOGNITION Now, let's talk about something that can be challenging.
Sometimes we do good things for the wrong reasons.
Maybe we want people to notice.
Maybe we want recognition.
Maybe we want someone to thank us.
Or maybe we want others to know how much we've done.
Now, there's nothing wrong with appreciating encouragement.
And there's nothing wrong with recognizing volunteers or thanking people for their service.
But our motivation matters.
Are we serving because we genuinely care?
Or are we serving primarily because we want attention?
Now, that's an important question.
Because sometimes genuine service happens where nobody sees it.
Someone quietly pays for another person's groceries.
Someone prepares a meal.
Someone checks on an elderly neighbor.
Someone prays for a person who may never know about it.
Now, those actions may never receive public recognition.
But they can still be meaningful expressions of love.
JOHN 13 — JESUS WASHES THE DISCIPLES' FEET Now, let's turn to John chapter 13.
We're going to read verses 12 through 17.
In this passage, Jesus has washed His disciples' feet.
Now, in that culture, washing feet was associated with hospitality and humble service.
And Jesus uses this action to teach His disciples.
Let's read. "So after he had washed their feet, and had taken his garments, and was set down again, he said unto them, Know ye what I have done to you? Ye call me Master and Lord: and ye say well; for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet. For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you. Verily, verily, I say unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord; neither he that is sent greater than he that sent him. If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them."
Now, I want you to notice something. Jesus doesn't simply tell His disciples to serve.
He gives them an example.
He takes on a humble task.
And He demonstrates the kind of love and humility He wants them to practice.
Now, I think that's something we need to remember.
Because sometimes we think serving God means doing something extraordinary.
We think about standing on a stage.
Leading a ministry.
Or organizing a major event.
Now, those things can be meaningful.
But sometimes serving God looks like doing something simple.
Helping someone clean up.
Preparing a meal.
Giving someone a ride.
Or listening when someone needs encouragement.
Now, those things may not seem impressive.
But they can reflect the humility and love of Christ.
WHEN SERVICE BECOMES EXHAUSTING Now, I want to talk about something important.
Sometimes people who love helping others become exhausted.
They say yes to everything.
They take on more responsibilities than they can manage.
And they begin feeling guilty whenever they need to rest.
Now, I want you to hear something. Serving others doesn't mean ignoring your own limitations.
And it doesn't mean that every request for help is yours to fulfill.
Sometimes we need to say no.
Sometimes we need to ask someone else to help.
And sometimes we need to rest.
Now, think about Jesus.
Throughout the Gospels, we see Him ministering to people.
But we also see Him withdrawing to pray.
He wasn't driven by a need to satisfy every demand people placed on Him.
His ministry was guided by His relationship with the Father and His divine mission.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Healthy boundaries can help us serve faithfully without neglecting important responsibilities or our own well-being.
And sometimes accepting help is just as important as offering it.
2 CORINTHIANS 9 — GOD LOVES A CHEERFUL GIVER Now, let's turn to 2 Corinthians chapter 9.
We're going to read verses 6 through 8.
In this passage, Paul is encouraging believers to participate in a collection for Christians in need.
He emphasizes generosity and willingness.
Let's read. "But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully. Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver. And God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work:"
Now, I want you to notice something important. Paul says... "Not grudgingly, or of necessity."
Now, that matters.
Because genuine generosity shouldn't be based on manipulation.
It shouldn't be based on shame.
And it shouldn't be based on pressure.
Paul encourages believers to give willingly.
Now, here's something else we need to understand. This passage isn't a guarantee that donating money will make us wealthy.
And it shouldn't be used to pressure people into giving beyond their means.
Instead, Paul is encouraging sincere generosity in support of others.
Now, I want you to remember something. The heart behind our giving matters.
We can give thoughtfully.
Responsibly.
And willingly.
And sometimes our ability to give may look different in different seasons.
That's okay.
LUKE 21 — THE WIDOW'S OFFERING Now, let's turn to Luke chapter 21.
We're going to read verses 1 through 4. The King James Version says: "And he looked up, and saw the rich men casting their gifts into the treasury. And he saw also a certain poor widow casting in thither two mites. And he said, Of a truth I say unto you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all: For all these have of their abundance cast in unto the offerings of God: but she of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had."
Now, this passage deserves careful attention.
Jesus notices a widow giving two small coins.
And He contrasts her contribution with the larger gifts of wealthy people.
Now, the passage also appears near Jesus' warning about religious leaders who exploit vulnerable widows.
So we should be careful not to use this account to pressure people who are struggling financially to give away what they need to survive.
Instead, the passage challenges us to consider how God sees what others might overlook.
A contribution that seems small in monetary value may represent a great deal to the person giving it.
Now, here's something important. We shouldn't judge someone's generosity by comparing dollar amounts.
And we shouldn't assume that everyone has the same resources.
Generosity can take different forms.
And it should be approached with wisdom and compassion.
PAUSE AND PRAY — GIVE ME A HEART TO SERVE Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about someone in your life who may need encouragement.
Maybe it's a family member.
A friend.
A neighbor.
Or someone in your church.
Now, ask yourself... Is there a meaningful way I can help?
Maybe it's a phone call.
Maybe it's a meal.
Maybe it's offering practical assistance.
Or maybe it's simply listening. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for the example of Jesus Christ. Thank You for showing us what genuine love and service look like. Lord, help us become more attentive to the needs of others. Give us wisdom to recognize where we can help. And help us serve with compassion rather than a desire for recognition. Father, teach us to give willingly. Help us respect our own limitations. And remind us that even small acts of kindness can be meaningful. May our lives reflect the love of Christ. In His precious name, Amen.
MATTHEW 25 — SERVING THOSE IN NEED Now, let's turn to Matthew chapter 25.
We're going to read verses 34 through 40.
In this passage, Jesus describes the judgment of the nations.
And He speaks about acts of compassion shown to those in need.
Let's read. "Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me. Then shall the righteous answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee? or thirsty, and gave thee drink? When saw we thee a stranger, and took thee in? or naked, and clothed thee? Or when saw we thee sick, or in prison, and came unto thee? And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."
Now, I want you to think about the acts Jesus describes.
Feeding the hungry.
Giving water to the thirsty.
Welcoming strangers.
Providing clothing.
Visiting the sick.
And remembering those in prison.
Now, those are practical expressions of compassion.
They're not simply words.
They're actions.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Christian love is meant to be expressed through the way we treat people.
And sometimes that means responding to needs that others overlook.
Now, this passage also reminds us to take the needs of vulnerable people seriously.
We shouldn't treat service as a performance.
And we shouldn't use someone's hardship as an opportunity to draw attention to ourselves.
Instead, we can serve with dignity, respect, and compassion.
THE JOY OF SERVING WITHOUT EXPECTING SOMETHING BACK Now, let's talk about something that can be challenging.
Sometimes we help someone and expect a particular response.
Maybe we expect a thank-you.
Maybe we expect recognition.
Or maybe we expect that person to help us in return.
Now, it's natural to appreciate gratitude.
And healthy relationships often involve mutual care.
But genuine generosity isn't simply a transaction.
We don't have to measure every act of kindness by what we receive in return.
Now, here's something important. That doesn't mean we should allow people to exploit us.
And it doesn't mean we should ignore unhealthy patterns.
But when we choose to serve, we can do so with a sincere desire to help.
And sometimes the blessing is simply knowing that we responded with compassion.
GALATIANS 6 — DON'T GROW WEARY IN DOING GOOD Now, let's turn to Galatians chapter 6.
We're going to read verses 9 and 10. The King James Version says: "And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith."
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul encourages believers not to grow weary in doing good.
But he also says... "As we have therefore opportunity..."
Now, that's meaningful.
Because not every opportunity belongs to every person.
We have different responsibilities.
Different abilities.
Different resources.
And different seasons of life.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Faithful service isn't about doing everything. It's about responding wisely to the opportunities God places before us.
Sometimes we can help directly.
Sometimes we can connect someone with another resource.
Sometimes we can pray.
And sometimes we need to recognize that another person is better equipped to meet a particular need.
Now, those are all important considerations.
1 PETER 4 — USING OUR GIFTS TO SERVE Now, let's turn to 1 Peter chapter 4.
We're going to read verse 10. The King James Version says: "As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God."
Now, let's think about that.
Peter encourages believers to use the gifts they've received in service to one another.
Now, I love that.
Because not everyone serves in the same way.
Some people are gifted at teaching.
Some are gifted at organizing.
Some are gifted at encouraging.
Some are skilled at preparing meals.
Some are good listeners.
And some have practical abilities that can help meet important needs.
Now, here's something important. We don't have to compare our gifts with someone else's.
We can recognize the abilities and opportunities we have.
And use them to serve faithfully.
Now, let me ask you something. What is something you do well?
Maybe you enjoy writing.
Maybe you're good at organizing.
Maybe you enjoy cooking.
Maybe you have a talent for encouraging others.
Or maybe you're someone who listens carefully.
Now, think about how that ability could become an opportunity to serve.
Because sometimes the things we do naturally can become meaningful ways to help others.
SERVING IN THE SEASON YOU'RE IN Now, I want to talk about something important.
Our ability to serve can change throughout life.
Maybe there was a time when you had more energy.
More free time.
Or more financial resources.
But now your circumstances are different.
Maybe you're caring for a family member.
Maybe you're dealing with health concerns.
Maybe you're raising young children.
Or maybe you're facing responsibilities that require most of your attention.
Now, I want you to hear something. You don't have to compare your present capacity with what you could do in another season.
Sometimes serving faithfully looks different.
Maybe you can no longer volunteer for an entire afternoon.
But you can send an encouraging message.
Maybe you can't contribute financially.
But you can offer a skill.
Maybe you can't attend every event.
But you can pray for the people involved.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Your worth isn't measured by how much you accomplish for other people.
And your relationship with God isn't dependent on constant productivity.
We serve because of His grace.
Not to earn it.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... What does generosity look like in my current season of life?
Maybe it's financial support.
Maybe it's time.
Maybe it's encouragement.
Or maybe it's sharing a skill. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... Have I been comparing my ability to serve with someone else's?
Think about whether you've been feeling pressure to do more than you're able.
And remember that people have different capacities and responsibilities. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... What gifts or abilities could I use to encourage someone else?
Maybe it's organizing.
Teaching.
Cooking.
Listening.
Or offering practical assistance. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... Who is one person I could serve or encourage this week?
Maybe it's a family member.
A friend.
A neighbor.
Or someone in your church or community. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — JESUS SERVED US FIRST Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because the foundation of Christian service is found in Him.
Jesus didn't simply teach about love.
He demonstrated it.
He cared for people.
He showed compassion.
And ultimately, He gave His life for our salvation.
Now, that's the greatest example of sacrificial love.
Jesus lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn salvation by serving enough people.
We don't earn God's love by giving enough money.
And we don't have to prove our worth through constant sacrifice.
Our salvation rests in God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And our service is a response to that grace.
Now, I want you to remember something. We don't serve to earn God's love. We serve because we've received His love through Jesus Christ.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. You don't have to change the whole world to make a meaningful difference in someone's life. Sometimes one sincere act of kindness becomes an expression of Christ's love.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we think our contribution has to be extraordinary.
But service can begin with something simple.
A conversation.
A meal.
A helping hand.
Or a moment of compassion.
LIVING IT OUT — ONE ACT OF LOVE Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... One Act of Love.
Now, beneath that heading, answer three questions.
First... Who is someone I could encourage?
Maybe it's a family member.
A friend.
A neighbor.
Or someone in your community.
Second... What is one practical way I could help?
Maybe it's sending a message.
Preparing a meal.
Offering transportation.
Or simply listening.
And third... How can I serve with a sincere heart?
Think about your motivation.
And ask God to help you serve with compassion.
Now, after you've written those answers down, choose one appropriate action you can take this week.
It doesn't have to be expensive.
And it doesn't have to be complicated.
Just something meaningful.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, one person You've placed on my heart to encourage is...
Our second prompt is... One gift or ability I could use to serve others is...
And our third prompt is... Help me serve with love and wisdom by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. I will serve others with love, generosity, and wisdom, remembering that my service is a response to God's grace.
Now, say that again. I will serve others with love, generosity, and wisdom, remembering that my service is a response to God's grace.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize Acts chapter 20, verse 35. And focus especially on these words: "It is more blessed to give than to receive."
Now, throughout the day, think about one meaningful way you can serve someone.
Maybe it's offering help.
Maybe it's giving encouragement.
Or maybe it's sharing something you have.
And remember... Giving isn't only about money.
Sometimes your time, attention, and compassion can be meaningful gifts.
AROUND THE FIRE — THE KINDNESS YOU NEVER FORGOT Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
And I ask you this question. Can you remember a time when someone helped you during a difficult season?
Maybe they brought you a meal.
Maybe they helped with a responsibility.
Maybe they offered encouragement.
Or maybe they simply sat beside you when you needed someone. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. What made that act of kindness meaningful?
Was it the amount of money they spent?
Was it the size of the gift?
Or was it the fact that someone cared enough to notice your need? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to think about something. Sometimes the acts of kindness we remember most are the simplest ones.
Someone showing up.
Someone listening.
Someone helping without being asked.
Now, those things matter.
And maybe today, you have an opportunity to offer that same kind of compassion to someone else.
CLOSING REFLECTION — THE JOY OF A GENEROUS HEART Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Sometimes we spend so much time thinking about what we need that we overlook opportunities to encourage someone else.
Now, that doesn't mean our own needs aren't important.
And it doesn't mean we should ignore our responsibilities.
But it does mean we can remain attentive to the people around us.
Sometimes someone needs a meal.
Sometimes someone needs a ride.
Sometimes someone needs encouragement.
And sometimes someone simply needs to know they haven't been forgotten.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to have everything figured out in your own life before you can show kindness to someone else.
But you also don't have to neglect yourself to prove that you care.
We can serve with wisdom.
With compassion.
And with healthy boundaries.
Now, remember the words of Jesus.
"It is more blessed to give than to receive."
And remember His example.
He came not to be served, but to serve.
So today, I want to encourage you.
Look for one opportunity to show kindness.
One opportunity to encourage someone.
And one opportunity to reflect the love of Christ.
It doesn't have to be big.
It doesn't have to be expensive.
And it doesn't have to receive recognition.
Sometimes one sincere act of love can be deeply meaningful.
And that is a beautiful way to live faithfully.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for reminding us of the blessing of generosity and service. Lord, You know every person listening. You know the resources they have. The responsibilities they carry. And the limitations they face. Father, help us serve with wisdom. Help us recognize the needs of others. And help us respond with compassion. Lord, I pray for the person who's feeling overwhelmed. Remind them that they don't have to do everything. I pray for the person who wants to help but has limited resources. Show them meaningful ways to offer encouragement. I pray for the person who's been serving faithfully but feels exhausted. Help them find rest and support. And I pray for those who are in need. Surround them with people who can offer practical assistance and genuine care. Father, teach us to serve without seeking recognition. Help us give willingly. And help us reflect the love of Jesus Christ. Thank You for His sacrifice. His resurrection. And the promise of eternal life through Him. May our lives be shaped by Your grace. And may our service become an expression of our gratitude. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY SIX Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Nine, Day Five!
And I hope today's lesson has encouraged you to remember that generosity is about so much more than money.
Sometimes the most meaningful gift we can offer is our time. Our attention. Our encouragement. Or our compassion.
Tomorrow, we're continuing our study of Finding Joy in Every Season. And we're going to gather around the fire for a special time of reflection. Our next lesson is called... Around the Fire — Choosing Joy Through Gratitude, Grief, and Generosity.
We'll reflect on what we've learned this week and explore how joy can remain rooted in Jesus Christ through every season.
Until then, remember... You don't have to change the whole world to show someone the love of Christ.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: Around the Fire: Choosing Joy Through Gratitude, Grief, and Generosity
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — COME SIT AROUND THE FIRE Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Nine, Day Six. And that means it's time for one of my favorite parts of our weekly Bible study. Our Around the Fire reflection.
Now, if you've been walking through this study with me, you know that our Around the Fire episodes are a little different.
This is where we slow down. Where we reflect. Where we ask ourselves some honest questions. And where we take what we've learned from Scripture and consider what it means for our everyday lives.
Now, I want you to imagine something. Imagine we're sitting together around a warm fire.
Maybe we're outside on a cool evening. Maybe the stars are shining. Maybe there's a cup of coffee sitting beside you. And maybe, for the first time all day, you don't feel like you have to rush anywhere.
You don't have to answer another message. You don't have to solve another problem. And you don't have to pretend that everything is fine.
You can simply sit. Breathe. And spend a little time reflecting on God's Word.
Now, that's what I want this episode to feel like. A conversation. Not a performance. Not a lecture. Just a meaningful time of reflection.
Because this week, we've been talking about something that sounds simple... But can actually be difficult. Joy.
We've talked about finding joy in the Lord. We've talked about gratitude. We've talked about appreciating ordinary moments. We've talked about grief. And we've talked about the joy of serving others.
Now, today I want to bring all of those lessons together.
Because here's something I've learned. Life doesn't always give us one emotion at a time.
Sometimes we're thankful and disappointed. Sometimes we're grieving and laughing. Sometimes we're exhausted and encouraged. And sometimes we're celebrating something beautiful while still carrying a burden nobody else can see.
Now, that's real life.
And I believe Scripture gives us room to acknowledge all of it.
So today, we're going to talk about what it means to choose joy without pretending. To practice gratitude without denying pain. And to serve others without forgetting that we need care, too.
Our lesson today is called... Around the Fire — Choosing Joy Through Gratitude, Grief, and Generosity.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together today. Thank You for another opportunity to open Your Word. Lord, this week we've been studying joy. And You know that for some people listening, joy feels close. But for others, it feels very far away. You know the people who are grieving. The people who are discouraged. The people who are carrying responsibilities that feel overwhelming. And the people who are trying to remain faithful through difficult circumstances. Father, help us reflect honestly today. Help us remember what Scripture teaches about Your goodness. Teach us to practice gratitude. To offer compassion. And to remain rooted in the hope we have through Jesus Christ. Lord, may this time of reflection bring encouragement. And may everything we discuss draw us closer to You. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — ROMANS 12:12 Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 12.
We're going to focus on verse 12. But before we read it, let's understand the context.
In Romans chapter 12, Paul begins describing what a life transformed by God's mercy should look like.
He talks about humility. Using our gifts. Showing sincere love. Serving others. And living faithfully.
Then he gives a short instruction that connects beautifully with everything we've been studying this week.
Let's read Romans chapter 12, verse 12, from the King James Version. "Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer;"
Now, I want you to hear those words again. "Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer."
Now, isn't that a beautiful picture of Christian living?
Rejoicing in hope.
Patient in tribulation.
Continuing in prayer.
Now, notice something. Paul doesn't say that believers will never experience tribulation.
He acknowledges it.
And he encourages them to remain patient and prayerful through it.
Now, that's important. Because sometimes we think joy means the absence of hardship.
But Scripture gives us a different picture.
Our joy is connected to hope.
Our endurance is needed because hardship is real.
And prayer remains part of our relationship with God through every season.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH Christian joy isn't about pretending life is easy. It's about remaining rooted in hope, practicing gratitude, and walking faithfully with Jesus through every season.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we place unrealistic expectations on ourselves.
We think we should always be smiling. Always encouraged. Always positive.
But faith doesn't erase our humanity.
And Christian joy doesn't require pretending.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHAT HAS THIS WEEK TAUGHT YOU? Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
And I ask you this question. What has this week taught you about joy?
Maybe you've realized that joy and happiness aren't exactly the same thing.
Maybe you've recognized that gratitude doesn't mean ignoring difficult circumstances.
Maybe you've been reminded to appreciate ordinary moments.
Maybe you've found comfort in knowing that grief and joy can exist together.
Or maybe you've been encouraged to serve someone else.
Now, I want you to take a moment and think about that. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Because sometimes we hear a lesson. We agree with it. And then we move on.
But spiritual growth involves more than hearing information.
It involves reflecting on what Scripture teaches.
And considering how we should respond.
So today, I want us to do exactly that.
REFLECTION ONE — JOY ROOTED IN THE LORD Now, let's go back to our first lesson this week.
We studied Nehemiah chapter 8.
And we focused on these words from verse 10. "For the joy of the LORD is your strength."
Now, remember the context.
God's people had gathered to hear His Word.
They were responding emotionally.
And their leaders encouraged them to recognize the holiness of the occasion and celebrate.
Now, I want you to think about something. Where have you been looking for joy lately?
Have you been waiting for a particular circumstance to change?
Have you been waiting for someone to make a decision?
Have you been waiting for an answer?
Or have you been thinking that you'll finally experience joy once everything settles down?
Now, there's nothing wrong with hoping for better circumstances.
But here's something important. Our relationship with God doesn't have to be placed on hold while we're waiting.
We can continue praying.
We can continue studying Scripture.
And we can continue remembering the hope we have through Jesus Christ.
Now, I want you to ask yourself something. Have I been treating joy as something I can only experience after my circumstances improve? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, be honest with yourself.
Because sometimes recognizing that pattern is an important first step.
REFLECTION TWO — GRATITUDE WITHOUT PRETENDING Now, let's talk about gratitude.
Earlier this week, we studied 1 Thessalonians chapter 5.
And we learned about giving thanks in every circumstance.
Now, I want you to remember something important. That doesn't mean every circumstance is good.
And it doesn't mean we should be thankful for wrongdoing, suffering, or injustice.
But we can continue recognizing God's goodness while acknowledging the difficulties we face.
Now, let me ask you something. What is one thing you're genuinely thankful for today?
Not something you think you should say.
Not something you feel pressured to appreciate.
But something meaningful.
Maybe it's a person.
Maybe it's a memory.
Maybe it's an opportunity.
Or maybe it's simply the hope you have through Jesus Christ. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's something else I want you to consider. Have you been putting pressure on yourself to feel thankful when you're actually hurting?
Because gratitude doesn't require denying pain.
You can say... "Lord, I'm thankful for Your faithfulness."
And also say... "Lord, I'm struggling today."
Those prayers can exist together.
And both can be honest.
REFLECTION THREE — THE LITTLE THINGS Now, let's talk about something that can be easy to overlook.
The little things.
Earlier this week, we studied James chapter 1, verse 17.
And we were reminded that every good and perfect gift comes from above.
Now, sometimes we're so focused on the next big thing that we overlook meaningful moments already happening around us.
We wait for the vacation.
The celebration.
The achievement.
Or the next milestone.
But ordinary life continues happening.
And sometimes those ordinary moments are deeply meaningful.
Now, I want you to think about something. What little thing brought you joy this week?
Maybe it was hearing a child laugh.
Maybe it was a phone call.
Maybe it was a beautiful sunrise.
Maybe it was a song.
Or maybe it was simply a peaceful moment. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to ask yourself another question. Did I really appreciate that moment?
Or was I already thinking about the next thing?
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Ordinary moments can be meaningful gifts.
And sometimes we need to slow down long enough to recognize them.
REFLECTION FOUR — WHEN JOY AND SORROW MEET Now, let's talk about something especially important.
Grief.
Earlier this week, we studied 2 Corinthians chapter 1.
And we were reminded that God is the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort.
We also studied John chapter 11.
And we remembered that Jesus wept.
Now, I want you to think about something. Sometimes we feel pressure to hide our grief.
We think we should be stronger.
We think we should have moved on.
Or we worry that our tears will make other people uncomfortable.
But Scripture makes room for sorrow.
And it reminds us to show compassion to those who are hurting.
Now, I want to ask you something. Is there a grief you've been carrying quietly?
Maybe you're missing someone.
Maybe you're grieving a relationship.
Maybe you're disappointed about something that didn't happen.
Or maybe you're struggling with a change you never expected. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to hide your sorrow to have faith.
And you don't have to feel guilty when you experience moments of joy.
You can grieve.
You can laugh.
You can remember.
And you can continue placing your hope in Jesus Christ.
REFLECTION FIVE — THE JOY OF GIVING Now, let's talk about our most recent lesson.
The joy of giving.
We studied Acts chapter 20, verse 35.
And we remembered the words of Jesus. "It is more blessed to give than to receive."
Now, I want you to think about something. Who has shown you kindness during a difficult season?
Maybe someone brought you a meal.
Maybe someone helped you with a responsibility.
Maybe someone encouraged you.
Or maybe someone simply listened. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to think about another question. Who might need that same kind of compassion from you?
Maybe it's a family member.
A friend.
A neighbor.
Or someone in your community.
Now, here's something important. Serving others doesn't mean doing everything.
And it doesn't mean ignoring your own limitations.
But it does mean remaining attentive to opportunities for kindness.
Sometimes a simple act of love can be deeply meaningful.
HABAKKUK — THE POWER OF "YET" Now, I want us to revisit a passage from earlier this week.
Habakkuk chapter 3.
Remember, Habakkuk described a situation in which the harvest failed.
The fields produced no food.
And the flocks were gone.
Yet he expressed confidence in the Lord.
Let's read Habakkuk chapter 3, verses 17 through 19. "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments."
Now, I want you to focus on that one word. Yet.
Now, sometimes one word can remind us of an important truth.
I'm disappointed... Yet I can still pray.
I'm grieving... Yet I can still seek comfort.
I'm uncertain... Yet I can still make wise decisions.
I'm struggling... Yet I can still ask for help.
Now, that word doesn't erase the difficulty.
It doesn't make the pain disappear.
But it reminds us that hardship isn't the only reality we can acknowledge.
We can recognize our struggles.
And still remember God's faithfulness.
Now, I want you to think about something. What would your "yet" statement be today?
Maybe it's... "Lord, I'm tired, yet I'm still seeking You."
Maybe it's... "Lord, I'm disappointed, yet I still believe Your Word."
Or maybe it's simply... "Lord, I'm hurting, yet I'm bringing my pain before You." [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, hold on to that thought.
Because sometimes a simple, honest prayer is a meaningful expression of faith.
PHILIPPIANS 4 — PRAYER IN EVERY SEASON Now, let's turn to Philippians chapter 4.
We're going to read verses 4 through 7. The King James Version says: "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand. Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus."
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul brings together rejoicing, prayer, thanksgiving, and peace.
Now, that's meaningful.
Because sometimes we think we need to get our emotions under control before we pray.
We think we need to feel better first.
Or we think we need to have the right words.
But Scripture encourages us to bring our requests before God.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to wait until you feel joyful to pray.
You can pray when you're discouraged.
You can pray when you're grieving.
You can pray when you're thankful.
And you can pray when you're uncertain.
Our relationship with God isn't limited to one emotional state.
PAUSE AND PRAY — LORD, MEET ME IN THIS SEASON Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about the season of life you're in right now.
Maybe it's a season of celebration.
Maybe it's a season of waiting.
Maybe it's a season of grief.
Maybe it's a season of change.
Or maybe it's a season where you're experiencing several of those things at once.
Now, take a moment to acknowledge that honestly. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, You know the season each of us is walking through. You know the circumstances we're facing. The emotions we're experiencing. And the burdens we're carrying. Lord, help us remember that we can bring our whole hearts before You. Help us practice gratitude without denying our pain. Help us recognize moments of goodness. And help us offer compassion to others. Father, teach us to remain rooted in the hope we have through Jesus Christ. Give us wisdom for the decisions before us. And help us continue walking faithfully. In His precious name, Amen.
ROMANS 12 — REJOICE AND WEEP TOGETHER Now, let's stay in Romans chapter 12.
We began today with verse 12. But I also want us to read verse 15. The King James Version says: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep."
Now, I love how those two verses connect.
Verse 12 encourages believers to rejoice in hope, remain patient in tribulation, and continue in prayer.
And verse 15 reminds them to enter into the experiences of others with compassion.
Now, that's important.
Because Christian joy isn't simply about our own emotions.
It's also connected to the way we love others.
We can celebrate when someone receives good news.
And we can sit beside someone who's grieving.
We can share encouragement.
And we can offer practical help.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Sometimes the most meaningful expression of Christian love is simply being present with someone in the season they're experiencing.
We don't have to force them to feel differently.
We don't have to explain everything.
And we don't have to solve every problem.
Sometimes we simply need to love them well.
JOHN 15 — JOY ROOTED IN CHRIST Now, let's turn to John chapter 15.
We're going to read verses 9 through 11. The King James Version says: "As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you: continue ye in my love. If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love; even as I have kept my Father's commandments, and abide in his love. These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full."
Now, let's think about that.
Jesus connects joy with remaining in His love.
Now, that's the foundation of everything we've been studying.
Our deepest joy isn't simply about having a good day.
It's about our relationship with Jesus Christ.
Now, that relationship doesn't eliminate every hardship.
But it gives us a foundation of hope.
And it reminds us that our lives are connected to something greater than our changing circumstances.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn God's love by feeling joyful enough.
We don't earn salvation by practicing gratitude perfectly.
And we don't have to prove our worth through constant service.
Our salvation rests in God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And our joy, gratitude, and service grow out of that relationship.
FIVE QUESTIONS AROUND THE FIRE Now, before we move into our closing reflection, I want us to take a few minutes with five questions.
If you have your journal nearby, this is a good time to write.
And if you're listening while driving or doing something else, you can always return to these questions later.
Our first question is... Where have I been looking for joy lately?
Have I been waiting for circumstances to change?
Or have I been remembering the hope I have through Jesus Christ? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... What is one thing I can sincerely thank God for today?
Not something I feel pressured to say.
But something meaningful. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... What sorrow or disappointment do I need to acknowledge honestly?
Maybe it's grief.
Maybe it's uncertainty.
Or maybe it's something I've been carrying quietly. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... Who has shown me meaningful kindness during a difficult season?
And have I taken time to thank them? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fifth question is... What is one practical way I can share encouragement or compassion with someone else?
Maybe it's a message.
A phone call.
A meal.
Or simply listening. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, take a moment to look at those answers.
Because sometimes reflection helps us recognize what needs our attention.
And it can help us respond thoughtfully to what we've learned from Scripture.
CHRIST CONNECTION — THE HOPE THAT HOLDS US Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because He's the foundation of our hope.
Jesus lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, that's the foundation of Christian joy.
Not perfect circumstances.
Not constant happiness.
And not a life without sorrow.
But the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Our hope is not that life will always be easy. Our hope is that Jesus Christ is our Savior, and His promises remain true.
And that hope can sustain our faith through changing seasons.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. You don't have to choose between acknowledging your pain and remembering God's goodness. Joy, gratitude, grief, and compassion can all be part of a life rooted in Jesus Christ.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we think faith should make life simple.
But life can be complicated.
And our emotions can be complicated.
Yet we can continue bringing our whole hearts before the Lord.
LIVING IT OUT — MY JOY REFLECTION Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... My Joy Reflection.
Now, beneath that heading, write down four things.
First... One truth about God that gives you hope.
Second... One meaningful thing you're grateful for.
Third... One sorrow or disappointment you want to bring before the Lord.
And fourth... One opportunity to encourage someone else.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Bring your gratitude before God.
Bring your concerns before Him.
And ask Him to help you live faithfully in the season you're experiencing.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, the season I'm walking through right now feels like...
Our second prompt is... One truth from Your Word that gives me hope is...
And our third prompt is... Help me practice joy, gratitude, and compassion by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. I will remain rooted in the hope of Jesus Christ, practice sincere gratitude, acknowledge my emotions honestly, and seek opportunities to love others well.
Now, say that again. I will remain rooted in the hope of Jesus Christ, practice sincere gratitude, acknowledge my emotions honestly, and seek opportunities to love others well.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize Romans chapter 12, verse 12. "Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer;"
Now, throughout the day, return to those three instructions.
Rejoicing in hope.
Patient in tribulation.
Continuing in prayer.
And think about one practical way you can apply each of them.
Maybe you'll spend time remembering the hope you have in Christ.
Maybe you'll respond patiently to a difficult situation.
Or maybe you'll take a few minutes to pray honestly.
AROUND THE FIRE — THE SEASON YOU'RE IN Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire one more time.
The evening has grown quiet.
The fire is still burning.
And we're sitting together, reflecting on everything we've discussed.
Now, I want to ask you one final question. What does joy look like in the season you're in right now?
Maybe joy looks like celebration.
Maybe it looks like gratitude.
Maybe it looks like a quiet moment of peace.
Maybe it looks like serving someone else.
Or maybe it looks like continuing to pray while you're still hurting. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's something I want you to remember. Joy doesn't have to look the same in every season.
And it doesn't have to look the same for every person.
But our hope in Jesus Christ remains the foundation of Christian joy.
And that hope is worth remembering.
CLOSING REFLECTION — JOY FOR THE JOURNEY Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Maybe this week has been wonderful.
Maybe you've experienced answered prayers.
Meaningful moments.
And opportunities to celebrate.
Or maybe this week has been difficult.
Maybe you've experienced disappointment.
Grief.
Or uncertainty.
Now, whatever kind of week you've had, I want you to remember something.
Your relationship with Jesus Christ isn't measured by how happy you've felt.
And your faith isn't measured by whether you've cried.
You can bring your whole heart before the Lord.
Your gratitude.
Your questions.
Your joy.
And your sorrow.
Now, remember the words of Romans chapter 12, verse 12.
"Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer."
That's a beautiful reminder for the journey.
We can rejoice in the hope we have through Jesus Christ.
We can seek patience through difficult circumstances.
And we can continue praying.
One day at a time.
So today, I want to encourage you.
Don't feel pressured to pretend.
Don't overlook the meaningful moments.
Don't be ashamed of your tears.
And don't underestimate the value of kindness.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep seeking the Lord.
And keep remembering the hope we have through Jesus Christ.
Because joy isn't simply about having an easy journey.
It's about remaining rooted in the Savior who gives our journey its deepest hope.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for allowing us to reflect on everything we've learned this week. Lord, You know every person listening. You know the season they're experiencing. The emotions they're carrying. And the circumstances they're facing. Father, help us remain rooted in the hope we have through Jesus Christ. Teach us to practice sincere gratitude. Help us recognize meaningful moments. And give us compassion for those who are hurting. Lord, I pray for the person who's grieving. Surround them with care and support. I pray for the person who's discouraged. Give them encouragement and wisdom. I pray for the person who's feeling overwhelmed. Help them find rest and appropriate assistance. And I pray for the person who's experiencing joy. Help them celebrate with gratitude and share kindness with others. Father, teach us to rejoice with those who rejoice. And to weep with those who weep. Help us serve with love. And help us remember that our salvation rests in Your grace through faith in Jesus Christ. Thank You for His sacrifice. His resurrection. And the promise of eternal life through Him. May our lives reflect Your love. And may we continue walking faithfully through every season. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY SEVEN Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Nine, Day Six!
And I hope today's Around the Fire reflection has encouraged you to remember that joy, gratitude, grief, and compassion can all be part of a life rooted in Jesus Christ.
Tomorrow, we're going to finish Week Nine with a special closing lesson. It's called... Joy for the Journey — Carrying God's Goodness into Every Season.
We'll reflect on the hope we have through Christ and how we can continue practicing joy and gratitude as we move forward.
Until then, remember... You don't have to pretend life is easy to remain faithful.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: Joy for the Journey: Carrying God's Goodness into Every Season
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — JOY FOR THE ROAD AHEAD Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Nine, Day Seven. And that means we've reached the final day of our study called... Finding Joy in Every Season.
Now, I want to begin today's lesson by asking you something. Have you ever finished a difficult season and looked back at everything you experienced?
Maybe you remembered the things that challenged you. The moments when you felt discouraged. The prayers you prayed. And the people who helped you along the way.
Maybe you remembered moments of joy, too.
A conversation that encouraged you. A kindness you didn't expect. A memory that made you smile. Or a moment when you recognized God's goodness.
Now, here's something I want us to think about today. Life is made up of many different seasons.
Some are filled with celebration. Some involve waiting. Some bring unexpected changes. And some are marked by grief or uncertainty.
But through all of those seasons, our relationship with Jesus Christ remains the foundation of our hope.
Now, this week we've been learning that biblical joy isn't the same as constant happiness.
We've learned that gratitude doesn't require pretending everything is good.
We've learned that ordinary moments can be meaningful gifts.
We've learned that grief and joy can exist together.
And we've learned that serving others can become an expression of Christ's love.
Now, today, I want us to bring all of those lessons together.
Because it's one thing to study joy.
But it's another thing to carry those truths into everyday life.
What happens when the next disappointment comes?
What happens when our plans change?
What happens when we're waiting for an answer?
Or when we're facing circumstances we didn't expect?
How do we continue walking faithfully?
Now, that's what we're going to explore today.
Our lesson is called... Joy for the Journey — Carrying God's Goodness into Every Season.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for everything we've learned throughout this week. Lord, help us understand what it means to remain rooted in the joy and hope we have through Jesus Christ. You know the seasons we're walking through. You know the circumstances we're facing. And You know the burdens we're carrying. Father, teach us to remember Your goodness. Help us practice sincere gratitude. Give us compassion for those who are hurting. And help us continue walking faithfully, even when life becomes difficult. May Your Word encourage us today. And may everything we learn draw us closer to Jesus Christ. In His precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — ROMANS 15:13 Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 15.
We're going to focus on verse 13. But before we read it, let's understand the context.
In Romans chapter 15, Paul is encouraging believers to live in unity.
He reminds them that Christ has welcomed them.
And he points to the promises of Scripture concerning the hope that extends to the Gentiles.
Then he offers a beautiful prayer.
Let's read Romans chapter 15, verse 13, from the King James Version. "Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost."
Now, I want you to hear those words again. "Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing..."
Now, isn't that beautiful?
Paul describes God as the God of hope.
And he prays that believers will be filled with joy and peace as they trust in Him.
