Now, I want you to notice something important. Paul connects joy with believing.
And he connects hope with the work of the Holy Spirit.
Now, that reminds us that Christian joy is rooted in our relationship with God.
It's not simply a reaction to pleasant circumstances.
And it's not something we manufacture by pretending everything is fine.
Instead, it's connected to the hope we have through Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something important. This verse is a prayer.
It's not a promise that believers will always feel happy.
And it doesn't mean that faithful Christians never experience sadness, anxiety, or grief.
But it does remind us that God is the source of our hope.
And that we can continue seeking Him through every season.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH The joy we carry into tomorrow is rooted not in knowing what tomorrow holds, but in the hope we have through Jesus Christ.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we become so focused on what might happen next that we forget the promises we already have.
We worry about the future.
We wonder whether things will work out.
And we try to prepare for every possible outcome.
Now, planning is important.
And making wise decisions is important.
But our hope in Christ isn't dependent on being able to predict every circumstance.
We can plan responsibly.
We can seek wisdom.
And we can continue trusting God.
LOOKING BACK AT WEEK NINE Now, before we move forward, I want us to look back at what we've studied this week.
Because sometimes we learn something meaningful and then move on without taking time to reflect.
And I don't want us to do that.
I want us to remember these truths.
On Day One, we studied joy that doesn't depend on circumstances.
We learned that biblical joy is deeper than temporary happiness.
On Day Two, we studied gratitude.
We learned that giving thanks doesn't mean denying difficult circumstances.
On Day Three, we talked about finding joy in the little things.
We learned to appreciate ordinary moments and recognize God's goodness.
On Day Four, we talked about grief.
We learned that joy and sorrow can exist together.
On Day Five, we studied generosity.
We learned that serving others can become an expression of Christ's love.
And yesterday, during our Around the Fire reflection, we brought those lessons together.
Now, today, I want us to consider how we can carry those truths into the future.
Because spiritual growth involves more than learning information.
It involves allowing Scripture to shape the way we live.
PSALM 16 — JOY IN GOD'S PRESENCE Now, let's turn to Psalm chapter 16.
We're going to read verse 11. The King James Version says: "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore."
Now, I love that verse.
Because it reminds us that our deepest joy is found in God.
Now, Psalm 16 is a psalm of trust.
David expresses confidence in the Lord.
And this final verse speaks about the path of life and the joy found in God's presence.
Now, in the New Testament, Peter also refers to this psalm when proclaiming the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
So this passage has a beautiful connection to our hope in the risen Savior.
Now, here's something I want you to think about. Sometimes we look for joy in things that cannot provide lasting security.
We look for it in accomplishments.
In recognition.
In possessions.
Or in circumstances going exactly the way we planned.
Now, those things may bring temporary happiness.
And some of them can be meaningful gifts.
But they cannot replace our relationship with God.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The deepest foundation of Christian joy is not what we accomplish or possess. It's the relationship we have with God through Jesus Christ.
CARRYING JOY INTO UNCERTAIN SEASONS Now, let's talk about uncertainty.
Because life doesn't always unfold the way we expect.
Sometimes we make plans.
We set goals.
We prepare.
And then something changes.
Maybe an opportunity doesn't work out.
Maybe a relationship changes.
Maybe a health concern interrupts our plans.
Or maybe we're simply facing a future that feels uncertain.
Now, I want you to hear something. Uncertainty doesn't mean we have to abandon hope.
But it also doesn't mean we should ignore the practical realities before us.
We can seek medical care when needed.
We can ask for financial guidance.
We can establish healthy boundaries.
And we can make thoughtful decisions.
Now, here's something important. Trusting God and taking responsible action are not opposites.
We can do both.
And through it all, we can remain rooted in the hope we have through Jesus Christ.
HABAKKUK — YET I WILL REJOICE Now, let's turn to Habakkuk chapter 3.
We're going to read verses 17 through 19.
Now, remember the context.
Habakkuk describes a situation where crops fail.
The fields produce no food.
And the flocks and herds are gone.
These are serious circumstances.
They represent economic hardship and the loss of essential resources.
Yet Habakkuk expresses confidence in the Lord.
Let's read. "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments."
Now, I want you to focus on one word. Yet.
Now, I think that's one of the most meaningful words in this passage.
Habakkuk doesn't deny the seriousness of the situation.
He doesn't pretend that the harvest is successful.
And he doesn't ignore the loss of essential resources.
But he expresses confidence in the Lord.
Now, that's something we can learn from.
Sometimes we may need to say... "Lord, I'm disappointed, yet I'm still praying."
"Lord, I'm grieving, yet I'm still seeking Your comfort."
"Lord, I'm uncertain, yet I'm still asking for wisdom."
Or... "Lord, I'm struggling, yet I'm still bringing my concerns before You."
Now, those statements don't erase the difficulty.
But they remind us that hardship doesn't have to end our relationship with God.
GRATITUDE FOR THE JOURNEY Now, let's talk about gratitude.
Because as we move forward, gratitude can remain part of our everyday lives.
Remember what we studied in 1 Thessalonians chapter 5.
Verses 16 through 18 say: "Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you."
Now, I want you to remember something important. Giving thanks in every circumstance doesn't mean every circumstance is good.
It doesn't mean we should be grateful for wrongdoing.
And it doesn't mean we should pretend that suffering is a blessing.
But we can continue recognizing God's goodness while acknowledging difficult realities.
Now, sometimes gratitude involves remembering.
Remembering a kindness.
Remembering an encouraging conversation.
Remembering someone who helped us.
Or remembering the promises of Scripture.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Gratitude doesn't require a perfect journey. It invites us to recognize God's goodness along the way.
JOY IN ORDINARY MOMENTS Now, let's talk about something we've discussed throughout this week.
The little things.
Sometimes we're so focused on reaching the next milestone that we overlook meaningful moments already happening around us.
We wait for the weekend.
The vacation.
The promotion.
Or the next celebration.
But ordinary life continues happening.
And sometimes those ordinary moments become the ones we remember most.
A conversation around the table.
A child's laughter.
A beautiful sunrise.
A song that encourages us.
Or a quiet moment of prayer.
Now, those things may seem small.
But they can be meaningful.
And they can become opportunities to recognize God's goodness.
Now, let's read James chapter 1, verse 17. "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning."
Now, James reminds us of God's goodness and unchanging character.
And as we recognize the good gifts in our lives, we can respond with sincere gratitude.
WHEN JOY AND GRIEF WALK TOGETHER Now, I want to talk about something important.
Because not everyone listening today is experiencing a joyful season.
Some people are grieving.
Some are facing disappointment.
Some are dealing with illness.
And some are carrying burdens that other people cannot see.
Now, I don't want anyone to feel pressured to pretend everything is fine.
Grief is real.
Disappointment is real.
And difficult emotions are part of the human experience.
Now, remember what we studied earlier this week.
Jesus wept.
And Paul described himself as sorrowful, yet rejoicing.
Now, those passages remind us that sorrow and Christian hope can exist together.
You can grieve.
And still trust God.
You can miss someone.
And still experience meaningful moments.
You can cry.
And still remain rooted in the hope of Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to hide your pain to carry Christian hope into tomorrow.
And if you're struggling, it's okay to seek support.
Sometimes that means talking with someone you trust.
A pastor.
A support group.
Or a qualified mental health professional.
Those steps can be meaningful parts of caring for yourself.
PAUSE AND PRAY — JOY FOR THE JOURNEY Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about the season you're in right now.
Maybe it's a season of celebration.
Maybe it's a season of waiting.
Maybe it's a season of grief.
Or maybe it's a season of change.
Now, take a moment to acknowledge that honestly. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, You know the season each of us is walking through. You know the circumstances we're facing. The emotions we're experiencing. And the questions we're carrying. Lord, help us remember that our hope is rooted in Jesus Christ. Teach us to practice gratitude without denying our pain. Help us recognize meaningful moments. And give us wisdom for the decisions before us. Father, help us continue walking faithfully. One day at a time. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
PHILIPPIANS 4 — REJOICE IN THE LORD Now, let's turn to Philippians chapter 4.
We're going to read verses 4 through 7. The King James Version says: "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand. Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus."
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul connects rejoicing with prayer.
And he connects prayer with thanksgiving.
Now, that's meaningful.
Because sometimes we think we need to feel joyful before we can pray.
But Scripture encourages us to bring our concerns before God.
We can pray when we're thankful.
We can pray when we're discouraged.
We can pray when we're grieving.
And we can pray when we're uncertain.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Prayer isn't reserved for the moments when everything feels peaceful. It's part of our relationship with God through every season.
THE JOY OF SERVING OTHERS Now, let's talk about something else we've learned this week.
The joy of giving.
Remember the words of Jesus recorded in Acts chapter 20, verse 35. "It is more blessed to give than to receive."
Now, serving others can become a meaningful expression of our faith.
Sometimes it looks like preparing a meal.
Sometimes it looks like helping a neighbor.
Sometimes it looks like encouraging someone.
And sometimes it looks like simply listening.
Now, here's something important. Serving others doesn't mean ignoring our own needs.
And it doesn't mean giving beyond our ability.
But we can remain attentive to opportunities for kindness.
We can serve with wisdom.
With compassion.
And with a sincere desire to reflect the love of Christ.
Now, sometimes a simple act of kindness becomes a meaningful encouragement to someone else.
And that's worth remembering.
JOHN 15 — JOY THAT REMAINS Now, let's turn to John chapter 15.
We're going to read verses 9 through 11. The King James Version says: "As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you: continue ye in my love. If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love; even as I have kept my Father's commandments, and abide in his love. These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "That my joy might remain in you..."
Now, Jesus connects joy with remaining in His love.
And that's the foundation of everything we've studied this week.
Our deepest joy isn't simply about having good circumstances.
It's about our relationship with Jesus Christ.
Now, that relationship doesn't eliminate every hardship.
But it gives us a foundation of hope.
And it reminds us that our lives are connected to the saving work of our Savior.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... What has Week Nine taught me about biblical joy?
Maybe you've learned that joy is deeper than happiness.
Maybe you've learned that gratitude doesn't require pretending.
Or maybe you've learned that grief and joy can exist together. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... What is one truth from Scripture I want to carry into the next season of my life?
Maybe it's Romans 15:13.
Maybe it's Psalm 16:11.
Or maybe it's another passage we've studied. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... What is one practical way I can continue practicing gratitude and recognizing God's goodness?
Maybe it's keeping a journal.
Maybe it's spending time in prayer.
Or maybe it's intentionally appreciating ordinary moments. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... How can I share the hope and love of Jesus Christ with someone else?
Maybe it's offering encouragement.
Maybe it's helping someone.
Or maybe it's simply listening with compassion. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — OUR JOY IS ROOTED IN JESUS Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because He's the foundation of our hope.
Jesus lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, that's the foundation of Christian joy.
Not perfect circumstances.
Not constant happiness.
And not a life without sorrow.
But the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn God's love by feeling joyful enough.
We don't earn salvation by practicing gratitude perfectly.
And we don't have to prove our worth through constant service.
Our salvation rests in God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And our gratitude, joy, and service grow out of that relationship.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. You don't have to know what the next season holds to carry the hope of Jesus Christ into it. His goodness is not measured by the ease of your circumstances, and His promises remain true through every season.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we think we need all the answers before we can move forward.
But we can continue walking faithfully.
We can seek wisdom.
We can make thoughtful decisions.
And we can remain rooted in the hope we have through Jesus Christ.
LIVING IT OUT — MY JOY FOR THE JOURNEY PLAN Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... My Joy for the Journey Plan.
Now, beneath that heading, write down four things.
First... One Scripture that gives you hope.
Second... One meaningful thing you're grateful for.
Third... One challenge you want to bring before God in prayer.
And fourth... One opportunity to encourage or serve someone else.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Thank God for His goodness.
Bring your concerns before Him.
And ask Him to help you continue walking faithfully.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, one truth from Your Word I want to carry into the next season is...
Our second prompt is... One area where I need to remember Your faithfulness is...
And our third prompt is... Help me practice joy, gratitude, and compassion by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. My joy is rooted in Jesus Christ. I will continue seeking Him, practicing gratitude, and walking faithfully through every season.
Now, say that again. My joy is rooted in Jesus Christ. I will continue seeking Him, practicing gratitude, and walking faithfully through every season.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize Romans chapter 15, verse 13. "Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost."
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about one practical way you can carry the truths we've studied this week into your everyday life.
Maybe it's spending time in prayer.
Maybe it's keeping a gratitude journal.
Maybe it's offering encouragement.
Or maybe it's simply remembering the hope you have through Jesus Christ.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHAT WILL YOU CARRY FORWARD? Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire one more time.
The evening is quiet.
The fire is still burning.
And we're reflecting on everything we've learned.
Now, I want to ask you something. What will you carry forward from this week?
Maybe it's the reminder that joy isn't the same as happiness.
Maybe it's the understanding that gratitude doesn't require pretending.
Maybe it's the reminder that grief and joy can exist together.
Or maybe it's the encouragement to serve others with compassion. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to think about another question. What is one thing you want to do differently because of what you've learned?
Maybe you'll spend more time in prayer.
Maybe you'll become more intentional about expressing gratitude.
Maybe you'll reach out to someone who's grieving.
Or maybe you'll simply slow down long enough to appreciate an ordinary moment. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's something I want you to remember. Spiritual growth often happens through faithful, everyday choices.
We open our Bibles.
We pray.
We seek wisdom.
And we respond to opportunities to love others.
One day at a time.
CLOSING REFLECTION — KEEP WALKING WITH JOY Now, before we close Week Nine, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Maybe this week has been wonderful.
Maybe you've experienced meaningful moments.
Answered prayers.
And opportunities to celebrate.
Or maybe this week has been difficult.
Maybe you've experienced disappointment.
Grief.
Or uncertainty.
Now, whatever kind of week you've had, I want you to remember something.
Your relationship with Jesus Christ isn't measured by how happy you've felt.
And your faith isn't measured by whether you've cried.
You can bring your whole heart before the Lord.
Your gratitude.
Your questions.
Your joy.
And your sorrow.
Now, remember the words of Romans chapter 15, verse 13.
"Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing..."
Now, that's a beautiful prayer for the journey.
That we would continue trusting God.
That we would remain rooted in the hope of Jesus Christ.
And that we would allow His Word to shape the way we live.
Now, I can't promise that every season will be easy.
I can't promise that every prayer will be answered the way we hope.
And I can't promise that we won't experience sorrow.
But I can remind you of the hope we have through Jesus Christ.
And I can encourage you to keep seeking Him.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep praying.
Keep showing compassion.
And keep walking faithfully.
Because our deepest joy isn't found in having a perfect journey.
It's found in the Savior who gives us hope for the journey.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us through another week of Walking Through the Word. Thank You for everything we've learned about joy. Lord, help us remember that our deepest hope is found in Jesus Christ. Teach us to practice gratitude without denying our pain. Help us appreciate ordinary moments. Give us compassion for those who are grieving. And help us serve others with love and wisdom. Father, You know the season each person listening is experiencing. You know the challenges they're facing. The questions they're carrying. And the hopes they have for the future. Lord, give them wisdom for the decisions before them. Encourage those who are discouraged. Comfort those who are grieving. And help those who are overwhelmed find meaningful support. Father, may Your Word continue shaping our lives. Help us remain faithful through changing circumstances. And remind us of the hope we have through Jesus Christ. Thank You for His sacrifice. His resurrection. And the promise of eternal life through Him. May our lives reflect Your love. And may we continue walking with You through every season. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — WEEK NINE COMPLETE Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Nine!
And what a meaningful week it's been.
We've studied joy. Gratitude. Ordinary blessings. Grief. Generosity. And the hope we have through Jesus Christ.
Now, as we move forward, I want you to carry those truths with you.
Because our journey through God's Word continues.
And next week, we're beginning something special.
We're entering Week Ten. And our new study is called... The Greatest Gift — Preparing Our Hearts for Christmas.
Over the next seven days, we'll begin looking at the promises of God, the coming of Jesus Christ, and the meaning of His birth.
We'll explore how the Christmas story points us toward God's love, His faithfulness, and the hope of salvation.
And we'll prepare our hearts to celebrate the greatest gift of all. Jesus Christ.
Until then, remember... Your joy doesn't have to depend on perfect circumstances.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you next week!

weeks.title: The Greatest Gift — Preparing Our Hearts for Christmas

lessons.title: The Greatest Gift: God's Promise of a Savior
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — CHRISTMAS BEGAN WITH A PROMISE Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Ten, Day One. And we're beginning a brand-new study together.
For the next seven days, we're going to prepare our hearts for Christmas.
Now, I know that when we think about Christmas, there are probably several things that come to mind.
Maybe it's decorating the Christmas tree.
Hanging lights.
Wrapping presents.
Baking cookies.
Or gathering with family and friends.
And those can be beautiful traditions.
But today, I want us to look beyond the decorations. Beyond the presents. And beyond the busy schedules.
Because Christmas is about something far greater.
It's about the coming of Jesus Christ.
The Savior of the world.
Now, here's something I want you to think about. The Christmas story didn't begin in Bethlehem.
It didn't begin with Mary and Joseph traveling to be counted in the census.
And it didn't begin when the shepherds heard the angels announcing the birth of Jesus.
The story of God's plan of redemption reaches much farther back.
Throughout the Old Testament, we find promises and expectations pointing toward the coming of the Messiah.
And when we turn to the New Testament, we see how Jesus Christ fulfills God's saving purposes.
Now, I want you to imagine something. Imagine living in a time when God's people were waiting for the promised Messiah.
Generations came and went.
People experienced hardship.
Nations rose and fell.
And still, the hope of God's promise remained.
Now, sometimes we struggle to wait a few days for an answer.
Sometimes we become discouraged when our plans don't unfold according to our preferred timeline.
But the coming of Jesus reminds us that God's redemptive plan unfolded across generations.
And His promises were not forgotten.
Now, today, we're going to explore one of the most beautiful passages in the Old Testament.
A passage that Christians have long understood as pointing toward Jesus Christ.
Our lesson today is called... The Greatest Gift — God's Promise of a Savior.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for allowing us to begin this special Christmas study. Lord, during this season, our schedules can become busy. Our attention can become divided. And sometimes we become so focused on preparations that we forget to reflect on the meaning of Christ's coming. Father, help us slow down. Help us open our hearts to Your Word. Teach us about the promises of Scripture. And help us understand how those promises point us toward Jesus Christ. Lord, for those who are celebrating this season, help them celebrate with gratitude. For those who are grieving, provide comfort. And for those who are struggling, help them find meaningful support and encouragement. May this study draw us closer to our Savior. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — ISAIAH 9:6–7 Now, let's turn to Isaiah chapter 9.
We're going to read verses 6 and 7. But before we read them, let's understand the setting.
The prophet Isaiah ministered during a time of political uncertainty and spiritual struggle in Judah.
The people faced threats from powerful nations.
And throughout Isaiah's message, we find warnings about judgment alongside promises of hope and restoration.
In Isaiah chapter 9, the prophet describes light coming to people who have experienced darkness.
And he announces the birth of a child associated with righteous rule and lasting peace.
Christians understand this passage as pointing ultimately toward Jesus Christ, the promised Messiah.
Now, let's read Isaiah chapter 9, verses 6 and 7, from the King James Version. "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order it, and to establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will perform this."
Now, I want you to hear those first words again. "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given..."
Now, isn't that beautiful?
A child is born.
A son is given.
And through this promised ruler, Isaiah speaks of justice, righteousness, and peace.
Now, when we read this passage as Christians, we see its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The One who came into the world as a child.
The One who revealed God's love.
And the One whose kingdom will never end.
Now, here's something I want us to remember. Christmas isn't simply about the birth of a baby.
It's about the arrival of the promised Savior.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH The greatest gift of Christmas is Jesus Christ, the promised Savior through whom God brings salvation and lasting hope.
Now, I want you to carry that truth with you throughout this week.
Because when we understand who Jesus is, the Christmas story becomes much more than a familiar tradition.
It becomes a reminder of God's faithfulness.
His love.
And His plan of redemption.
THE PROMISE BEGAN LONG BEFORE BETHLEHEM Now, let's go all the way back to the beginning of the Bible.
To Genesis chapter 3.
In this chapter, Adam and Eve have disobeyed God.
Sin has entered the human story.
And the consequences of that disobedience are being revealed.
But even in this difficult passage, Christians have long recognized an early indication of God's redemptive plan.
Let's read Genesis chapter 3, verse 15. "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel."
Now, this verse is spoken as part of God's judgment upon the serpent.
And in Christian theology, it has often been understood as an early foreshadowing of Christ's victory over evil.
Now, I want you to think about that. At the beginning of the biblical story, we see the devastating reality of sin.
But as Scripture unfolds, we also see God's plan to redeem.
Now, here's something important. The Bible doesn't present humanity as capable of saving itself through good intentions or religious effort.
Instead, the New Testament points us toward Jesus Christ as our Savior.
And that is why His coming matters so much.
ISAIAH 7 — IMMANUEL, GOD WITH US Now, let's turn to Isaiah chapter 7.
We're going to read verse 14. The King James Version says: "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."
Now, the original setting of this prophecy involves King Ahaz and a time of political crisis.
And when we turn to Matthew's Gospel, we find that Matthew connects this passage with the birth of Jesus Christ.
The name Immanuel means... God with us.
Now, I want you to think about those words. God with us.
Not a distant God who has no concern for humanity.
But the God who entered human history through the incarnation of Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something important. When Christians say Jesus is Immanuel, we're speaking about who He is.
Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man.
And through His coming, we see God's saving purposes revealed.
Now, that's a truth worth celebrating.
THE NAMES OF THE PROMISED CHILD Now, let's return to Isaiah chapter 9.
Because I want us to spend a few minutes looking at the names and titles Isaiah gives to this promised ruler.
The first is... Wonderful Counsellor.
Now, that title points toward extraordinary wisdom.
And when we look at the life and teachings of Jesus, we see wisdom that challenges human assumptions.
He teaches about love.
Forgiveness.
Humility.
And the kingdom of God.
Now, sometimes we look for wisdom everywhere except Scripture.
We seek advice.
We listen to opinions.
And we try to figure everything out ourselves.
But Jesus invites His followers to learn from Him.
And His teachings continue shaping Christian life today.
The next title is... The Mighty God.
Now, this is a remarkable title.
And Christians understand it as pointing toward the divine identity of Jesus Christ.
He isn't merely a moral teacher.
And He isn't simply an inspiring historical figure.
He is the eternal Son of God who became flesh.
Now, the next title is... The Everlasting Father.
Now, I want to clarify something here.
Christians believe in one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
So this title doesn't mean that Jesus is the same person as God the Father.
Rather, in the context of Isaiah's royal prophecy, it describes the enduring, fatherly care associated with the promised ruler.
And finally... The Prince of Peace.
Now, I love that title.
Because we live in a world where peace can feel difficult to find.
There are conflicts.
Broken relationships.
Fear.
And uncertainty.
But Isaiah points toward a ruler whose reign is characterized by justice and peace.
And Christians understand that promise as finding its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something important. The peace Jesus brings doesn't mean believers will never experience hardship.
And it doesn't mean every conflict in the world has already disappeared.
But through Christ, we can be reconciled to God.
And we look forward to the full realization of His kingdom.
MICAH 5 — A PROMISE CONNECTED TO BETHLEHEM Now, let's turn to Micah chapter 5.
We're going to read verse 2. The King James Version says: "But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting."
Now, I want you to notice something. Bethlehem was not a great imperial capital.
It was a relatively small town.
Yet Micah speaks of a ruler coming from Bethlehem.
And in the New Testament, this prophecy is connected with the birth of Jesus.
Now, I think that's meaningful.
Because sometimes we assume that important things must happen in impressive places.
We think greatness must come with recognition.
Power.
Or public attention.
But the Christmas story challenges those assumptions.
Jesus was born in humble circumstances.
And His coming reveals God's purposes in ways the world might not have expected.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. God's work is not measured by the world's standards of importance.
And the Christmas story reminds us to look beyond outward appearances.
THE LONG WAIT FOR THE MESSIAH Now, let's talk about waiting.
Because between the promises of the Old Testament and the birth of Jesus, generations passed.
God's people experienced political upheaval.
Exile.
Foreign rule.
And changing circumstances.
And throughout those generations, the hope of God's promised deliverance remained significant.
Now, I want you to think about something. We often struggle with waiting.
We want answers.
We want clarity.
And we want to know what happens next.
Now, waiting can be difficult.
Especially when the circumstances are serious.
But the coming of Jesus reminds us that God's redemptive plan unfolded according to His purposes.
Now, here's something important. That doesn't mean every personal desire we have is a promise from God.
And it doesn't mean every situation will unfold the way we hope.
But we can trust the promises God has actually given us in Scripture.
And the coming of Jesus Christ is central to those promises.
GALATIANS 4 — THE FULNESS OF TIME Now, let's turn to Galatians chapter 4.
We're going to read verses 4 and 5. The King James Version says: "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons."
Now, I want you to hear those first words again. "But when the fulness of the time was come..."
Now, that's a beautiful phrase.
Paul is explaining how God sent His Son to accomplish redemption.
And he connects Christ's coming with the fulfillment of God's saving plan.
Now, I want you to think about that. Jesus didn't simply appear as an unexpected figure disconnected from the rest of Scripture.
His coming belongs to the unfolding story of God's redemption.
And that's why studying the Old Testament promises helps us understand the significance of Christmas.
PAUSE AND PRAY — THANK YOU FOR THE PROMISE Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about the promises we've studied today.
Isaiah's prophecy.
The promise connected to Bethlehem.
And Paul's words about the fullness of time.
Now, take a moment to reflect on what those passages reveal about God's faithfulness. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for the promises of Your Word. Thank You for the coming of Jesus Christ. Lord, help us understand the significance of His birth. Help us remember that Christmas is about more than traditions and celebrations. It's about Your saving love revealed through our Savior. Father, teach us to trust the promises You've given us in Scripture. Give us wisdom when we're uncertain. And help us continue walking faithfully. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
LUKE 1 — THE ANGEL'S ANNOUNCEMENT Now, let's turn to Luke chapter 1.
We're going to read verses 26 through 33.
This is where we begin seeing the announcement of Jesus' coming in the New Testament.
Let's read. "And in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee, named Nazareth, To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary. And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women. And when she saw him, she was troubled at his saying, and cast in her mind what manner of salutation this should be. And the angel said unto her, Fear not, Mary: for thou hast found favour with God. And, behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS. He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David: And he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end."
Now, I want you to notice something. Gabriel connects Jesus with the throne of David.
And with a kingdom that will never end.
Now, remember what we read in Isaiah chapter 9.
Isaiah spoke about a ruler associated with David's throne.
And a kingdom characterized by lasting peace and justice.
Now, when we read Luke's Gospel, we see how the announcement of Jesus' birth connects with those earlier promises.
And that's something worth celebrating.
Because Christmas is not an isolated story.
It's part of the larger biblical account of God's redemption.
MARY'S RESPONSE — TRUSTING GOD WITHOUT KNOWING EVERYTHING Now, I want us to think about Mary for a moment.
Imagine receiving such an extraordinary announcement.
Mary was troubled by Gabriel's greeting.
And later in the passage, she asks how the announced birth will happen.
Now, I think that's important.
Because Mary wasn't given a detailed explanation of every challenge she would face.
She didn't know every event that would unfold.
But she responded to God's message with humility and willingness.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Faith doesn't always mean having every answer.
But it does involve responding to what God has revealed.
And for us today, that means continuing to seek His wisdom through Scripture.
Now, we should be careful not to assume that every unexpected circumstance is a special message from God.
But we can learn from Mary's willingness to respond faithfully to God's revealed word.
MATTHEW 1 — WHY HIS NAME IS JESUS Now, let's turn to Matthew chapter 1.
We're going to read verses 21 through 23. The King James Version says: "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins. Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."
Now, I want you to focus on those words. "For he shall save his people from their sins."
Now, that tells us something essential about why Jesus came.
He came to save.
Not merely to provide an inspiring example.
Not simply to teach good morals.
But to accomplish salvation.
Now, that's the heart of the Christmas message.
The baby born in Bethlehem is the Savior who would die for our sins and rise again.
And through Him, we have the hope of forgiveness and eternal life.
JOHN 3 — THE GREATEST GIFT Now, let's turn to John chapter 3.
We're going to read verses 16 and 17. The King James Version says: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved."
Now, I want you to hear those first words again. "For God so loved the world, that he gave..."
Now, isn't that beautiful?
God's love is expressed through the giving of His Son.
And that's why we call Jesus the greatest gift.
Now, when we think about Christmas gifts, we often think about things wrapped in paper.
Things placed beneath a tree.
Things we give to the people we love.
And there's nothing wrong with those traditions.
But the greatest gift of Christmas cannot be purchased in a store.
It isn't something we can earn through good behavior.
And it isn't something we can deserve through religious effort.
Salvation is God's gracious gift through Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The greatest gift of Christmas isn't something we place beneath a tree. It's the Savior who came into the world to redeem us.
WHEN CHRISTMAS IS DIFFICULT Now, I want to talk about something important.
Because not everyone experiences Christmas as a joyful season.
For some people, Christmas brings excitement.
Family gatherings.
Celebrations.
And meaningful traditions.
But for others, Christmas can be difficult.
Maybe someone they love is no longer here.
Maybe they're facing financial hardship.
Maybe their family relationships are strained.
Or maybe they're simply feeling lonely.
Now, if that's where you are this Christmas season, I want you to hear something. You don't have to pretend that everything is wonderful.
And you don't have to feel guilty if the holidays are difficult.
The meaning of Christmas doesn't depend on having a perfect celebration.
It doesn't depend on expensive gifts.
And it doesn't depend on having every tradition go according to plan.
The meaning of Christmas is rooted in Jesus Christ.
And the hope of the gospel remains meaningful even during difficult seasons.
Now, if you're grieving, it's okay to grieve.
If you're struggling, it's okay to seek support.
And if your Christmas looks different this year, that doesn't make it less meaningful.
You can remember Christ's coming in simple ways.
Through Scripture.
Prayer.
Worship.
And acts of kindness.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... When I think about Christmas, what usually receives most of my attention?
Maybe it's decorating.
Shopping.
Planning.
Or spending time with family.
Now, think about how you can make room to reflect on Jesus Christ. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... What does God's promise of a Savior reveal about His character?
Think about His faithfulness.
His love.
And His saving purposes. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... What part of the Christmas story gives me the greatest hope?
Maybe it's the announcement to Mary.
Maybe it's the promise of Immanuel.
Or maybe it's the reminder that Jesus came to save His people from their sins. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... How can I prepare my heart to celebrate Jesus this Christmas?
Maybe it's spending more time in Scripture.
Maybe it's making time for prayer.
Maybe it's serving someone.
Or maybe it's simplifying part of your holiday schedule. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — FROM THE MANGER TO THE CROSS Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because the Christmas story doesn't end at the manger.
The baby born in Bethlehem grew up.
He lived a sinless life.
He taught about the kingdom of God.
He demonstrated compassion.
And ultimately, He died on the cross for our sins.
But the story doesn't end at the cross, either.
Jesus rose again.
And through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, that's the heart of the gospel.
And it's why the coming of Jesus Christ matters so much.
Christmas points us toward the Savior.
And the Savior points us toward God's gracious gift of salvation.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn that gift by being good enough.
We don't earn it through perfect religious performance.
And we don't earn it by having a perfect Christmas celebration.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And that's the greatest gift of all.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. Before there was a manger in Bethlehem, God had already revealed His promise of redemption. Christmas reminds us that Jesus Christ is the promised Savior and the greatest gift of God's love.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we become so busy preparing for Christmas that we forget what we're celebrating.
We're celebrating the coming of Jesus Christ.
The Savior of the world.
LIVING IT OUT — PREPARING MY HEART FOR CHRISTMAS Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... Preparing My Heart for Christmas.
Now, beneath that heading, write down four things.
First... One truth about Jesus Christ that gives you hope.
Second... One Christmas tradition that helps you remember Him.
Third... One distraction you may need to manage during this season.
And fourth... One meaningful way you can share Christ's love with someone else.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Thank God for sending Jesus Christ.
Ask Him to help you remain focused on the meaning of Christmas.
And seek His wisdom for the season ahead.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, the promise of Jesus Christ reminds me that...
Our second prompt is... One area where I need to remember Your faithfulness is...
And our third prompt is... Help me prepare my heart for Christmas by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. Jesus Christ is the promised Savior and the greatest gift of God's love. I will prepare my heart to celebrate His coming with gratitude and faith.
Now, say that again. Jesus Christ is the promised Savior and the greatest gift of God's love. I will prepare my heart to celebrate His coming with gratitude and faith.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize Isaiah chapter 9, verse 6. "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace."
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about what they reveal about Jesus Christ.
Maybe you'll spend time reflecting on His wisdom.
His divine identity.
His care.
Or His promise of peace.
And ask God to help you keep Christ at the center of this Christmas season.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHAT DOES CHRISTMAS MEAN TO YOU? Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
The evening is quiet.
The fire is burning.
And maybe somewhere nearby, there are Christmas lights shining.
Now, I want to ask you something. What does Christmas mean to you?
Maybe it brings back childhood memories.
Maybe it reminds you of family traditions.
Maybe it brings excitement.
Or maybe it brings a mixture of joy and sadness. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. When you think about the birth of Jesus Christ, what part of the story speaks most deeply to your heart?
Maybe it's the humility of His birth.
Maybe it's the announcement of the angels.
Maybe it's the promise of Immanuel.
Or maybe it's the reminder that Jesus came to save us from our sins. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to think about something. Christmas can be celebrated in many different ways.
Some families have elaborate traditions.
Others keep things simple.
And some people may be facing circumstances that make celebration difficult.
But the meaning of Christmas remains centered on Jesus Christ.
And that's something we can remember wherever we are.
CLOSING REFLECTION — THE GIFT THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Every Christmas, people spend time choosing gifts.
We think about what someone might like.
We try to find something meaningful.
And we look forward to seeing their reaction.
Now, giving gifts can be a beautiful expression of love.
But I want you to remember something. The greatest gift of Christmas wasn't wrapped in colorful paper.
It wasn't placed beneath a decorated tree.
And it wasn't purchased with money.
The greatest gift was Jesus Christ.
The promised Savior.
The Son of God.
The One who came into the world to accomplish our salvation.
Now, think about the promises we've studied today.
Isaiah spoke of a child who would be born.
Micah spoke of a ruler connected to Bethlehem.
Gabriel announced that Mary would give birth to Jesus.
And Matthew reminds us that His name means He would save His people from their sins.
Now, those passages help us understand the significance of Christ's coming.
And they remind us that Christmas belongs to the larger story of God's redemption.
So today, I want to encourage you.
As you prepare for Christmas... Make room for Jesus.
Make room for Scripture.
Make room for prayer.
And make room to reflect on the gift of salvation.
Because when the decorations are taken down... When the presents have been opened... And when the celebrations are over...
The hope we have through Jesus Christ remains.
And that's the greatest gift of all.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for allowing us to begin this Christmas study. Lord, thank You for the promises of Scripture. Thank You for revealing Your saving purposes throughout the biblical story. And thank You for sending Jesus Christ. Father, help us remember the true meaning of Christmas. When our schedules become busy, help us make time for Your Word. When we become distracted, help us refocus on our Savior. And when we're facing difficult circumstances, remind us of the hope we have through Him. Lord, I pray for the person who's grieving this Christmas season. Surround them with compassion and care. I pray for the person who's struggling financially. Help them find practical support and encouragement. I pray for the person who's feeling lonely. Help them experience meaningful connection. And I pray for families gathering together. Help them show kindness, patience, and love. Father, may this Christmas season draw us closer to Jesus Christ. Thank You for His birth. His sinless life. His sacrifice on the cross. And His resurrection. Thank You for the promise of forgiveness and eternal life through Him. May our hearts remain rooted in the greatest gift of all. Jesus Christ, our Savior. In His precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY TWO Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Ten, Day One!
And what a beautiful way to begin our Christmas study.
Today, we learned that Christmas is about more than traditions and celebrations.
It's about the promised Savior. Jesus Christ.
Tomorrow, we're continuing our study called The Greatest Gift — Preparing Our Hearts for Christmas. And our next lesson is... The Light in the Darkness — Why the World Needed a Savior.
We'll explore what Scripture teaches about sin, spiritual darkness, and the hope that comes through Jesus Christ.
Until then, remember... The greatest gift of Christmas isn't something we can buy.
It's the Savior who came into the world to redeem us.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: The Light in the Darkness: Why the World Needed a Savior
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — A LIGHT THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Ten, Day Two. And we're continuing our Christmas study called... The Greatest Gift — Preparing Our Hearts for Christmas. Yesterday, we went back into the Old Testament and explored God's promise of a Savior. We studied Isaiah's prophecy. We talked about Bethlehem. And we learned how the coming of Jesus Christ fulfills God's redemptive purposes.
But today, I want us to talk about something that makes the Christmas story even more meaningful. Why did the world need a Savior in the first place?
Now, I want you to imagine something with me. Imagine you're standing in a room. It's completely dark. There are no windows. No lamps. And no light coming through the doorway.
You can reach out your hands, but you can't see what's around you. You know there are things in the room. But you can't clearly make out where they are.
Now, imagine someone opens the door. And suddenly, light begins pouring into the room.
You can see where you're standing. You can see the things around you. And you can begin to understand what was hidden in the darkness.
Now, light changes what we can see. It reveals what was previously hidden.
And throughout Scripture, light is often used to communicate truth, holiness, revelation, and salvation.
Now, here's something important. When the Bible describes spiritual darkness, it isn't talking about ordinary nighttime.
And it isn't saying that people who are grieving, depressed, or struggling emotionally are somehow spiritually inferior.
It's describing the reality of sin, separation from God, and humanity's need for His saving grace.
Now, that's why today's lesson matters. Because Christmas isn't simply the story of a beautiful baby being born.
It's the story of the eternal Son of God entering the world.
The Light coming into the darkness.
The Savior coming to redeem sinners.
And the hope of salvation being revealed through Jesus Christ.
Our lesson today is called... The Light in the Darkness — Why the World Needed a Savior. Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for the opportunity to continue learning about the coming of Jesus Christ. Lord, today we're studying what Scripture teaches about sin, salvation, and the light of Christ. Help us approach these truths with humility. Give us understanding as we read. Help us recognize our need for Your grace. And remind us of the hope we have through Jesus Christ. Father, may this Christmas season become an opportunity for us to grow in our faith. And may everything we learn draw us closer to our Savior. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — JOHN 1:1–5 Now, let's turn to the Gospel of John. Chapter 1.
Now, when we think about the Christmas story, we often turn to Matthew or Luke. We think about Mary and Joseph. The manger. The shepherds. And the angels.
But John begins his Gospel differently. He doesn't begin with a description of Bethlehem. He begins by telling us who Jesus is.
Let's read John chapter 1, verses 1 through 5, from the King James Version. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life; and the life was the light of men. And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not."
Now, I want you to hear that final verse again. "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not."
Now, that's a powerful statement. But let's look carefully at what John is teaching. He begins with the words... "In the beginning."
Now, those words remind us of Genesis chapter 1. The beginning of creation.
But John is telling us something extraordinary about Jesus. The Word already existed in the beginning. The Word was with God. And the Word was God.
Now, Christians understand the Word to be Jesus Christ. The eternal Son of God.
And John tells us that all things were made through Him.
Now, think about that. The One who came into the world as a baby is the eternal Son through whom all things were created.
Christmas isn't the beginning of Jesus' existence. It's the celebration of His coming into the world as a human being.
And that's what we call the incarnation.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH Jesus Christ came into a world affected by sin and spiritual darkness to reveal God's truth and accomplish the salvation we could never earn for ourselves.
Now, I want you to remember that. Because sometimes we think of Christmas only in terms of what happened in Bethlehem.
But to understand the significance of Christ's birth, we also need to understand why He came.
JOHN 1 — THE WORD BECAME FLESH Now, let's continue in John chapter 1. We're going to read verses 9 through 14.
"That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not. He came unto his own, and his own received him not. But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name: Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."
Now, I want you to focus on verse 14. "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us..."
Now, that's the heart of the incarnation. The eternal Son of God became truly human.
Jesus wasn't merely appearing to be human. He entered human history. He experienced hunger. He experienced tiredness. He experienced sorrow. And He lived among people in a world affected by sin.
Yet Scripture teaches that Jesus Himself was without sin.
Now, I want you to think about something. God didn't send humanity a message from a distance and leave us to save ourselves.
He sent His Son.
And through Jesus Christ, God's saving grace is revealed.
Now, that's why Christmas matters.
ISAIAH 9 — PEOPLE WALKING IN DARKNESS Now, let's go back to Isaiah chapter 9.
Yesterday, we studied verses 6 and 7. But today, I want us to look at verse 2. The King James Version says: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined."
Now, remember the setting. Isaiah was speaking to people living through serious national and spiritual difficulties.
There was fear. There was uncertainty. And there were threats from surrounding nations.
But Isaiah announced hope. A great light.
And when Matthew describes the beginning of Jesus' ministry, he connects this prophecy with Christ.
Now, here's something important. The darkness described in Scripture isn't simply a difficult mood or an unpleasant season.
It includes the spiritual condition of humanity and the need for God's saving intervention.
And the coming of Jesus reveals the hope of salvation.
Now, I want you to remember something. The Christmas story is a story of hope because the Savior came into a world that needed redemption.
WHY DID HUMANITY NEED A SAVIOR? Now, let's talk about something that isn't always easy to discuss. Sin.
Because if we don't understand the problem of sin, we won't fully understand why the coming of Jesus is such good news.
Now, when we hear the word sin, we sometimes think only about particularly serious wrongdoing.
But Scripture describes sin more broadly.
It includes our failure to live according to God's holy character and commands.
Our thoughts. Our words. Our actions. And our hearts.
Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 3. We're going to read verse 23. The King James Version says: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;"
Now, I want you to notice one word. All.
Not just certain people. Not just people whose mistakes are public. And not just people whose lives look different from ours.
All have sinned.
Now, that's important. Because the gospel doesn't invite us to look down on other people.
It calls us to recognize our own need for God's grace.
Now, sometimes we compare ourselves with others.
We say... "Well, at least I've never done what they did."
Or... "I'm not as bad as that person."
But the standard of God's holiness isn't based on comparing ourselves with other human beings.
Scripture reminds us that every one of us needs salvation.
And that's why Jesus came.
ROMANS 6 — THE GIFT OF ETERNAL LIFE Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 6. We're going to read verse 23. The King James Version says: "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord."
Now, let's look at both parts of that verse.
First... "The wages of sin is death."
Sin has serious consequences.
It isn't something Scripture treats lightly.
But then Paul says... "But the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord."
Now, isn't that beautiful?
The verse moves from the consequence of sin to the gift of God.
And that gift is eternal life through Jesus Christ.
Now, notice something. Paul doesn't say eternal life is a reward we purchase.
He doesn't say it's something we earn by being better than someone else.
He calls it a gift.
And that's why the Christmas story is so meaningful.
Because the One born in Bethlehem came to accomplish the salvation we could never earn for ourselves.
WHEN WE TRY TO SAVE OURSELVES Now, let's talk about something I think many of us can relate to.
Sometimes we try to fix everything ourselves.
We think that if we work hard enough, we'll become good enough.
If we make enough improvements, we'll finally deserve God's approval.
Or if we do enough good things, maybe they'll outweigh the wrong things we've done.
Now, good works matter.
Obedience matters.
And living faithfully matters.
But Scripture doesn't teach that we can earn salvation through our own efforts.
Let's turn to Ephesians chapter 2. We're going to read verses 8 through 10. The King James Version says: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them."
Now, I want you to notice the order.
We are saved by grace through faith.
Not by our own works.
And then, as people who belong to Christ, we're called to live in ways that reflect His grace.
Now, that's important. We don't do good works to purchase salvation.
We seek to do good because we've received God's grace.
And that changes the way we understand Christmas.
Because the greatest gift isn't something we earn.
It's something God has graciously provided through His Son.
JOHN 8 — JESUS, THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD Now, let's turn to John chapter 8. We're going to read verse 12. The King James Version says: "Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life."
Now, I want you to hear those words again. "I am the light of the world..."
Now, that's a remarkable statement. Jesus isn't simply saying that He can point people toward the light.
He identifies Himself as the Light of the World.
And He calls people to follow Him.
Now, I want you to think about what light does.
Light reveals.
It helps us see clearly.
And it makes visible what darkness conceals.
Now, spiritually speaking, Jesus reveals God's truth.
He exposes sin.
He teaches us about the Father.
And He provides the way of salvation.
Now, here's something important. Following Jesus doesn't mean we'll never experience confusion or difficult circumstances.
And it doesn't mean we'll never need advice, guidance, or practical help.
But it does mean that our spiritual hope is rooted in Him.
WHEN THE CHRISTMAS LIGHTS COME ON Now, I want you to imagine something.
Maybe you've seen a neighborhood where people decorate their homes for Christmas.
During the day, the decorations are beautiful.
But when evening comes and the lights turn on, everything looks different.
The trees are glowing.
The houses are illuminated.
And suddenly, what was difficult to see becomes visible.
Now, I think that's a beautiful reminder of the language Scripture uses to describe Jesus.
But here's something I want us to remember. Christmas lights are temporary.
Eventually, they'll be taken down.
The decorations will be packed away.
And the holiday season will end.
But Jesus Christ is not a temporary source of hope.
His saving work isn't limited to one holiday.
And His truth doesn't disappear when Christmas is over.
Now, that's something worth celebrating.
1 JOHN — WALKING IN THE LIGHT Now, let's turn to 1 John chapter 1. We're going to read verses 5 through 9. The King James Version says: "This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. If we say that we have fellowship with him, and walk in darkness, we lie, and do not the truth: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Now, I want you to notice something. John connects walking in the light with honesty about sin.
He doesn't encourage believers to pretend they're perfect.
In fact, he warns against claiming to have no sin.
Instead, he encourages confession and points to the cleansing available through Jesus Christ.
Now, that's important. Because sometimes people think Christianity is about pretending to have everything together.
But the gospel calls us to acknowledge our need for grace.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Walking in the light doesn't mean pretending we're sinless. It means responding honestly to God's truth and trusting in the cleansing work of Jesus Christ.
PAUSE AND PRAY — LORD, HELP ME WALK IN YOUR LIGHT Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about what we've studied so far.
We've talked about Jesus as the Light of the World.
We've talked about humanity's need for salvation.
And we've talked about the grace of God.
Now, I want you to ask yourself something. Is there an area of my life where I need to respond more faithfully to God's Word?
Maybe it's an attitude.
Maybe it's a relationship.
Maybe it's a decision.
Or maybe it's something you've been avoiding. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for sending Jesus Christ. Thank You for the light of Your truth. Lord, help us recognize our need for Your grace. Give us humility to acknowledge our sins. And help us respond faithfully to Your Word. Father, teach us to walk in truth. Help us make wise decisions. And remind us that forgiveness and salvation are found through Jesus Christ. May our lives reflect His love. In His precious name, Amen.
LUKE 2 — GOOD TIDINGS OF GREAT JOY Now, let's turn to Luke chapter 2. We're going to read verses 8 through 11.
This is one of the most familiar passages in the Christmas story.
Let's read. "And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid. And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord."
Now, I want you to focus on those last words. "A Saviour, which is Christ the Lord."
Now, that's the announcement.
The Savior has been born.
The promised Messiah has come.
And the angel describes this as good news of great joy.
Now, I want you to think about that. The shepherds weren't simply being told that a baby had been born.
They were being told that the Savior had arrived.
And that's why the Christmas story is good news.
Because Jesus came to save.
WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO RECEIVE THE LIGHT? Now, let's talk about something personal.
Because it's one thing to know the Christmas story.
And it's another thing to understand what it means to trust Jesus Christ.
Now, maybe you've heard about Jesus your entire life.
Maybe you grew up attending church.
Maybe you've heard the Christmas story every December.
Or maybe you're learning about Him for the first time.
Now, I want you to understand something. Knowing facts about Jesus isn't the same as placing your faith in Him.
The gospel calls us to recognize our sin.
To turn to God.
And to trust in Jesus Christ as Savior and Lord.
Now, that isn't something we accomplish through perfect behavior.
It's a response of faith to God's grace.
And if you're listening today and have questions about following Jesus, I encourage you to continue reading the Gospels.
Talk with a trusted Christian pastor or mature believer.
And seek to understand what Scripture teaches about salvation.
Because the greatest gift of Christmas is not simply a story to admire.
It's the Savior we're called to trust.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... What does the title "Light of the World" teach me about Jesus Christ?
Think about His truth.
His holiness.
And His saving work. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... Why is it important to understand our need for salvation when we celebrate Christmas?
Think about what Scripture teaches concerning sin and grace. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... Is there an area of my life where I need to respond more faithfully to God's Word?
Maybe it's a decision.
A relationship.
An attitude.
Or a responsibility. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... How can I share the hope of Jesus Christ with someone this Christmas season?
Maybe it's through a conversation.
An invitation to church.
An act of kindness.
Or sharing a Scripture that has encouraged you. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — THE LIGHT CAME TO SAVE Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because He's the center of everything we've studied today.
The eternal Son of God became flesh.
He entered human history.
He lived a sinless life.
He taught God's truth.
And He died on the cross for our sins.
But the story doesn't end there.
Jesus rose again.
And through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, that's why the Christmas story matters.
The baby born in Bethlehem is the Savior who came to redeem us.
And His coming reveals the love and grace of God.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn salvation by being good enough.
We don't earn it by attending enough church services.
And we don't earn it by performing enough acts of kindness.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ.
And that's the greatest gift of all.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. The darkness of sin revealed humanity's need for a Savior, and Jesus Christ came as the Light of the World to reveal God's truth and accomplish our salvation.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because Christmas is about more than decorations and traditions.
It's about the coming of the Savior.
The Light of the World.
LIVING IT OUT — LET YOUR LIGHT POINT TO JESUS Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... Let Your Light Point to Jesus.
Now, beneath that heading, write down three things.
First... One truth about Jesus Christ that gives you hope.
Second... One area where you want to respond more faithfully to God's Word.
And third... One meaningful way you can share Christ's love with someone else.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Thank God for sending Jesus Christ.
Ask Him to help you live according to His Word.
And seek opportunities to share the hope of the gospel.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, knowing that Jesus is the Light of the World reminds me that...
Our second prompt is... One area where I need Your wisdom and truth is...
And our third prompt is... Help me reflect the love of Christ this Christmas by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. Jesus Christ is the Light of the World. Through Him, I have the hope of forgiveness, salvation, and eternal life.
Now, say that again. Jesus Christ is the Light of the World. Through Him, I have the hope of forgiveness, salvation, and eternal life.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize John chapter 8, verse 12. "Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life."
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about what it means to follow Jesus.
Maybe you'll spend time reading one of the Gospels.
Maybe you'll pray about a decision.
Or maybe you'll share a Scripture with someone who needs encouragement.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHAT DOES LIGHT MEAN TO YOU? Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
The evening is quiet.
And the fire is casting light into the darkness around us.
Now, I want you to think about something. What does light help us do?
It helps us see.
It reveals what's around us.
And it helps us recognize where we're going.
Now, spiritually speaking, Jesus reveals God's truth and provides the way of salvation.
So here's my question. What has studying Jesus Christ helped you understand more clearly?
Maybe it's God's love.
Maybe it's your need for grace.
Maybe it's the meaning of forgiveness.
Or maybe it's the hope of eternal life. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. How can you help someone else understand the hope of the gospel?
Maybe it's through a sincere conversation.
Maybe it's sharing Scripture.
Maybe it's inviting someone to study the Bible with you.
Or maybe it's simply living in a way that reflects the love of Christ. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to remember something. We don't have to pressure people.
And we don't have to pretend we have every answer.
We can share the truth of Scripture with humility.
And we can trust God with the results.
CLOSING REFLECTION — THE LIGHT HAS COME Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
When we think about Christmas, we often picture beautiful lights.
Lights on houses.
Lights on trees.
Lights shining through windows.
And those lights can make the season feel special.
But I want you to remember something. The greatest light of Christmas isn't something we hang on a tree.
It's Jesus Christ.
The Light of the World.
The eternal Son of God.
The Savior who came to redeem us.
Now, Scripture reminds us that all have sinned.
And that the wages of sin is death.
But it also reminds us that the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
Now, that's the hope of Christmas.
Not that humanity can save itself.
Not that we can become good enough through our own efforts.
But that God has provided salvation through His Son.
So today, I want to encourage you.
As you see Christmas lights this season... Remember Jesus.
As you hear familiar Christmas songs... Remember the Savior.
And as you prepare to celebrate His birth... Remember why He came.
He came to save.
He came to reveal God's truth.
And through Him, we have the hope of forgiveness and eternal life.
That's the greatest gift of all.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for reminding us why the world needed a Savior. Lord, we acknowledge that all have sinned and fallen short of Your glory. And we thank You for the gift of salvation through Jesus Christ. Father, thank You for sending Your Son into the world. Thank You for the light of His truth. His sinless life. His sacrifice on the cross. And His resurrection. Lord, help us walk faithfully according to Your Word. Give us humility to acknowledge our need for grace. Give us wisdom for the decisions before us. And help us reflect the love of Christ in the way we treat others. Father, I pray for the person who's struggling this Christmas season. Surround them with care and support. I pray for the person who's searching for answers about faith. Help them understand the truth of Your Word. And I pray for those who already know Jesus as Savior. Help us continue growing in our faith and sharing His love with others. Thank You for the greatest gift of all. Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior. In His precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY THREE Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Ten, Day Two!
And I hope today's lesson has reminded you why the coming of Jesus Christ is such good news.
The world needed a Savior.
And God sent His Son.
Tomorrow, we're continuing our Christmas study. And our next lesson is called... Mary's Yes — Trusting God When His Plans Surprise Us.
We'll explore the angel's announcement to Mary, her response of faith, and what we can learn about humility and obedience.
Until then, remember... Jesus Christ is the Light of the World.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: Mary's Yes: Trusting God When His Plans Surprise Us
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — WHEN LIFE DOESN'T FOLLOW THE PLAN Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Ten, Day Three. And we're continuing our Christmas study called... The Greatest Gift — Preparing Our Hearts for Christmas.
Yesterday, we talked about Jesus being the Light of the World. We studied why humanity needed a Savior. And we learned that the coming of Jesus Christ is good news because salvation is God's gracious gift.
But today, I want us to look at the Christmas story from a different perspective.
We're going to look at the experience of a young woman named Mary.
Now, I want to begin by asking you something. Have you ever had your life planned out?
Maybe you knew what you wanted to accomplish. Maybe you had a timeline. Maybe you had a particular picture of how your future would unfold.
And then something happened that you didn't expect.
Maybe you received news that changed your plans. Maybe an opportunity came along. Maybe a responsibility appeared that you hadn't anticipated. Or maybe you found yourself facing a decision you never imagined having to make.
Now, unexpected circumstances can bring many different emotions. Sometimes excitement. Sometimes uncertainty. Sometimes fear. And sometimes all of those emotions at once.
Now, I want you to think about Mary. She was betrothed to Joseph. She was living in Nazareth. And then the angel Gabriel appeared with an extraordinary announcement.
She would give birth to Jesus. The promised Messiah. The Son of the Highest.
Now, Mary didn't receive a detailed explanation of everything that would happen in the years ahead. She didn't know every challenge she would face. And she didn't know every sorrow she would eventually experience.
But she responded to God's message with humility and faith.
Now, here's something I want us to understand today. Mary's experience was unique.
We shouldn't assume that every surprising circumstance in our own lives is a special revelation from God.
But we can learn from the way Mary responded to God's clearly revealed message.
We can learn about humility. About faith. About asking sincere questions. And about responding faithfully to God's Word.
Our lesson today is called... Mary's Yes — Trusting God When His Plans Surprise Us.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for the opportunity to continue studying the coming of Jesus Christ.
