The evening is quiet.
Maybe the Christmas lights are glowing nearby.
And we're reflecting on everything we've studied today.
Now, I want to ask you something. When you think about your favorite Christmas memories, what do you remember most?
Maybe it's a particular gift.
Maybe it's a family gathering.
Maybe it's a tradition.
Or maybe it's simply being with someone you love. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. If you could simplify one part of Christmas this year, what would it be?
Maybe it's spending less money.
Maybe it's attending fewer events.
Maybe it's placing less pressure on yourself.
Or maybe it's making more room for meaningful moments. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to remember something. The most meaningful parts of Christmas aren't always the most expensive.
And they aren't always the most elaborate.
Sometimes the moments we remember most are the simplest.
A conversation.
A prayer.
A shared meal.
Or reading the Christmas story together.
CLOSING REFLECTION — THERE IS ROOM FOR JESUS Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
When Mary gave birth to Jesus, Luke tells us that she laid Him in a manger because there was no room in the lodging place.
Now, that was a detail about the circumstances of His birth.
But today, we've used it as an opportunity to reflect on our own priorities.
And I want you to think about something. Maybe your schedule is full.
Maybe your responsibilities are heavy.
Maybe you're preparing for Christmas while also managing difficult circumstances.
Or maybe you're simply exhausted.
Now, I want you to hear something. You don't have to create a perfect schedule to seek Jesus.
You don't have to have an elaborate devotional routine.
And you don't have to compare your spiritual life with someone else's.
You can begin with what you have.
A few minutes in Scripture.
A sincere prayer.
A moment of gratitude.
Or an opportunity to serve someone with love.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Making room for Jesus isn't about making your life look perfect. It's about allowing His Word and His love to shape the life you're living.
So this Christmas season...
Enjoy the traditions.
Celebrate with the people you love.
And appreciate the meaningful moments.
But don't forget the Savior.
The One whose birth we're celebrating.
Jesus Christ.
The greatest gift of all.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for reminding us of the importance of seeking You. Lord, You know how busy our lives can become. You know the responsibilities we carry. And You know the things that compete for our attention. Father, help us recognize what matters most. Give us wisdom to simplify where we can. Teach us to make meaningful time for Scripture and prayer. And help us honor You in our everyday responsibilities. Lord, I pray for the person who feels overwhelmed. Give them wisdom and support. I pray for the person who's facing a difficult Christmas season. Surround them with compassion and care. And I pray for the person who's placing pressure on themselves to create a perfect celebration. Help them remember that the meaning of Christmas is rooted in Jesus Christ. Father, thank You for sending Your Son. Thank You for His humble birth. His sinless life. His sacrifice on the cross. And His resurrection. Thank You for the hope of salvation through Him. May this Christmas season draw us closer to our Savior. And may our lives reflect His grace and love. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY SIX Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Ten, Day Five!
And I hope today's lesson has encouraged you to remember what matters most.
You don't have to create a perfect Christmas.
You don't have to do everything.
And you don't have to compare your celebrations with anyone else's.
You can make meaningful room for Jesus Christ in the middle of everyday life.
Tomorrow, we're continuing our Christmas study with our special Around the Fire reflection. And our next lesson is called... Around the Fire — Remembering the Greatest Gift in the Middle of the Christmas Rush.
We'll reflect on everything we've learned this week and consider how we can keep Christ at the center of our celebrations.
Until then, remember... The greatest gift of Christmas isn't found beneath a tree.
It's found in Jesus Christ.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: Around the Fire: Remembering the Greatest Gift in the Middle of the Christmas Rush
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — COME SIT AROUND THE FIRE Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles. And today, I want to invite you to do something a little different.
I want you to imagine we're sitting together around a warm fire.
Maybe it's a cool December evening.
The Christmas lights are glowing.
There's a warm cup of coffee or hot chocolate nearby.
And for just a little while, we don't have anywhere else we need to be.
No shopping lists. No wrapping paper. No schedules to rearrange. And no pressure to make everything perfect.
Just a quiet moment. You. Me. Our Bibles. And the opportunity to reflect on the goodness of God.
Now, if you've been walking through this study with me, you know we've covered a lot this week.
We began with God's promise of a Savior.
We learned that Jesus Christ is the Light of the World.
We studied Mary's response of faith.
We looked at Joseph's compassion and obedience.
And yesterday, we talked about making room for Jesus when life becomes too busy.
But today, I don't want us to rush into another lesson.
I want us to reflect.
Because sometimes we spend so much time learning that we forget to stop and consider how God's Word is shaping our hearts.
And that's what our Around the Fire episodes are all about.
A moment to slow down. To remember. To pray. And to carry what we've learned into everyday life.
Now, I want to ask you something. When you think about Christmas, what's the first thing that comes to mind?
Is it the decorations?
The presents?
The music?
Or maybe the people you love?
Now, those can all be meaningful parts of the season.
But today, I want us to remember the reason Christians celebrate Christmas.
Jesus Christ.
The promised Savior.
The greatest gift of all.
Our lesson today is called... Around the Fire — Remembering the Greatest Gift in the Middle of the Christmas Rush.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for this opportunity to slow down and reflect. Lord, You know how busy our lives can become. You know the responsibilities we carry. The expectations we place on ourselves. And the emotions we may experience during this season. Father, help us remember the true meaning of Christmas. Help us reflect on the coming of Jesus Christ. And remind us that our hope is found in Him. Lord, for those who are celebrating, help them celebrate with gratitude. For those who are grieving, provide comfort and support. And for those who are overwhelmed, give wisdom and encouragement. May today's time together draw us closer to our Savior. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — GOOD TIDINGS OF GREAT JOY Now, let's turn to Luke chapter 2. We're going to read verses 10 and 11.
The King James Version says: "And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord."
Now, I want you to hear those final words again. "For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord."
Now, isn't that beautiful?
The announcement wasn't simply that a baby had been born.
It was that the Savior had come.
The promised Messiah.
Christ the Lord.
And that's the reason the Christmas story is good news.
Because Jesus came to save.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH The greatest gift of Christmas isn't found in what we purchase, prepare, or accomplish. It's found in Jesus Christ, the Savior God sent into the world.
Now, I want you to carry that truth with you today.
Because the Christmas season can become filled with expectations.
And sometimes those expectations distract us from the meaning of Christ's coming.
REFLECTION ONE — GOD KEPT HIS PROMISE Now, let's think back to Day One.
We studied Isaiah chapter 9.
And we read about the promised child.
Let's read Isaiah chapter 9, verse 6, from the King James Version. "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace."
Now, I want you to think about that passage.
Christians understand Isaiah's words as pointing toward Jesus Christ.
The promised Savior.
The One whose kingdom will never end.
Now, here's something important. God's redemptive plan unfolded across generations.
And the coming of Jesus Christ stands at the center of that plan.
Now, I want you to think about something. Sometimes we become discouraged when things don't happen according to our preferred timeline.
We want answers quickly.
We want circumstances to change.
And we want to know what comes next.
But the Christmas story reminds us of God's faithfulness to His redemptive promises.
Now, that doesn't mean every personal desire we have is a promise from God.
And it doesn't mean every situation will unfold the way we hope.
But we can trust the promises God has actually given us in Scripture.
And the coming of Jesus Christ is central to those promises.
Now, here's my first Around the Fire question. What does God's faithfulness in sending Jesus Christ teach you about His character?
Think about His love.
His wisdom.
And His saving purposes. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
REFLECTION TWO — THE LIGHT CAME INTO THE WORLD Now, let's think back to Day Two.
We studied Jesus as the Light of the World.
Let's read John chapter 1, verse 14. The King James Version says: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "The Word was made flesh..."
The eternal Son of God entered human history.
He became truly human.
And through Him, God's grace and truth were revealed.
Now, that's the miracle of the incarnation.
And that's why Christmas is about more than the birth of a child.
It's about the coming of the Savior.
Now, I want you to think about something. During Christmas, we see lights everywhere.
On houses.
On trees.
In windows.
And throughout our communities.
Now, those lights can be beautiful.
But they can also remind us of Jesus Christ.
The Light of the World.
The One who reveals God's truth.
And the One through whom salvation is found.
Now, here's my next question. When you see Christmas lights this season, how can you use that moment to remember Jesus Christ?
Maybe you'll pause and thank God for sending His Son.
Maybe you'll remember a Scripture.
Or maybe you'll take a moment to pray. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
REFLECTION THREE — MARY'S FAITH Now, let's think back to Day Three.
We studied Mary's response to the angel Gabriel.
Let's read Luke chapter 1, verse 38. The King James Version says: "And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. And the angel departed from her."
Now, I want you to remember something. Mary received an extraordinary message.
She asked a sincere question.
And she responded with humility.
Now, her experience was unique.
She was chosen to bear Jesus Christ.
And we shouldn't assume that every unexpected circumstance in our own lives is a special revelation from God.
But we can learn from her willingness to respond to God's revealed Word.
Now, here's something I want you to think about. Sometimes we want to understand everything before taking a step.
We want every question answered.
Every detail explained.
And every outcome guaranteed.
But faithful living often involves seeking wisdom and responding responsibly with the information we have.
Now, here's my next Around the Fire question. Is there an area of your life where you need to seek God's wisdom rather than trying to control every outcome?
Maybe it's a decision.
A responsibility.
A relationship.
Or a situation that feels uncertain. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
REFLECTION FOUR — JOSEPH'S QUIET FAITHFULNESS Now, let's think back to Day Four.
We studied Joseph.
A man whose actions speak loudly in the Christmas story.
Matthew tells us that Joseph was a just man.
He considered Mary's dignity.
He thought carefully about his situation.
And when he received the angel's message, he responded with obedience.
Now, let's read Matthew chapter 1, verse 21. The King James Version says: "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins."
Now, I want you to notice something. Joseph's story is ultimately centered on Jesus Christ.
The Savior who came to redeem His people.
But Joseph's example also reminds us that faithfulness can be quiet.
Sometimes it looks like taking responsibility.
Sometimes it looks like treating people with compassion.
And sometimes it looks like doing the right thing without public recognition.
Now, here's my next question. What does quiet faithfulness look like in your life right now?
Maybe it's caring for someone.
Keeping a commitment.
Being honest.
Or helping someone who's facing a difficult situation. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
REFLECTION FIVE — MAKING ROOM FOR JESUS Now, let's think back to yesterday.
We talked about making room for Jesus during the Christmas season.
We studied the circumstances surrounding His birth.
And we reflected on the importance of keeping Christ at the center of our lives.
Now, let's turn to Luke chapter 10. We're going to read verses 41 and 42. The King James Version says: "And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her."
Now, remember the setting.
Martha was busy serving.
And Mary of Bethany was sitting at Jesus' feet, listening to His teaching.
Now, Jesus wasn't saying that serving others is wrong.
But He was reminding Martha of the importance of listening to Him.
Now, I want you to think about something. Sometimes we become so busy preparing for Christmas that we forget to spend time reflecting on the Savior.
We plan.
We shop.
We decorate.
And we organize.
But do we intentionally make time for Scripture?
For prayer?
And for worship?
Now, here's something important. Making room for Jesus doesn't require a perfect schedule.
And it doesn't mean neglecting necessary responsibilities.
It means seeking meaningful ways to keep Christ central in the life we're living.
Now, here's my next question. What is one thing you could simplify this Christmas season to make more meaningful room for Jesus?
Maybe it's reducing unnecessary commitments.
Maybe it's spending less time comparing your celebrations with others.
Or maybe it's setting aside a few minutes each day for Scripture and prayer. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
WHEN CHRISTMAS BRINGS MIXED EMOTIONS Now, I want to spend a few minutes talking about something important.
Because Christmas doesn't feel the same for everyone.
For some people, it's a season of excitement.
They look forward to family gatherings.
Decorating.
And celebrating traditions.
But for others, Christmas can be difficult.
Maybe someone they love is no longer here.
Maybe they're facing financial hardship.
Maybe family relationships are strained.
Or maybe they're simply feeling lonely.
Now, I want you to hear something. You don't have to pretend that everything is wonderful.
And you don't have to feel guilty if this season is difficult.
The meaning of Christmas doesn't depend on having a perfect celebration.
It doesn't depend on expensive gifts.
And it doesn't depend on everyone being together.
The meaning of Christmas is rooted in Jesus Christ.
And the hope of the gospel remains meaningful even during difficult seasons.
Now, here's something important. Faith doesn't require denying grief.
And trusting God doesn't mean refusing to acknowledge pain.
You can bring your sorrow before Him.
You can seek support.
And you can remember the hope of Christ even when the holidays feel different.
A MOMENT FOR THE PERSON WHO'S GRIEVING Now, if you're listening today and you're missing someone you love, I want to speak to you for a moment.
Maybe there's an empty chair at your Christmas table.
Maybe there's a tradition that doesn't feel the same anymore.
Maybe there's a song that brings back memories.
Or maybe you're facing your first Christmas without someone who meant the world to you.
Now, I want you to know that it's okay to remember them.
It's okay to talk about them.
And it's okay to acknowledge that their absence hurts.
You don't have to erase your grief to celebrate the coming of Jesus Christ.
And you don't have to force yourself to feel cheerful.
Sometimes a meaningful Christmas moment may simply be lighting a candle in remembrance.
Looking at a photograph.
Sharing a favorite memory.
Or spending time with someone who understands.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The hope of the gospel doesn't make every sorrow disappear.
But it gives Christians a reason to look toward the resurrection and the promises of God.
And that's a hope worth holding on to.
PAUSE AND PRAY — FOR THE WEARY HEART Now, let's take a moment to pause.
Maybe you've been carrying a lot this Christmas season.
Maybe you're tired.
Maybe you're grieving.
Maybe you're worried about finances.
Or maybe you're simply overwhelmed by responsibilities.
Now, take a moment to bring those concerns before the Lord. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for hearing our prayers. Lord, You know the burdens people are carrying. You know the grief. The uncertainty. The financial concerns. And the responsibilities that can feel overwhelming. Father, provide wisdom and encouragement. Help those who are grieving find comfort and meaningful support. Help those who are struggling financially find practical assistance. And help those who are overwhelmed recognize what they can simplify. Lord, remind us of the hope we have through Jesus Christ. And help us approach this Christmas season with gratitude and compassion. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
THE GREATEST GIFT CANNOT BE PURCHASED Now, I want us to return to the heart of our Christmas study.
The greatest gift.
Let's turn to John chapter 3. We're going to read verse 16. The King James Version says: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life."
Now, I want you to focus on those words. "For God so loved the world, that he gave..."
Now, that's the heart of Christmas.
God's love is revealed through the giving of His Son.
And through Jesus Christ, we have the hope of salvation.
Now, think about the gifts we exchange at Christmas.
We spend time choosing them.
We wrap them.
And we give them to people we love.
Now, giving gifts can be a beautiful tradition.
But the greatest gift of Christmas cannot be purchased.
It cannot be earned.
And it cannot be deserved through our own efforts.
Salvation is God's gracious gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
Now, that's something worth celebrating.
THE CHRISTMAS RUSH — WHAT ARE WE REALLY CHASING? Now, I want to ask you something.
What are we really chasing during Christmas?
Are we trying to create beautiful memories?
Are we trying to meet expectations?
Are we trying to make everyone happy?
Or are we trying to create a celebration that looks impressive?
Now, those questions aren't meant to make anyone feel guilty.
But they can help us examine our priorities.
Because sometimes we become so focused on making everything perfect that we forget to enjoy what's meaningful.
We spend money we don't have.
We take on commitments we can't reasonably manage.
And we place pressure on ourselves to meet expectations that may not even be necessary.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to exhaust yourself to make Christmas meaningful.
You can celebrate simply.
You can set healthy boundaries.
You can be thoughtful about spending.
And you can make meaningful time for Christ.
PHILIPPIANS 4 — PRAYER IN THE MIDDLE OF THE BUSYNESS Now, let's turn to Philippians chapter 4. We're going to read verses 6 and 7. The King James Version says: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus."
Now, I want you to think about those words.
Paul encourages believers to bring their concerns before God.
Through prayer.
Supplication.
And thanksgiving.
Now, this passage isn't telling us that faithful Christians never experience anxiety.
And it isn't a reason to avoid seeking professional care when it's needed.
But it does encourage us to bring our concerns before the Lord.
Now, during a busy Christmas season, that can be a meaningful practice.
We can pause.
We can pray.
And we can remember the peace we have through Jesus Christ.
A CHRISTMAS HEART CHECK Now, I want us to do something together.
We're going to take a few moments for a Christmas heart check.
Now, this isn't a test.
And there are no perfect answers.
It's simply an opportunity to reflect honestly.
Here's the first question. Am I spending more time worrying about Christmas preparations than reflecting on the meaning of Christ's coming? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Here's the second question. Have I placed unnecessary expectations on myself or others? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Here's the third question. Is there someone who may need compassion or encouragement from me this season? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] And here's the fourth question. What is one meaningful way I can honor Jesus Christ this Christmas? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, take a moment to think about your answers.
Maybe you want to simplify something.
Maybe you want to spend more time in Scripture.
Maybe you want to reach out to someone.
Or maybe you simply want to approach the season with greater gratitude.
CHRIST CONNECTION — THE REASON WE CELEBRATE Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because He's the reason we're studying the Christmas story.
The eternal Son of God became flesh.
He entered human history.
He lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, that's the heart of the gospel.
And it's why the coming of Jesus Christ is such good news.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn salvation by having a perfect Christmas.
We don't earn it by giving expensive gifts.
And we don't earn it by attending every church activity.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And our celebrations can become opportunities to express gratitude for that gift.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. When Christmas becomes busy, remember that the greatest gift isn't something you have to purchase, prepare, or earn. The greatest gift is Jesus Christ, the Savior God has given.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes we become so focused on the details that we forget the meaning.
And Christmas is an opportunity to remember God's saving love.
LIVING IT OUT — A CHRIST-CENTERED CHRISTMAS Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... A Christ-Centered Christmas.
Now, beneath that heading, write down four things.
First... One truth about Jesus Christ that you want to remember this season.
Second... One Christmas activity you could simplify.
Third... One meaningful way you can spend time in Scripture or prayer.
And fourth... One person you could encourage or serve.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Thank God for sending Jesus Christ.
Ask Him for wisdom in how you use your time.
And seek opportunities to reflect His love.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, the greatest gift of Christmas reminds me that...
Our second prompt is... One thing I want to simplify this season is...
And our third prompt is... Help me keep Christ at the center of my Christmas by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. Jesus Christ is the greatest gift of Christmas. I will celebrate His coming with gratitude, seek His Word, and share His love with others.
Now, say that again. Jesus Christ is the greatest gift of Christmas. I will celebrate His coming with gratitude, seek His Word, and share His love with others.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize Luke chapter 2, verse 11. "For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord."
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about the meaning of Christ's coming.
Maybe you'll read the Christmas story with your family.
Maybe you'll spend a few minutes in prayer.
Or maybe you'll reach out to someone who may be facing a difficult season.
AROUND THE FIRE — ONE FINAL QUESTION Now, before we close, I want to ask you one final question.
Imagine that all the Christmas decorations were gone.
There were no presents beneath the tree.
No elaborate meals.
And no special events on the calendar.
Now, what would Christmas mean to you? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] I hope it would still remind you of Jesus Christ.
The promised Savior.
The Light of the World.
The Son of God.
And the One who came to redeem us.
Because the meaning of Christmas doesn't depend on the decorations.
Or the gifts.
Or the celebrations.
It depends on the Savior.
And that's the greatest gift of all.
CLOSING REFLECTION — DON'T MISS THE GIFT Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Christmas can be a beautiful season.
But it can also become overwhelming.
We plan.
We prepare.
We shop.
We decorate.
And we try to make everything special.
But sometimes, in the middle of all those preparations, we forget to slow down.
We forget to reflect.
And we forget to remember why we're celebrating.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Don't become so busy preparing for Christmas that you forget to celebrate Christ.
Make room for Scripture.
Make room for prayer.
Make room for worship.
And make room for meaningful moments with the people you love.
But above all... Remember Jesus.
The promised Savior.
The Light of the World.
The One who came to save His people from their sins.
And the greatest gift of all.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for allowing us to slow down and reflect. Lord, thank You for the promises of Scripture. Thank You for sending Jesus Christ. Thank You for His birth. His sinless life. His sacrifice on the cross. And His resurrection. Father, help us remember the true meaning of Christmas. When our schedules become busy, help us recognize what matters most. When we become overwhelmed, give us wisdom. When we're grieving, surround us with comfort and support. And when we're celebrating, help us celebrate with gratitude. Lord, teach us to make meaningful room for Scripture, prayer, and worship. Help us treat others with compassion. And give us opportunities to share the hope of Jesus Christ. Father, may this Christmas season draw us closer to our Savior. And may our lives reflect His love. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY SEVEN Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Ten, Day Six!
And I hope today's Around the Fire reflection has encouraged you to slow down and remember the greatest gift of all.
Jesus Christ.
Tomorrow, we're finishing Week Ten with our final lesson. And our next episode is called... The Gift That Changes Everything — Carrying the Hope of Christmas into Everyday Life.
We'll bring this week's study together and reflect on how the coming of Jesus Christ should shape the way we live beyond the Christmas season.
Until then, remember... Christmas isn't about creating a perfect celebration.
It's about remembering the perfect Savior.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: The Gift That Changes Everything: Carrying the Hope of Christmas into Everyday Life
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — WHEN CHRISTMAS IS OVER Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I am so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Ten, Day Seven. And that means we're finishing another full week of walking through God's Word together.
This week, we've been studying something beautiful. The Greatest Gift — Preparing Our Hearts for Christmas.
We've talked about God's promise of a Savior. We've studied Jesus as the Light of the World. We've looked at Mary's faith. Joseph's obedience. And the importance of making room for Jesus in the middle of our busy lives.
Yesterday, during our Around the Fire episode, we reflected on the greatest gift of Christmas. And today, I want to ask you something.
What happens when Christmas is over?
What happens when the decorations come down? When the Christmas music stops playing? When the presents have all been opened? And when life returns to its ordinary routine?
Does the meaning of Christmas get packed away with the decorations?
Or does it continue shaping the way we live?
Now, I want you to imagine something. It's a few days after Christmas. The wrapping paper has been thrown away. The leftovers are almost gone. And the house is beginning to look normal again.
Maybe you've returned to work. Maybe the children are getting ready to return to school. Maybe you're looking at the calendar and realizing a new year is approaching.
And suddenly, the excitement of the holiday season begins to fade.
Now, here's what I want you to remember. The meaning of Christmas doesn't end when Christmas Day is over.
Because Jesus Christ didn't come into the world simply to give us one beautiful holiday.
He came to save.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
And through His death and resurrection, He provides the hope of forgiveness and eternal life.
Now, that's not something we celebrate for just one day.
That's something that changes our understanding of life itself.
Our identity. Our priorities. Our relationships. And the way we respond to the world around us.
So today, as we finish Week Ten, we're going to talk about what it means to carry the hope of Christmas into everyday life.
Our lesson is called... The Gift That Changes Everything — Carrying the Hope of Christmas into Everyday Life.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for carrying us through another week of Bible study. Lord, we've spent this week reflecting on the coming of Jesus Christ. We've studied Your promises. We've learned about the faith of Mary and Joseph. And we've been reminded that Jesus is the greatest gift of all. Father, today, help us understand what that gift means for our everyday lives. Teach us to live with gratitude. Help us grow in faith. Show us how to reflect the love of Christ in our relationships and responsibilities. And remind us that our hope is found in Jesus, not in a particular season or celebration. May today's lesson encourage us to continue walking faithfully with You. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — 2 CORINTHIANS 5:17–21 Now, let's turn to 2 Corinthians chapter 5. We're going to read verses 17 through 21.
This passage is going to help us understand something important. The coming of Jesus Christ is connected to God's work of reconciliation.
And through Christ, believers receive a new identity and a new purpose.
Let's read from the King James Version. "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation; To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation. Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God. For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him."
Now, I want you to hear verse 17 again. "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
Now, isn't that powerful?
Paul isn't simply talking about making a few improvements to our behavior.
He's describing the transforming reality of belonging to Jesus Christ.
A new relationship with God. A new identity. And a new direction for life.
Now, let's look more closely at what this means.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH The greatest gift of Christmas is Jesus Christ, and through faith in Him, we receive salvation, a new identity, and a calling to reflect His love throughout our lives.
Now, I want you to hold on to that truth. Because Christmas is not just about remembering that Jesus was born.
It's about understanding who He is. Why He came. And what His saving work means for us.
PART ONE — THE GIFT WE COULD NEVER EARN Now, let's begin with something we've talked about several times this week. Grace.
Sometimes we have a difficult time receiving gifts.
We feel like we need to repay the person who gave them.
Or we feel uncomfortable accepting something we didn't earn.
Now, when it comes to salvation, Scripture teaches us something extraordinary.
We cannot earn it.
Let's turn to Ephesians chapter 2. We're going to read verses 8 through 10. The King James Version says: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them."
Now, I want you to notice the order. We are saved by grace through faith.
And then, as people who belong to Christ, we are called to live in ways that reflect that grace.
Now, that's important. Because sometimes we get the order backward.
We think we need to become good enough before we can come to Jesus.
We think we need to clean up every part of our lives.
Fix every mistake.
And prove that we deserve His love.
But the gospel tells us that salvation is God's gracious gift.
We come to Christ in faith.
And as we grow in Him, our lives begin to reflect His work within us.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Good works are not the price of salvation. They are part of the life we're called to live because of God's grace.
And that changes everything.
PART TWO — A NEW CREATION DOESN'T MEAN A PERFECT LIFE Now, let's return to 2 Corinthians chapter 5, verse 17.
"If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature..."
Now, I want to talk about something important. Because sometimes people hear that verse and assume it means becoming a Christian will immediately remove every struggle from their lives.
But that's not what Scripture teaches.
Becoming a new creation in Christ doesn't mean we'll never experience grief.
It doesn't mean we'll never become discouraged.
It doesn't mean we'll never face temptation.
And it doesn't mean every painful memory will suddenly disappear.
But it does mean that through Christ, we have a new standing before God.
We belong to Him.
And we're called to grow in holiness.
Now, here's something I want you to hear. Your past may still be part of your story.
But through faith in Jesus Christ, your identity is not limited to the mistakes you've made or the circumstances you've experienced.
Now, that doesn't mean the consequences of past choices automatically disappear.
And it doesn't mean healing from painful experiences happens overnight.
But it does mean that our hope is rooted in Christ.
And we can continue growing in faith.
One day at a time.
PART THREE — THE CHRISTMAS STORY POINTS TO THE CROSS Now, I want us to think about something.
When we picture Christmas, we often picture a baby lying in a manger.
And that's a beautiful part of the story.
But we cannot fully understand the significance of Jesus' birth without understanding His mission.
Let's turn to Matthew chapter 1, verse 21. The King James Version says: "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins."
Now, notice those words. "He shall save his people from their sins."
Jesus came to save.
And the salvation He came to accomplish would involve His death and resurrection.
Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 5, verse 8. The King James Version says: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
Now, I want you to think about that. God's love is demonstrated through Christ's sacrifice.
Not because humanity had earned salvation.
But because of His grace.
Now, here's something important. The manger and the cross belong to the same redemptive story.
The baby born in Bethlehem is the Savior who would give His life for our sins.
And He rose again.
So when we celebrate Christmas, we're remembering the beginning of Christ's earthly life.
But we're also remembering the Savior's mission.
And that's why the gift of Jesus changes everything.
PART FOUR — CARRYING THE HOPE OF CHRIST INTO EVERYDAY LIFE Now, let's talk about what all of this means practically.
Because sometimes it's easier to feel inspired during a special season.
We hear Christmas music.
We attend worship services.
We read familiar Bible passages.
And we spend time reflecting on Jesus.
But what happens when life returns to normal?
What happens when the calendar is full again?
When work becomes stressful?
When relationships become difficult?
And when the excitement of the holiday season fades?
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The truth of the gospel doesn't change when our circumstances change.
Jesus Christ remains the same.
Let's turn to Hebrews chapter 13, verse 8. The King James Version says: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever."
Now, isn't that encouraging?
The Savior we celebrate at Christmas is the same Lord we follow throughout the year.
His character doesn't change with the calendar.
His saving work doesn't become less meaningful when the decorations come down.
And the truth of His Word remains relevant to everyday life.
Now, that means our faith isn't something we put away after a holiday.
It's something that shapes our daily decisions.
Our relationships.
Our priorities.
And the way we treat others.
PART FIVE — LET THE LOVE OF CHRIST CHANGE YOUR RELATIONSHIPS Now, let's turn to Colossians chapter 3. We're going to read verses 12 through 14. The King James Version says: "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness."
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul describes the character believers are called to demonstrate.
Compassion.
Kindness.
Humility.
Patience.
Forgiveness.
And love.
Now, I want you to think about how those qualities could change our relationships.
What if we responded with patience instead of immediately becoming angry?
What if we listened more carefully?
What if we looked for opportunities to show kindness?
What if we were willing to acknowledge our own mistakes?
Now, here's something important. Forgiveness doesn't mean pretending that wrongdoing never happened.
And it doesn't require remaining in an abusive or unsafe situation.
But Scripture calls us to reflect the mercy and love we've received through Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. One of the ways we carry the hope of Christmas into everyday life is through the way we treat people.
Not just during December.
But throughout the year.
PART SIX — LET YOUR LIGHT SHINE Now, let's turn to Matthew chapter 5. We're going to read verses 14 through 16. The King James Version says: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid. Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "Let your light so shine before men..."
Now, earlier this week, we studied Jesus as the Light of the World.
And here, Jesus teaches His followers that their lives should reflect God's truth and goodness.
Now, here's something important. We're not the source of salvation.
Jesus Christ is.
But our lives can point others toward Him.
Through kindness.
Through honesty.
Through generosity.
And through the way we respond to others.
Now, sometimes we think sharing our faith requires doing something dramatic.
But often, meaningful opportunities begin with ordinary moments.
Helping someone who needs assistance.
Encouraging someone who's discouraged.
Listening to someone who's grieving.
Or speaking about the hope we have in Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Our lives should point people toward Jesus, not simply toward ourselves.
And that is a meaningful way to carry the hope of Christmas into everyday life.
PAUSE AND PRAY — LORD, LET MY LIFE REFLECT YOU Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about the people you encounter throughout an ordinary week.
Your family.
Your coworkers.
Your neighbors.
The people you see at church.
And even the strangers you encounter.
Now, ask yourself something. How can my life reflect the love of Jesus Christ? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for the gift of Jesus Christ. Thank You for the salvation we have through Him. Lord, help us remember that our faith isn't limited to one season. Teach us to reflect Your love throughout the year. Help us demonstrate kindness. Patience. Humility. And compassion. Father, give us wisdom in our relationships. Help us recognize opportunities to encourage others. And remind us that our actions can point people toward Jesus. May our lives bring glory to You. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
PART SEVEN — DON'T PACK AWAY YOUR FAITH Now, I want to share something with you.
Every year, when Christmas is over, people begin putting things away.
The ornaments come off the tree.
The decorations go back into storage.
The Christmas lights are taken down.
And eventually, everything returns to normal.
Now, there's nothing wrong with that.
But I want you to imagine something. What if we treated our relationship with Jesus the same way?
What if we spent December talking about His birth...
But then rarely opened our Bibles throughout the rest of the year?
What if we celebrated His coming...
But didn't allow His teaching to shape our decisions?
What if we sang about His love...
But neglected opportunities to show that love to others?
Now, I don't say that to make anyone feel guilty.
I say it because Christmas can be a beautiful reminder to renew our focus on Christ.
Not just for one day.
Not just for one month.
But throughout our lives.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The decorations may come down, but our devotion to Jesus Christ should continue growing.
PART EIGHT — THE GIFT OF RECONCILIATION Now, let's return to our main Scripture. 2 Corinthians chapter 5.
Paul tells us that God has reconciled us to Himself through Jesus Christ.
Now, reconciliation is an important word.
It speaks of a relationship being restored.
And in this passage, Paul is describing God's work of bringing sinners into a right relationship with Himself through Christ.
Now, think about that. Sin separates humanity from God.
But through Jesus Christ, God has provided the way of reconciliation.
And Paul goes on to describe the message of reconciliation entrusted to believers.
Now, that means the gospel isn't simply something we receive and then forget.
It's a message we're called to share.
Not through pressure.
Not through manipulation.
And not through pretending we have every answer.
But through faithful witness to Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The greatest gift we can point someone toward isn't something we can purchase. It's the hope of salvation through Jesus Christ.
PART NINE — THE GIFT OF HOPE IN DIFFICULT SEASONS Now, I want to speak to someone who's facing a difficult season.
Maybe this Christmas hasn't looked the way you expected.
Maybe you're grieving.
Maybe you're dealing with illness.
Maybe you're facing financial uncertainty.
Or maybe you're simply exhausted.
Now, I want you to hear something. The hope of the gospel doesn't depend on having an easy life.
It doesn't depend on everything working out the way we planned.
And it doesn't require pretending that our circumstances are better than they are.
Christian hope is rooted in Jesus Christ.
His death.
His resurrection.
And the promises of God.
Now, that doesn't mean we won't need support.
And it doesn't mean we shouldn't seek practical help when we're struggling.
But it does mean that our spiritual hope is anchored in something greater than the circumstances of one particular season.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The greatest gift of Christmas remains meaningful even when life is difficult, because our hope is found in the Savior, not in perfect circumstances.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... How has this week's Christmas study helped me understand Jesus Christ more deeply?
Think about His identity.
His coming into the world.
And His mission to save. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... What does being a new creation in Christ mean for the way I understand my identity?
Think about grace.
Forgiveness.
And spiritual growth. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... How can I carry the hope of Christmas into my relationships and responsibilities?
Maybe it's through patience.
Kindness.
Honesty.
Or serving others. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... What is one spiritual habit I want to continue developing after the Christmas season?
Maybe it's reading Scripture.
Prayer.
Worship.
Or participating in Christian fellowship. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — THE GREATEST GIFT OF ALL Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because He's the center of everything we've studied this week.
God promised a Savior.
And Jesus Christ came into the world.
The eternal Son of God became flesh.
He lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, let's read John chapter 3, verses 16 and 17. The King James Version says: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved."
Now, that's the heart of the gospel.
God's love.
God's gift.
And salvation through Jesus Christ.
Now, if you're listening today and you've never placed your faith in Jesus Christ, I encourage you to continue exploring what Scripture teaches about Him.
Read the Gospels.
Ask sincere questions.
And speak with a trusted Christian pastor or mature believer.
Because the greatest gift of Christmas isn't simply a story to admire.
It's the Savior we're called to trust.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. Christmas reminds us that God gave the greatest gift through Jesus Christ. That gift isn't meant to be remembered for one day and forgotten—it gives us a reason to live with faith, gratitude, and hope throughout the year.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because the Christmas season will eventually pass.
But Jesus Christ remains the same.
LIVING IT OUT — CARRYING CHRISTMAS INTO EVERYDAY LIFE Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... Carrying the Hope of Christmas into Everyday Life.
Now, beneath that heading, write down four things.
First... One truth about Jesus Christ that you want to remember throughout the year.
Second... One spiritual habit you want to continue developing.
Third... One relationship where you can demonstrate greater kindness or compassion.
And fourth... One meaningful way you can share the hope of Christ with someone else.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Thank God for sending Jesus Christ.
Ask Him to help you grow in faith.
And seek opportunities to reflect His love throughout the year.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, the greatest gift of Christmas has reminded me that...
Our second prompt is... One way I want my relationship with Jesus Christ to grow is...
And our third prompt is... Help me carry the hope of Christ into everyday life by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. Jesus Christ is the greatest gift of all. Through faith in Him, I have the hope of salvation, and I will seek to reflect His love throughout my life.
Now, say that again. Jesus Christ is the greatest gift of all. Through faith in Him, I have the hope of salvation, and I will seek to reflect His love throughout my life.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize 2 Corinthians chapter 5, verse 17. "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about what it means to belong to Jesus Christ.
Maybe you'll spend time reflecting on God's grace.
Maybe you'll encourage someone.
Or maybe you'll begin developing a spiritual habit that you want to continue throughout the coming year.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHAT WILL YOU CARRY WITH YOU? Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire one more time this week.
The evening is quiet.
The fire is burning.
And we're looking back over everything we've studied.
Now, I want to ask you something. What is the most meaningful thing you've learned about Jesus Christ during this Christmas study?
Maybe it's the faithfulness of God's promises.
Maybe it's the meaning of the incarnation.
Maybe it's the humility of Christ's birth.
Or maybe it's the reminder that salvation is God's gracious gift. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. What do you want to carry with you when this Christmas season is over?
Maybe it's a deeper commitment to Scripture.
Maybe it's a more consistent prayer life.
Maybe it's greater compassion for others.
Or maybe it's a renewed appreciation for the gospel. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to remember something. We don't have to wait for a special holiday to seek Jesus Christ.
We can study His Word today.
We can pray today.
We can show kindness today.
And we can continue growing in faith throughout the year.
CLOSING REFLECTION — THE GIFT THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Every Christmas, we exchange gifts.
Some are expensive.
Some are simple.
Some are practical.
And some become treasured memories.
But eventually, many of those gifts will wear out.
They'll be replaced.
Or they'll be forgotten.
But the greatest gift of Christmas is different.
Because the greatest gift is Jesus Christ.
The promised Savior.
The Light of the World.
The eternal Son of God who became flesh.
The One who died for our sins.
And the One who rose again.
Now, that's a gift that changes everything.
Not because it guarantees an easy life.
Not because it removes every hardship.
And not because it makes us perfect overnight.
But because through Jesus Christ, we have the hope of reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness.
A new identity.
And eternal life.
So when the Christmas decorations come down...
Keep seeking Jesus.
When the holiday music stops...
Keep opening your Bible.
When life returns to its ordinary routine...
Keep praying.
And when you encounter someone who needs compassion...
Remember the love of Christ.
Because the greatest gift of Christmas isn't something we pack away.
It's the Savior we follow every day.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us through another week of Walking Through the Word. Thank You for every lesson we've studied. And thank You for the opportunity to reflect on the coming of Jesus Christ. Lord, we thank You for the greatest gift of all. Your Son. Our Savior. Jesus Christ. Father, thank You for His birth. His sinless life. His sacrifice on the cross. And His resurrection. Thank You for the hope of forgiveness and eternal life through Him. Lord, help us carry the meaning of Christmas into everyday life. Teach us to live with gratitude. Help us grow in faith. Give us compassion for others. And help us reflect the love of Christ in our words and actions. Father, I pray for the person who's facing a difficult season. Give them encouragement and meaningful support. I pray for the person who's grieving. Surround them with comfort and care. And I pray for the person who's seeking to grow closer to You. Help them continue studying Your Word and seeking Your wisdom. Lord, may our lives point others toward Jesus Christ. And may we remember that the greatest gift of Christmas remains meaningful throughout the entire year. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — WEEK TEN COMPLETE! Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Ten!
And what a meaningful week it has been.
We've studied God's promise of a Savior.
Jesus as the Light of the World.
Mary's faith.
Joseph's obedience.
And the importance of making room for Christ in our lives.
And today, we've been reminded that the greatest gift of Christmas is a gift that changes everything.
Now, tomorrow, we're beginning Week Eleven. And our new weekly theme is... The Promise of Christmas — Hope, Peace, and Jesus.
Our first lesson will be called... Hope Has a Name — Jesus Christ, Our Living Hope.
We'll explore what Scripture teaches about Christian hope and why that hope is rooted in the person and work of Jesus Christ.
Until then, remember... Christmas may come once a year.
But the hope we have through Jesus Christ is something we can carry every single day.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

weeks.title: The Promise of Christmas — Hope, Peace, and Jesus

lessons.title: Hope Has a Name: Jesus Christ, Our Living Hope
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — WHEN HOPE FEELS FAR AWAY Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Eleven, Day One. And we're beginning a brand-new week of studying God's Word together.
Our theme this week is... The Promise of Christmas — Hope, Peace, and Jesus.
Now, last week, we spent seven days reflecting on the greatest gift of Christmas. We studied God's promise of a Savior. We talked about Jesus being the Light of the World. We looked at Mary's faith. Joseph's obedience. And the importance of making room for Jesus in our lives.
And we finished the week by remembering that the greatest gift of Christmas isn't something we pack away when the holiday is over.
It's the Savior we follow every day.
Now, this week, I want us to go a little deeper.
Because Christmas is not only a celebration of Christ's birth.
It's also a reminder of the hope we have because of who He is and what He came to accomplish.
And today, we're beginning with one of my favorite subjects. Hope.
Now, let me ask you something. Have you ever been in a season of life where hope felt far away?
Maybe you were praying for something that hadn't happened.
Maybe you were facing a situation you couldn't control.
Maybe you were grieving someone you loved.
Or maybe you were simply exhausted from carrying responsibilities that seemed to have no end.
Now, I want you to think about something. Sometimes people tell us to just stay positive.
They tell us to look on the bright side.
Or to believe that everything will work out.
Now, encouragement can be helpful.
But Christian hope is deeper than positive thinking.
It's not simply convincing ourselves that life will become easier.
And it's not pretending that difficult circumstances don't exist.
Christian hope is rooted in Jesus Christ.
His death. His resurrection. And the promises of God.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Hope isn't the absence of hardship. Christian hope is confidence in the risen Savior, even when hardship remains.
And that's what we're going to study today.
Our lesson is called... Hope Has a Name — Jesus Christ, Our Living Hope.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for carrying us into another week of Bible study. Lord, today we're studying the hope we have through Jesus Christ. And You know that some people listening may be facing difficult circumstances. Some may be grieving. Some may be discouraged. Some may be worried about the future. And some may simply be tired. Father, help us understand what Your Word teaches about Christian hope. Remind us of the resurrection of Jesus Christ. Teach us to trust Your promises. And help us encourage one another with the truth of the gospel. May today's study strengthen our faith and draw us closer to our Savior. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — 1 PETER 1:3–9 Now, let's turn to 1 Peter chapter 1. We're going to read verses 3 through 9.
Before we begin, let's understand the setting. Peter was writing to Christians who were living as strangers and scattered believers across several regions.
These believers faced various trials.
And Peter wanted to remind them of the hope they possessed through Jesus Christ.
Now, I want you to notice something. Peter doesn't begin by promising that their difficulties will immediately disappear.
Instead, he points them toward the resurrection of Jesus and the inheritance God has prepared for His people.
Let's read 1 Peter chapter 1, verses 3 through 9, from the King James Version. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you, Who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation ready to be revealed in the last time. Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations: That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ: Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory: Receiving the end of your faith, even the salvation of your souls."
Now, I want you to hear that first verse again. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead."
Now, that is the foundation of today's lesson.
A living hope.
Not a hope built on circumstances.
Not a hope built on human promises.
But a hope rooted in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH Christian hope is living hope because Jesus Christ is risen. Our confidence rests in His saving work and God's promises, not in the certainty of an easy life.
Now, I want you to hold on to that truth.
Because sometimes we confuse hope with the expectation that everything will happen the way we want.
But Scripture teaches us something deeper.
PART ONE — WHAT IS LIVING HOPE? Now, let's look at the phrase Peter uses.
"A lively hope."
In many modern translations, that phrase is rendered "a living hope."
Now, what does that mean?
It means the hope Peter describes is grounded in the living Christ.
Jesus died.
But He did not remain in the grave.
He rose again.
And because He lives, believers have a future hope that cannot be destroyed by death.
Now, that's extraordinary.
Because so many things in this world are uncertain.
Our circumstances can change.
Our health can change.
Our finances can change.
And the people we love may experience hardship or loss.
But the resurrection of Jesus Christ is the foundation of Christian hope.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Living hope doesn't mean every circumstance is good. It means our hope is anchored in the living Savior.
PART TWO — HOPE IS NOT THE SAME AS WISHFUL THINKING Now, I want us to talk about something important.
Because we use the word hope in everyday conversation.
We say... "I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow."
"I hope I get the job."
"I hope everything works out."
Now, there's nothing wrong with expressing those desires.
But biblical hope is different.
Christian hope is confidence rooted in God's promises.
Not simply a wish for a particular outcome.
Now, that doesn't mean we shouldn't pray about our circumstances.
We absolutely can.
We can pray for healing.
For provision.
For reconciliation.
And for wisdom.
But we also recognize that God hasn't promised every circumstance will unfold according to our preferences.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Our hope isn't that every prayer will be answered exactly as we want. Our hope is that Jesus Christ is risen and God's promises are trustworthy.
PART THREE — AN INHERITANCE THAT DOESN'T FADE Now, let's look at verse 4. Peter describes an inheritance that is... "Incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away..."
Now, I want you to think about those words. Incorruptible.
Undefiled.
And unfading.
Now, so much of what we value in this world is temporary.
Possessions wear out.
Circumstances change.
And earthly accomplishments eventually become part of the past.
But Peter points believers toward an eternal inheritance.
One that isn't subject to decay.
Now, that's the hope of salvation.
And it's connected to our future with Christ.
Now, here's something important. This isn't a promise of earthly wealth.
It's not a guarantee of financial success.
And it isn't a declaration that believers will avoid hardship.
It's a promise concerning the eternal inheritance of God's people.
Now, that's something worth holding on to.
PART FOUR — HOPE IN THE MIDDLE OF TRIALS Now, let's look at verses 6 and 7.
Peter acknowledges that believers may experience heaviness through various trials.
Now, I want you to notice something. He doesn't deny their suffering.
He doesn't tell them to pretend everything is wonderful.
And he doesn't suggest that grief or hardship automatically means their faith is weak.
Instead, he recognizes that trials are part of their experience.
Now, I think that's important. Because sometimes people feel pressure to appear strong all the time.
They think that if they admit they're struggling, others will question their faith.
But Scripture gives us a more honest picture.
Believers can experience grief.
Fear.
Discouragement.
And hardship.
And they can still hold on to the hope of Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Faith doesn't require pretending that suffering doesn't hurt. Christian hope allows us to acknowledge hardship while trusting the risen Savior.
PART FIVE — FAITH REFINED THROUGH DIFFICULTY Now, let's look again at verse 7. Peter compares the testing of faith to gold being refined by fire.
Now, that's a powerful picture.
Gold is valuable.
And Peter says that tested faith is even more precious.
Now, I want you to think about something. Sometimes difficult experiences reveal what we're relying on.
They can expose our fears.
Our assumptions.
And our need for God's wisdom.
But here's something important. We shouldn't assume that every hardship is a punishment from God.
And we shouldn't tell someone who is suffering that their pain was necessary to make them stronger.
That can be deeply hurtful.
Instead, we can recognize that Scripture teaches believers to persevere in faith through trials.
And we can encourage one another with compassion.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The presence of hardship doesn't mean the absence of hope.
PART SIX — HOPE WHEN YOU CAN'T SEE Now, let's look at verse 8. Peter says: "Whom having not seen, ye love..."
Now, I want you to think about those words. Peter is writing to believers who had not seen Jesus with their own eyes.
And yet, they loved Him.
They believed in Him.
And they rejoiced in the hope of salvation.
Now, that's meaningful.
Because Christians today also live by faith in the risen Christ.
We haven't physically seen Him.
But we have the testimony of Scripture concerning His life, death, and resurrection.
And we place our trust in Him.
Now, here's something important. Faith isn't the same as pretending we know everything.
And it doesn't require ignoring sincere questions.
But it does involve trusting the testimony of God's Word.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Christian hope is grounded in the risen Christ, even though we do not yet see Him face to face.
PART SEVEN — THE HOPE OF CHRISTMAS Now, let's connect everything we've studied to the Christmas story.
Let's turn to Luke chapter 2. We're going to read verses 10 and 11. The King James Version says: "And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord."
Now, I want you to focus on those words. "A Saviour, which is Christ the Lord."
Now, that's the heart of Christmas.
The promised Savior has come.
And the hope of His coming is connected to His saving mission.
Now, here's something I want you to think about. When the shepherds heard the announcement, they were hearing good news about the birth of Jesus.
But we now look back on the Christmas story with the knowledge of His death and resurrection.
We understand that the baby born in Bethlehem is the risen Savior.
And that's why Christian hope is so powerful.
Because Christmas points us toward the gospel.
PART EIGHT — HOPE THAT DOESN'T DISAPPOINT Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 5. We're going to read verses 1 through 5. The King James Version says: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us."
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul connects hope with justification by faith.
Peace with God.
And the love of God.
Now, that's important. Because the hope Paul describes isn't simply optimism about earthly circumstances.
It's confidence in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The hope of the gospel isn't that life will always be easy. It's that through Jesus Christ, we have peace with God and the promise of eternal life.
PART NINE — HOPE WHEN YOU'RE GRIEVING Now, I want to spend a few minutes speaking to someone who's grieving.
Because the Christmas season can bring memories to the surface.
Maybe you're missing someone who used to celebrate with you.
Maybe there's an empty chair at the table.
Maybe a familiar Christmas song brings tears to your eyes.
Or maybe you're facing your first Christmas without someone you love.
Now, I want you to hear something. It's okay to grieve.
It's okay to remember.
And it's okay to acknowledge that someone's absence hurts.
Now, let's turn to 1 Thessalonians chapter 4. We're going to read verses 13 and 14. The King James Version says: "But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him."
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul doesn't tell believers that they must never grieve.
He points them toward the hope of the resurrection.
Now, that's important. Because Christian hope doesn't erase the pain of losing someone we love.
But it gives believers a reason to look toward the promises of God concerning resurrection and eternal life.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Grief and hope can exist together.
You can miss someone deeply.
And still hold on to the hope of Jesus Christ.
PART TEN — HOPE AS AN ANCHOR Now, let's turn to Hebrews chapter 6. We're going to read verse 19. The King James Version says: "Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;"
Now, I want you to think about that picture. An anchor.
Now, when a boat is on the water, an anchor helps keep it from drifting.
And Hebrews uses that image to describe the security of Christian hope.
Now, I want you to imagine a storm.
The wind is blowing.
The water is moving.
And everything feels uncertain.
Now, the anchor doesn't make the storm disappear.
But it provides stability.
Now, that's a helpful picture of Christian hope.
Our circumstances may change.
We may experience grief.
We may face hardship.
But our hope is anchored in God's promises through Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Hope doesn't mean the storm disappears. It means our confidence is anchored in the risen Savior.
PAUSE AND PRAY — LORD, STRENGTHEN MY HOPE Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about an area of your life where you need encouragement.
Maybe you're facing uncertainty.
Maybe you're grieving.
Maybe you're tired.
Or maybe you're struggling to remain hopeful.
Now, take a moment to bring that concern before the Lord. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for the hope we have through Jesus Christ. Thank You for His death and resurrection. Lord, You know the circumstances we're facing. You know the grief. The uncertainty. And the burdens we're carrying. Father, strengthen our faith. Help us remember Your promises. Teach us to place our hope in Jesus Christ rather than in perfect circumstances. And help us encourage others who may be struggling. Lord, may the truth of the resurrection give us confidence in Your saving work. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
PART ELEVEN — HOPE AND THE MERCIES OF GOD Now, let's turn to Lamentations chapter 3. We're going to read verses 21 through 23. The King James Version says: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "Great is thy faithfulness."
Now, Lamentations was written in the context of deep sorrow and national devastation.
And yet, in the middle of that grief, the writer remembers the Lord's mercy and faithfulness.
Now, that's meaningful.
Because hope doesn't require pretending that sorrow doesn't exist.
We can acknowledge difficult circumstances.
And still remember God's character.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Remembering God's faithfulness can help us hold on to hope when our circumstances feel uncertain.
PART TWELVE — THE GOD OF HOPE Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 15. We're going to read verse 13. The King James Version says: "Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost."
Now, I love that verse.
"The God of hope..."
Now, I want you to think about that. Our hope isn't simply something we manufacture through positive thinking.
It's rooted in God.
His character.
His promises.
And His saving work through Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something important. This doesn't mean believers will always feel joyful.
And it doesn't mean we should ignore emotional struggles.
But it does remind us that Christian hope is connected to the work of the Holy Spirit.
Now, that's something we can pray for.
That God would strengthen our faith.
That He would help us remember His promises.
And that He would encourage us through His Word.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... When I think about hope, am I usually thinking about a particular outcome or about the promises of God?
Now, there's nothing wrong with hoping for a particular outcome.
But today's lesson reminds us that Christian hope is rooted in Jesus Christ. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... How does the resurrection of Jesus Christ shape my understanding of hope?
Think about forgiveness.
Salvation.
And eternal life. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... What Scripture can I return to when I'm feeling discouraged?
Maybe it's 1 Peter chapter 1.
Romans chapter 15.
Or Lamentations chapter 3. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... Who in my life may need encouragement and compassion right now?
Maybe it's someone who's grieving.
Someone who's facing uncertainty.
Or someone who simply needs a listening ear. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — OUR LIVING HOPE Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because He is the foundation of Christian hope.
The eternal Son of God became flesh.
He lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, let's turn to John chapter 11. We're going to read verses 25 and 26. The King James Version says: "Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?"
Now, I want you to think about those words. "I am the resurrection, and the life..."
Now, that's the heart of Christian hope.
Jesus Christ is the risen Savior.
And through faith in Him, we have the promise of eternal life.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn salvation by being positive.
We don't earn it by never becoming discouraged.
And we don't earn it by having perfect faith.
Salvation is God's gracious gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
And our hope is rooted in His saving work.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. Hope has a name, and His name is Jesus. Our circumstances may change, but the resurrection of Christ remains the foundation of our living hope.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes life becomes difficult.
Sometimes prayers aren't answered the way we hoped.
And sometimes the future feels uncertain.
But Christian hope is rooted in the risen Savior.
LIVING IT OUT — ANCHORING MY HOPE IN CHRIST Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... Anchoring My Hope in Christ.
Now, beneath that heading, write down four things.
First... One situation where you're feeling discouraged or uncertain.
Second... One promise from Scripture that can strengthen your faith.
Third... One way you can remind yourself of the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And fourth... One person you can encourage with compassion and truth.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Ask God to strengthen your hope.
Thank Him for the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And seek opportunities to encourage others.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, one area where I need encouragement is...
Our second prompt is... The resurrection of Jesus Christ gives me hope because...
And our third prompt is... Help me anchor my hope in Your promises by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. My hope is anchored in Jesus Christ. Because He is risen, I can trust God's promises and look toward the future He has prepared for His people.
Now, say that again. My hope is anchored in Jesus Christ. Because He is risen, I can trust God's promises and look toward the future He has prepared for His people.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize 1 Peter chapter 1, verse 3. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,"
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about what it means to have a living hope.
Maybe you'll spend time studying the resurrection.
Maybe you'll pray for someone who's discouraged.
Or maybe you'll reach out to someone who needs encouragement.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHERE IS YOUR HOPE ANCHORED? Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
The evening is quiet.
The fire is burning.
And we're reflecting on everything we've studied today.
Now, I want to ask you something. When life becomes uncertain, what do you usually rely on for hope?
Maybe it's a particular outcome.
Maybe it's encouragement from someone you love.
Maybe it's your own ability to solve problems.
Or maybe it's the promises of Scripture. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. How would your perspective change if you remembered that Christian hope is rooted in the resurrection of Jesus Christ?
Maybe you would feel less pressure to control every outcome.
Maybe you would spend more time reflecting on Scripture.
Or maybe you would find encouragement in the promise of eternal life. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to remember something. Christian hope doesn't require pretending that life is easy.
It doesn't require denying grief.
And it doesn't require having every answer.
It means trusting the risen Savior.
And holding on to the promises of God.
CLOSING REFLECTION — HOPE HAS A NAME Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Sometimes hope feels fragile.
Sometimes life becomes overwhelming.
Sometimes the future feels uncertain.
And sometimes we're simply tired.
But I want you to remember something.
Christian hope isn't built on the certainty that everything will happen the way we want.
It's built on the truth that Jesus Christ is risen.
He came into the world.
He lived a sinless life.
He died for our sins.
And He rose again.
Now, that's the foundation of our hope.
