And that's why the Christmas story is such good news.
Because the baby born in Bethlehem is the risen Savior.
The One who conquered death.
And the One through whom we have the promise of eternal life.
So if you're facing uncertainty today...
Remember the risen Christ.
If you're grieving...
Remember the hope of the resurrection.
If you're discouraged...
Return to the promises of Scripture.
And if you're simply tired...
Remember that you don't have to pretend everything is easy.
You can bring your concerns before the Lord.
You can seek support.
And you can continue holding on to the hope of Jesus Christ.
Because hope has a name.
And His name is Jesus.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for the hope we have through Jesus Christ. Thank You for His birth. His sinless life. His sacrifice on the cross. And His resurrection. Lord, help us remember that Christian hope is rooted in Your promises. Not in perfect circumstances. Not in our ability to control every outcome. And not in the expectation that life will always be easy. Father, strengthen the faith of those who are discouraged. Provide comfort and meaningful support for those who are grieving. Give wisdom to those who are facing uncertainty. And help us encourage one another with the truth of the gospel. Lord, may the resurrection of Jesus Christ remain the foundation of our hope. And may we continue growing in faith as we walk through Your Word together. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY TWO Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Eleven, Day One!
And I hope today's lesson has reminded you that Christian hope is more than positive thinking.
It's confidence rooted in the risen Savior.
Tomorrow, we're continuing our study of The Promise of Christmas — Hope, Peace, and Jesus. And our next lesson is called... Peace in the Middle of the Storm — The Prince of Peace Has Come.
We'll explore what Scripture teaches about the peace Jesus gives and how that peace is different from simply having a trouble-free life.
Until then, remember... Hope has a name.
And His name is Jesus.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: Peace in the Middle of the Storm: The Prince of Peace Has Come
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — WHEN LIFE DOESN'T FEEL PEACEFUL Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Eleven, Day Two. And we're continuing our Christmas study called... The Promise of Christmas — Hope, Peace, and Jesus.
Yesterday, we talked about hope. Not just the kind of hope that wishes everything will turn out the way we want. But living hope. Hope rooted in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And today, we're talking about something that goes hand in hand with hope. Peace.
Now, let me ask you something. Have you ever looked around at your life and thought... Lord, I just need a little peace?
Maybe the bills are piling up. Maybe you're waiting on medical results. Maybe there's tension in your family. Maybe you're facing a difficult decision. Or maybe your mind just won't seem to slow down.
You go to bed thinking about everything you need to do tomorrow. You wake up remembering everything you didn't finish yesterday. And somewhere in the middle of it all, you find yourself longing for peace.
Now, during the Christmas season, we hear that word everywhere. Peace.
We see it written on Christmas cards. We hear it in Christmas songs. We see it hanging on decorations.
But sometimes our actual lives don't feel very peaceful.
And that raises an important question. What does the Bible really mean when it talks about peace?
Does peace mean everything is going well? Does it mean we never feel worried? Does it mean we never experience conflict?
Or could the peace Jesus gives be something deeper?
Now, here's something I want you to remember today. The peace Jesus gives is not the promise of a trouble-free life. It is rooted in who He is and what He has accomplished for us.
And that's what we're going to study.
Our lesson today is called... Peace in the Middle of the Storm — The Prince of Peace Has Come.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for the gift of Jesus Christ. And thank You for the peace we have through Him. Lord, You know the circumstances each person listening is facing. You know the worries. The responsibilities. The uncertainty. And the situations that may feel overwhelming. Father, help us understand what Your Word teaches about peace. Teach us the difference between peace with You and simply having comfortable circumstances. Help us bring our concerns before You in prayer. And remind us that Jesus Christ is the Prince of Peace. May today's study encourage us and draw us closer to our Savior. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — JOHN 14:25–27 Now, let's turn to John chapter 14. We're going to read verses 25 through 27.
Before we begin, let's understand the setting. Jesus is speaking to His disciples before His arrest and crucifixion.
He knows that difficult events are approaching.
His disciples will experience confusion, fear, and sorrow.
And in the middle of this conversation, Jesus speaks about peace.
Now, that's important. Because Jesus doesn't speak these words when everything is comfortable.
He speaks them as He prepares His disciples for what is coming.
Let's read John chapter 14, verses 25 through 27, from the King James Version. "These things have I spoken unto you, being yet present with you. But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you. Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid."
Now, I want you to hear those words again. "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you."
Now, isn't that beautiful?
Jesus speaks of a peace that is different from what the world gives.
And He speaks these words knowing that His disciples are about to face extraordinary difficulties.
Now, that tells us something important. The peace Jesus gives isn't dependent on everything around us being easy.
It's connected to our relationship with Him.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH Jesus Christ is the Prince of Peace. Through Him, believers have peace with God, and His promises give us a foundation for trust even when life is uncertain.
Now, I want you to hold on to that truth. Because sometimes we spend so much time trying to change our circumstances that we forget to consider the peace we have through Christ.
PART ONE — THE PRINCE OF PEACE Now, let's turn to Isaiah chapter 9. We're going to read verse 6. The King James Version says: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace."
Now, I want you to focus on those final words. "The Prince of Peace."
Now, Christians understand this prophecy as pointing toward Jesus Christ.
The promised Messiah.
The One whose reign is characterized by righteousness and peace.
Now, here's something important. When Isaiah speaks of the Prince of Peace, he's describing more than a temporary feeling of calm.
He's pointing toward the Messiah and His righteous rule.
And through Jesus Christ, we have reconciliation with God.
Now, that is the foundation of Christian peace.
PART TWO — PEACE WITH GOD Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 5. We're going to read verse 1. The King James Version says: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:"
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul doesn't simply say we feel peaceful.
He says we have peace with God.
Now, that's an important distinction.
Because sometimes we think peace is only an emotion.
We think peace means feeling calm.
Feeling relaxed.
Or having nothing to worry about.
But Romans chapter 5 is talking about something deeper.
Through Jesus Christ, those who are justified by faith have peace with God.
That means our relationship with God has been changed through Christ's saving work.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The foundation of Christian peace is not a peaceful feeling. It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
And that's something our circumstances cannot create for us.
It's something Christ has accomplished.
PART THREE — PEACE DOESN'T MEAN THERE WON'T BE STORMS Now, let's talk about something important.
Because sometimes we assume that if we're following Jesus, life should become easier.
We think our problems should disappear.
Our relationships should improve immediately.
And our circumstances should become comfortable.
But Scripture doesn't promise that.
In fact, Jesus told His followers that they would experience trouble in the world.
Now, let's turn to Mark chapter 4. We're going to read verses 35 through 41.
This is the account of Jesus calming the storm.
Let's read from the King James Version. "And the same day, when the even was come, he saith unto them, Let us pass over unto the other side. And when they had sent away the multitude, they took him even as he was in the ship. And there were also with him other little ships. And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full. And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish? And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. And he said unto them, Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith? And they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?"
Now, I want you to picture that scene.
The disciples are in a boat.
The wind is blowing.
The waves are coming into the boat.
And they're afraid.
Now, here's something I want you to notice. Jesus was with them.
And yet, they still encountered a storm.
Now, that's important. Because sometimes people assume that hardship means God has abandoned them.
But the presence of a storm doesn't automatically mean the absence of God's care.
Now, in this particular account, Jesus demonstrates His authority over creation by calming the wind and the sea.
And the disciples are left asking who He is.
Now, the central point of this passage is the extraordinary authority of Jesus Christ.
He's not merely a teacher offering encouragement.
He's the One whom even the wind and the sea obey.
Now, here's something important. This passage doesn't promise that every storm in our lives will immediately disappear when we pray.
But it does reveal the power and authority of Jesus Christ.
And that gives us a reason to trust Him.
PART FOUR — WHEN THE STORM IS INSIDE YOUR MIND Now, I want to talk about another kind of storm.
Not a storm with wind and rain.
But the kind that happens inside our minds.
Sometimes our circumstances may appear calm on the outside.
But inside, we're struggling.
We're thinking about things that haven't happened.
We're remembering difficult experiences.
We're worrying about decisions.
Or we're trying to figure out how to manage responsibilities.
Now, here's something I want you to hear. Experiencing anxiety or emotional distress doesn't mean you're failing as a Christian.
And it doesn't mean your faith is automatically weak.
Sometimes people need prayer.
Sometimes they need rest.
Sometimes they need practical support.
And sometimes they need professional care.
Those things are not enemies of faith.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Seeking God's peace doesn't mean ignoring the help and support we may need.
We can pray.
We can study Scripture.
And we can also take responsible steps to care for our well-being.
PART FIVE — BRING YOUR CONCERNS BEFORE GOD Now, let's turn to Philippians chapter 4. We're going to read verses 6 and 7. The King James Version says: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "Let your requests be made known unto God."
Now, isn't that encouraging?
Paul encourages believers to bring their concerns before the Lord.
Through prayer.
Supplication.
And thanksgiving.
Now, here's something important. Prayer isn't a way of pretending our problems don't exist.
It's an opportunity to bring those concerns honestly before God.
We can tell Him when we're afraid.
When we're uncertain.
When we're grieving.
And when we're overwhelmed.
Now, I want you to think about something. Sometimes we carry burdens without ever stopping to pray about them.
We spend hours thinking about what might happen.
We replay conversations.
We imagine different outcomes.
And we try to solve everything ourselves.
Now, prayer doesn't eliminate the need for responsible action.
But it reminds us that we can bring our concerns before our heavenly Father.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Prayer doesn't require having everything figured out. We can come to God honestly, even when we don't know what to do next.
PART SIX — THE PEACE OF GOD AND THE GOD OF PEACE Now, let's continue in Philippians chapter 4. We're going to read verses 8 and 9. The King James Version says: "Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things. Those things, which ye have both learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me, do: and the God of peace shall be with you."
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul speaks about what believers should think about.
And he also speaks about what they should do.
Now, that's important. Because Christian peace isn't simply about trying to feel calm.
It's connected to a life shaped by God's truth.
Now, here's something I want you to think about. What are you filling your mind with?
Are you constantly replaying frightening possibilities?
Are you comparing your life with other people?
Are you surrounding yourself with information that increases your worry?
Or are you also making meaningful room for truth, gratitude, and God's Word?
Now, I'm not suggesting that changing our thoughts will solve every emotional struggle.
But Scripture does encourage us to direct our attention toward what is true and good.
And that can be part of a faithful approach to daily life.
PART SEVEN — GOD IS OUR REFUGE Now, let's turn to Psalm chapter 46. We're going to read verses 1 through 3. The King James Version says: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea; Though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with the swelling thereof. Selah."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "God is our refuge and strength..."
Now, the psalmist describes extraordinary upheaval.
The earth being removed.
Mountains being carried into the sea.
And waters roaring.
Now, that's powerful imagery.
And in the middle of it, the psalmist declares that God is a refuge and strength.
Now, here's something important. God being our refuge doesn't mean trouble never comes.
It means He is worthy of our trust even when trouble exists.
Now, I want you to remember that. Because sometimes we think peace means the absence of problems.
But Scripture repeatedly points us toward God's character in the middle of difficult circumstances.
PART EIGHT — THE CHRISTMAS ANNOUNCEMENT OF PEACE Now, let's return to the Christmas story.
We're going to read Luke chapter 2, verses 13 and 14. The King James Version says: "And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying, Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men."
Now, I want you to think about that announcement.
The angels are praising God.
And they're announcing peace in connection with the birth of Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something important. The coming of Jesus didn't mean that every earthly conflict immediately ended.
Wars continued.
People still experienced suffering.
And the world remained affected by sin.
But through Jesus Christ, God's saving purposes were being fulfilled.
The promised Messiah had come.
And through Him, peace with God is possible.
Now, that's why the Christmas announcement is such good news.
Because the Prince of Peace has come.
PART NINE — PEACE IN OUR RELATIONSHIPS Now, let's talk about something practical.
Because sometimes the greatest challenges to peace happen in our relationships.
Maybe there's tension in your family.
Maybe you've had a disagreement with someone you love.
Maybe a friendship has become strained.
Or maybe you're trying to navigate a difficult situation.
Now, Scripture calls believers to pursue peace where possible.
But here's something important. Peace doesn't mean ignoring wrongdoing.
It doesn't mean refusing to establish boundaries.
And it doesn't require remaining in an unsafe relationship.
Sometimes pursuing peace involves honest conversations.
Sometimes it involves taking responsibility for our actions.
Sometimes it involves forgiveness.
And sometimes it involves maintaining appropriate distance for safety and well-being.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Biblical peace is not the same as pretending everything is okay. It involves truth, righteousness, and love.
PART TEN — LET THE PEACE OF GOD RULE Now, let's turn to Colossians chapter 3. We're going to read verse 15. The King James Version says: "And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to the which also ye are called in one body; and be ye thankful."
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul is speaking to believers about life together in the body of Christ.
He calls them to peace and gratitude.
Now, that's important. Because our faith isn't only about our individual feelings.
It also shapes the way we relate to other people.
How we respond to conflict.
How we demonstrate patience.
And how we seek unity in Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The peace of Christ should shape not only our hearts, but also the way we treat others.
PAUSE AND PRAY — LORD, TEACH ME YOUR PEACE Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about an area of your life where you're longing for peace.
Maybe it's a relationship.
Maybe it's a financial concern.
Maybe it's a health-related worry.
Or maybe it's a situation that feels uncertain.
Now, take a moment to bring that concern before the Lord. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for the peace we have through Jesus Christ. Thank You for sending the Prince of Peace into the world. Lord, You know the circumstances we're facing. You know the worries. The uncertainty. And the burdens we carry. Father, help us bring our concerns before You in prayer. Teach us to trust Your promises. Give us wisdom to take responsible action where needed. And help us seek appropriate support when we're struggling. Lord, may Your Word shape our hearts. And may the peace of Christ influence the way we treat others. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
PART ELEVEN — PEACE WHEN YOU DON'T HAVE ALL THE ANSWERS Now, I want to talk about something I think many of us can relate to.
Not knowing what comes next.
Sometimes we want answers.
We want to know how a situation will turn out.
We want to know when something will change.
And we want to know what the future holds.
But sometimes we don't have those answers.
Now, here's something important. Faith doesn't require pretending we know the future.
And trusting God doesn't mean ignoring uncertainty.
We can acknowledge what we don't know.
We can seek wisdom.
We can make responsible decisions.
And we can remember the promises God has given us in Scripture.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. We don't have to know every detail of tomorrow to trust the Savior who holds our eternal hope.
PART TWELVE — PEACE IS FOUND IN A PERSON Now, I want us to return to our main Scripture. John chapter 14, verse 27.
Jesus says: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you..."
Now, I want you to think about something. Jesus doesn't simply give His disciples a list of ways to create a peaceful life.
He speaks of His peace.
And in the larger conversation, He points them toward the work of the Holy Spirit and the promises of God.
Now, that's meaningful.
Because Christian peace is rooted in our relationship with Jesus Christ.
Not in the absence of responsibilities.
Not in perfect circumstances.
And not in our ability to control everything.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Peace isn't ultimately found in having a perfect life. Christian peace is rooted in the Prince of Peace.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... When I think about peace, do I usually think about my circumstances or my relationship with Jesus Christ? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... What concern have I been carrying that I need to bring honestly before God in prayer? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... How can I pursue peace in my relationships while still honoring truth and healthy boundaries? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... What Scripture can I return to when life feels overwhelming?
Maybe it's John chapter 14.
Philippians chapter 4.
Or Psalm chapter 46. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — THE PRINCE OF PEACE Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because He is the foundation of Christian peace.
The eternal Son of God became flesh.
He lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn peace with God by becoming calm enough.
We don't earn it by never worrying.
And we don't earn it by having perfect circumstances.
Peace with God comes through Jesus Christ.
And we receive salvation by God's grace through faith in Him.
Now, that's the greatest gift of Christmas.
The Prince of Peace has come.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. The peace Jesus gives is deeper than the absence of trouble. Through Him, we have peace with God and a foundation for trust even when life's storms continue.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes the storm doesn't immediately disappear.
But the truth of who Jesus is remains the same.
LIVING IT OUT — BRINGING MY STORMS TO JESUS Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... Bringing My Storms to Jesus.
Now, beneath that heading, write down four things.
First... One concern that's been weighing heavily on your heart.
Second... One truth from Scripture that can help you remember who Jesus is.
Third... One practical step you can take to address the concern responsibly.
And fourth... One way you can demonstrate peace, patience, or compassion in your relationships.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Bring your concerns before God.
Ask Him for wisdom.
And remember the peace you have through Jesus Christ.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, one situation where I'm longing for peace is...
Our second prompt is... The truth about Jesus Christ that I need to remember today is...
And our third prompt is... Help me pursue peace in a faithful and responsible way by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. Jesus Christ is my Prince of Peace. Through faith in Him, I have peace with God, and I will seek His wisdom when life feels uncertain.
Now, say that again. Jesus Christ is my Prince of Peace. Through faith in Him, I have peace with God, and I will seek His wisdom when life feels uncertain.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize John chapter 14, verse 27. "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid."
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about the peace Jesus gives.
Maybe you'll take a few minutes to pray.
Maybe you'll read John chapter 14 again.
Or maybe you'll take a responsible step toward addressing something that's been weighing on your heart.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHAT DOES PEACE LOOK LIKE? Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
The evening is quiet.
The fire is burning.
And we're reflecting on everything we've studied today.
Now, I want to ask you something. When was the last time you experienced a moment of peace in the middle of a difficult season?
Maybe it happened while you were praying.
Maybe while you were reading Scripture.
Maybe during a conversation with someone you trust.
Or maybe it was a quiet moment when you remembered that you didn't have to solve everything at once. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. What does it mean to you that Jesus is called the Prince of Peace?
Think about His saving work.
His authority.
And the peace with God we have through Him. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to remember something. Peace doesn't always mean silence.
It doesn't always mean comfort.
And it doesn't always mean the absence of difficulty.
But Christian peace is rooted in the Savior who came to reconcile us to God.
And that's something worth holding on to.
CLOSING REFLECTION — THE PRINCE OF PEACE HAS COME Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Sometimes life feels like a storm.
The wind is blowing.
The waves are rising.
And we don't know what comes next.
Sometimes the storm is around us.
And sometimes it feels like the storm is happening inside our hearts.
But I want you to remember something.
Jesus Christ is the Prince of Peace.
And through Him, we have peace with God.
Now, that doesn't mean every storm will disappear immediately.
It doesn't mean we'll never feel afraid.
And it doesn't mean we won't need help.
But it does mean that our hope is rooted in the Savior.
The One who came into the world.
The One who lived a sinless life.
The One who died for our sins.
And the One who rose again.
So if you're facing uncertainty today...
Bring your concerns before God.
If you're feeling overwhelmed...
Seek wisdom and support.
If you're experiencing conflict...
Pursue truth and peace where possible.
And if you're simply tired...
Remember that you don't have to pretend everything is easy.
You can come before the Lord honestly.
And you can continue growing in faith.
Because the Prince of Peace has come.
And that's the promise of Christmas.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for sending Jesus Christ, the Prince of Peace. Thank You for the peace we have with You through His saving work. Lord, You know the storms we're facing. You know the worries. The uncertainty. The grief. And the responsibilities that can feel overwhelming. Father, help us bring our concerns before You in prayer. Teach us to trust Your promises. Give us wisdom to take responsible action. And help us seek support when we need it. Lord, may Your peace shape our hearts. May Your Word guide our decisions. And may our relationships reflect the love of Jesus Christ. Thank You for the hope of salvation. And thank You for the promise of eternal life through our risen Savior. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY THREE Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Eleven, Day Two!
And I hope today's lesson has reminded you that the peace Jesus gives is deeper than the absence of trouble.
It's rooted in who He is. And what He has accomplished for us.
Tomorrow, we're continuing our study of The Promise of Christmas — Hope, Peace, and Jesus. And our next lesson is called... When God Feels Far Away — Remembering Emmanuel, God With Us.
We'll explore what Scripture teaches about the coming of Jesus Christ and how the name Emmanuel reminds us of God's saving presence.
Until then, remember... The Prince of Peace has come.
And our hope is found in Him.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: When God Feels Far Away: Remembering Emmanuel, God With Us
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — HAVE YOU EVER FELT ALONE? Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Eleven, Day Three. And we're continuing our Christmas study called... The Promise of Christmas — Hope, Peace, and Jesus.
On Day One, we talked about living hope. Hope rooted in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Yesterday, we talked about peace. Not simply the absence of trouble, but the peace we have with God through our Savior.
And today, we're talking about something that connects both of those truths.
The presence of God.
Now, let me ask you something. Have you ever felt completely alone, even when people were around you?
Maybe you were going through something difficult. Maybe you were facing a decision that nobody else could make for you. Maybe you were grieving someone you loved. Or maybe you were praying about a situation that seemed to have no answer.
And somewhere in the middle of it all, you found yourself wondering... God, where are You?
Lord, are You listening?
Do You see what's happening?
Do You understand how much this hurts?
Now, if you've ever asked questions like those, I want you to know something. You're not the first person to struggle with those feelings.
In fact, Scripture contains prayers from people who felt abandoned, confused, or overwhelmed.
And God has preserved those prayers in His Word.
Now, I think that's important. Because sometimes we assume that having strong faith means we should always feel close to God.
We think every prayer should feel powerful. Every worship service should feel emotional. And every difficult season should come with a clear sense of God's presence.
But that's not always how life works.
Sometimes we pray and feel encouraged.
And sometimes we pray while still feeling overwhelmed.
Sometimes we open our Bibles and immediately find comfort.
And sometimes we struggle to concentrate because we're carrying so much.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Our feelings about God's nearness can change, but the truth of who Jesus Christ is does not change.
And that's what we're studying today.
One of the most beautiful truths in the Christmas story.
Emmanuel.
God with us.
Our lesson today is called... When God Feels Far Away — Remembering Emmanuel, God With Us.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for the gift of Jesus Christ. And thank You for the truth revealed through His coming into the world. Lord, today we're studying what it means that Jesus is Emmanuel, God with us. And You know that some people listening may feel alone. Some may be grieving. Some may be discouraged. Some may be facing uncertainty. And some may be wondering whether their prayers are being heard. Father, help us understand what Scripture teaches about Your faithfulness. Remind us that our feelings are not always a reliable measure of spiritual reality. Teach us to bring our questions and concerns before You honestly. And help us find encouragement in the person and work of Jesus Christ. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — MATTHEW 1:22–23 Now, let's turn to Matthew chapter 1. We're going to read verses 22 and 23.
Before we begin, let's remember the setting. Joseph has learned that Mary is expecting a child.
And an angel of the Lord has appeared to him in a dream.
The angel explains that the child has been conceived by the Holy Ghost.
And Joseph is instructed to name Him Jesus.
Now, Matthew connects these events to the words of the prophet Isaiah.
Let's read Matthew chapter 1, verses 22 and 23, from the King James Version. "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."
Now, I want you to hear those final words again. "Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."
Now, isn't that beautiful?
God with us.
Not simply a message about God.
Not merely another prophet speaking on God's behalf.
But the coming of Jesus Christ.
The eternal Son of God who became flesh.
Now, here's something important. Matthew is making a claim about who Jesus is.
He's connecting Jesus' birth to the fulfillment of Scripture.
And he's showing us the significance of the incarnation.
God the Son entered human history.
And that is the heart of the name Emmanuel.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH Emmanuel means God with us. Through Jesus Christ, God has revealed Himself and accomplished salvation, giving believers a foundation for trust even when they don't feel His nearness.
Now, I want you to hold on to that truth.
Because sometimes our emotions change from one day to the next.
But the truth of the gospel doesn't depend on our emotions.
PART ONE — WHAT DOES EMMANUEL REALLY MEAN? Now, let's spend a few minutes talking about this name.
Emmanuel.
Or, as it's also commonly spelled, Immanuel.
The name comes from Hebrew and means... God with us.
Now, Matthew tells us exactly what the name means.
And he connects it to the birth of Jesus Christ.
Now, I want you to think about something. Throughout Scripture, God reveals Himself to His people.
He speaks through His prophets.
He makes covenants.
And He reveals His character and purposes.
But in Jesus Christ, something extraordinary happens.
The eternal Son of God becomes truly human.
Now, let's turn to John chapter 1. We're going to read verse 14. The King James Version says: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."
Now, I want you to focus on those words. "The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
Now, that's the miracle of the incarnation.
Jesus Christ is fully God and fully human.
And through Him, God has revealed His grace and truth.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Emmanuel isn't simply a comforting Christmas phrase. It points us toward the extraordinary truth of who Jesus Christ is.
PART TWO — GOD'S PRESENCE DOESN'T ALWAYS FEEL THE SAME Now, let's talk about something important.
Because sometimes people confuse God's presence with a particular emotional experience.
They think that if they don't feel encouraged during prayer, God must be far away.
Or if they don't experience strong emotions during worship, something must be wrong.
Now, emotional experiences can be meaningful.
But our feelings are not the foundation of Christian faith.
The foundation of our faith is Jesus Christ.
His identity.
His death.
His resurrection.
And the promises of God.
Now, here's something I want you to think about. Have you ever had a day when you felt spiritually encouraged?
Maybe you read a passage of Scripture that spoke directly to a concern you were facing.
Maybe you heard a sermon that helped you understand something more clearly.
Or maybe you spent time in prayer and felt comforted.
Now, those moments can be meaningful.
But what about the days when you don't feel that way?
What about the days when you're tired?
Or distracted?
Or grieving?
Now, here's something I want you to remember. A difficult emotional season doesn't automatically mean God has abandoned you.
We can continue seeking Him through Scripture, prayer, and Christian fellowship.
Even when our emotions are complicated.
PART THREE — WHEN DAVID FELT FORGOTTEN Now, let's turn to Psalm chapter 13.
We're going to read the entire psalm.
Now, this is a prayer of David.
And I want you to listen carefully to the honesty of his words.
Let's read Psalm chapter 13, verses 1 through 6, from the King James Version. "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me? How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me? Consider and hear me, O LORD my God: lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death; Lest mine enemy say, I have prevailed against him; and those that trouble me rejoice when I am moved. But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation. I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me."
Now, I want you to think about that first question. "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD?"
Now, David is expressing deep distress.
He feels forgotten.
He feels overwhelmed.
And he brings those feelings directly before God.
Now, here's something important. The psalm doesn't teach that God had actually forgotten David.
It shows us how David expressed his experience of suffering.
And I think that's meaningful.
Because sometimes people feel guilty for asking difficult questions.
They think they shouldn't admit that they're struggling.
But Scripture gives us examples of honest prayer.
We can bring our questions before God.
We can acknowledge our pain.
And we can seek Him even when we don't understand our circumstances.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Honest prayer doesn't require pretending that everything is okay.
PART FOUR — FROM QUESTIONS TO TRUST Now, let's look at how Psalm 13 ends.
David says: "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation."
Now, I want you to notice something. David begins the psalm with questions.
But he ends by remembering God's mercy.
Now, that doesn't mean every circumstance has suddenly changed.
The psalm doesn't tell us that all of David's problems disappeared.
But it shows a movement from lament toward trust.
Now, here's something I want you to think about. Sometimes we want our prayers to end with immediate answers.
We want to know exactly what God is going to do.
We want to know when things will change.
And we want every uncertainty resolved.
But sometimes faithful prayer involves bringing our concerns before God and continuing to trust His character.
Even when the answers aren't immediately clear.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You can bring your questions to God without having every answer.
PART FIVE — GOD IS NEAR TO THE BROKENHEARTED Now, let's turn to Psalm chapter 34. We're going to read verse 18. The King James Version says: "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart..."
Now, that's a beautiful reminder of God's compassion.
And I want to speak to someone who may be grieving today.
Maybe you're missing someone you love.
Maybe you're facing your first Christmas without them.
Maybe there's an empty chair at your table.
Or maybe a familiar song brings back memories that are difficult to carry.
Now, I want you to hear something. It's okay to grieve.
It's okay to remember.
And it's okay to acknowledge that someone's absence hurts.
Now, here's something important. Faith doesn't require denying grief.
And trusting God doesn't mean pretending that painful experiences didn't happen.
We can bring our sorrow before Him.
We can seek comfort through Scripture.
And we can receive support from people who care about us.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The Bible doesn't require us to hide our broken hearts from God.
PART SIX — I WILL NEVER LEAVE THEE Now, let's turn to Hebrews chapter 13. We're going to read verses 5 and 6.
Now, before we read, let's understand the context. The writer of Hebrews is encouraging believers toward faithful Christian living.
He speaks about love.
Hospitality.
Contentment.
And trust in God's provision.
Now, let's read Hebrews chapter 13, verses 5 and 6, from the King James Version. "Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee. So that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me."
Now, I want you to hear those words again. "I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee."
Now, that's a powerful promise.
And the writer connects it to contentment and confidence in God's help.
Now, here's something important. This passage isn't a promise that believers will never experience financial hardship.
And it doesn't mean that difficult circumstances will always be removed.
But it does remind God's people of His faithfulness.
Now, I want you to think about something. Sometimes we feel secure when everything is going well.
When the bills are paid.
When our health is good.
When our relationships are peaceful.
And when our plans are moving forward.
But what happens when those things change?
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Our confidence in God's faithfulness should be rooted in His promises, not in the stability of our circumstances.
PART SEVEN — WHEN PRAYERS SEEM UNANSWERED Now, I want to talk about something that can be especially difficult.
Praying about something for a long time.
Maybe you've been praying for healing.
Maybe you've been praying for a relationship.
Maybe you've been praying for financial provision.
Or maybe you've been asking God for wisdom about a decision.
And you still don't know what comes next.
Now, I want you to hear something. Waiting can be difficult.
And sometimes it can leave us feeling discouraged.
But here's something important. We shouldn't assume that every delay means God is displeased with us.
And we shouldn't assume that every personal desire is a promise God has made.
Instead, we can continue bringing our requests before Him.
We can seek wisdom.
We can take responsible action.
And we can remember the promises Scripture actually gives us.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. God's faithfulness isn't measured by whether every prayer is answered according to our preferred timeline.
PART EIGHT — EMMANUEL AND THE CHRISTMAS STORY Now, let's return to the Christmas story.
Because that's the heart of our study this week.
Let's turn to Luke chapter 2. We're going to read verses 10 and 11. The King James Version says: "And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "A Saviour, which is Christ the Lord."
Now, that's the good news of Christmas.
Jesus Christ has come.
The promised Savior.
The eternal Son of God.
Emmanuel.
God with us.
Now, here's something important. The coming of Jesus didn't mean that every earthly problem immediately disappeared.
People still experienced suffering.
Grief.
And hardship.
But through Jesus Christ, God's saving purposes were being fulfilled.
And that's why the Christmas story gives us hope.
Because the Savior has come.
PART NINE — NOTHING CAN SEPARATE US FROM THE LOVE OF GOD IN CHRIST Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 8. We're going to read verses 38 and 39. The King James Version says: "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "Nor things present, nor things to come..."
Now, that's a powerful reminder.
Paul is speaking about the security of God's love for His people in Jesus Christ.
And he lists circumstances and powers that cannot separate believers from that love.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Our hope isn't that life will never become difficult. Our hope is that God's saving love in Jesus Christ is secure.
And that's something worth holding on to.
PART TEN — THE PROMISE OF CHRIST'S PRESENCE Now, let's turn to Matthew chapter 28. We're going to read verses 18 through 20.
This passage comes after Jesus' resurrection.
And He is speaking to His disciples.
Let's read from the King James Version. "And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen."
Now, I want you to focus on those words. "I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world."
Now, Jesus gives this promise in the context of the Great Commission.
He's sending His disciples to make disciples of all nations.
And He assures them of His continuing presence as they carry out that mission.
Now, here's something beautiful. At the beginning of Matthew's Gospel, Jesus is identified as Emmanuel.
God with us.
And at the end of Matthew's Gospel, the risen Jesus promises His continuing presence with His disciples.
Now, that's a meaningful connection.
The Savior who came into the world is the risen Lord who remains with His people.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The promise of Emmanuel points us toward the identity of Jesus Christ, and the risen Savior continues to be present with His people.
PART ELEVEN — WHEN YOU DON'T FEEL SPIRITUALLY STRONG Now, I want to talk about something important.
Because sometimes people assume that being a faithful Christian means always feeling spiritually strong.
They think they should always feel confident.
Always feel encouraged.
And never struggle with questions.
But Scripture gives us a more honest picture.
Believers can experience discouragement.
They can become weary.
They can grieve.
And they can struggle to understand their circumstances.
Now, here's something I want you to hear. You don't have to pretend to feel spiritually strong every day.
You can acknowledge when you're struggling.
You can ask questions.
You can seek encouragement.
And you can continue studying God's Word.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Spiritual growth doesn't require pretending that every day is easy. It involves continuing to seek Christ through the realities of everyday life.
PAUSE AND PRAY — LORD, REMIND ME OF YOUR FAITHFULNESS Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about an area of your life where you've been feeling discouraged.
Maybe you're waiting for an answer.
Maybe you're grieving.
Maybe you're facing uncertainty.
Or maybe you're simply feeling spiritually distant.
Now, take a moment to bring that concern before the Lord. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for the truth of Your Word. Thank You for sending Jesus Christ into the world. And thank You for the hope we have through Him. Lord, You know the circumstances we're facing. You know the questions. The grief. The uncertainty. And the moments when we feel spiritually discouraged. Father, help us remember Your faithfulness. Teach us to bring our concerns before You honestly. Help us continue seeking You through Scripture and prayer. And give us wisdom to seek support when we need it. Lord, remind us of the truth of Emmanuel. God with us. And may the person and work of Jesus Christ remain the foundation of our hope. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
PART TWELVE — PRACTICING AWARENESS OF GOD'S TRUTH Now, let's talk about something practical.
Because sometimes we become so busy that we rarely stop to reflect on God's Word.
We move from one responsibility to another.
We answer messages.
We manage schedules.
And we try to keep up with everything happening around us.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Making meaningful time for Scripture and prayer doesn't require a perfect schedule.
Sometimes it's a few minutes in the morning.
Sometimes it's reading a Psalm during lunch.
Sometimes it's listening to Scripture while doing household responsibilities.
Or sometimes it's taking a moment to pray before going to bed.
Now, the goal isn't to create an impressive routine.
It's to continue growing in our relationship with Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something important. We shouldn't treat prayer or Bible reading like a way to force ourselves to feel a particular emotion.
Instead, we can approach those practices as meaningful ways to seek God and learn from His Word.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... When have I felt spiritually distant or discouraged?
Think about what was happening in your life during that time. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... How does the truth of Emmanuel help me understand who Jesus Christ is?
Think about the incarnation.
God's saving purposes.
And the identity of Jesus. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... What Scripture can I return to when I'm feeling alone or discouraged?
Maybe it's Psalm chapter 13.
Hebrews chapter 13.
Or Romans chapter 8. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... What is one meaningful way I can continue seeking God during difficult seasons?
Maybe it's prayer.
Scripture reading.
Christian fellowship.
Or speaking with someone who can offer wise encouragement. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — EMMANUEL, GOD WITH US Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because He's the center of the Christmas story.
The eternal Son of God became flesh.
He entered human history.
He lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn salvation by always feeling spiritually close to God.
We don't earn it by having perfect emotions.
And we don't earn it by never experiencing doubt or discouragement.
Salvation is God's gracious gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
And our hope is rooted in His saving work.
Now, that's the heart of Emmanuel.
God with us.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. When God feels far away, remember Emmanuel. The truth of Jesus Christ's coming into the world doesn't change with our emotions, and His saving love remains the foundation of Christian hope.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because sometimes our feelings change.
Sometimes life becomes difficult.
And sometimes we don't understand what comes next.
But the truth of who Jesus Christ is remains the same.
LIVING IT OUT — REMEMBERING EMMANUEL Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... Remembering Emmanuel — God With Us.
Now, beneath that heading, write down four things.
First... One situation where you've been feeling spiritually discouraged or alone.
Second... One truth from Scripture that reminds you of God's faithfulness.
Third... One meaningful way you can spend time in Scripture or prayer.
And fourth... One person you can reach out to for encouragement or support.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Bring your concerns before God.
Thank Him for sending Jesus Christ.
And remember the truth of Emmanuel.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, one area where I've been feeling distant or discouraged is...
Our second prompt is... The truth of Emmanuel reminds me that...
And our third prompt is... Help me continue seeking You through Scripture and prayer by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. Jesus Christ is Emmanuel, God with us. Even when my feelings change, I will remember His saving work and continue trusting the promises of Scripture.
Now, say that again. Jesus Christ is Emmanuel, God with us. Even when my feelings change, I will remember His saving work and continue trusting the promises of Scripture.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize Matthew chapter 1, verse 23. "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about what they teach us concerning Jesus Christ.
Maybe you'll read Matthew chapter 1 again.
Maybe you'll spend time reflecting on John chapter 1.
Or maybe you'll encourage someone who's feeling alone.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHEN GOD FEELS DISTANT Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
The evening is quiet.
The fire is burning.
And we're reflecting on everything we've studied today.
Now, I want to ask you something. Have you ever experienced a season when God felt far away?
Maybe you were grieving.
Maybe you were facing uncertainty.
Maybe you were overwhelmed.
Or maybe you simply felt spiritually discouraged. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. What would it mean to bring those feelings before God honestly rather than hiding them?
Maybe it would mean praying more openly.
Maybe it would mean reading a Psalm of lament.
Or maybe it would mean seeking encouragement from someone you trust. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to remember something. The Bible gives us examples of people who brought difficult questions before God.
And the Christmas story reminds us of the extraordinary truth of the incarnation.
Jesus Christ.
Emmanuel.
God with us.
CLOSING REFLECTION — HE IS EMMANUEL Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Sometimes life becomes difficult.
Sometimes we pray and don't immediately receive the answers we hoped for.
Sometimes we grieve.
Sometimes we feel discouraged.
And sometimes we wonder why God feels so far away.
But I want you to remember something.
The truth of Jesus Christ doesn't depend on how we feel on a particular day.
He is the eternal Son of God.
The Word made flesh.
The promised Savior.
And the risen Lord.
Now, that's the heart of Emmanuel.
God with us.
So if you're feeling discouraged today...
Return to Scripture.
If you're grieving...
Bring your sorrow before the Lord.
If you're facing uncertainty...
Seek wisdom and support.
And if you're struggling to feel spiritually connected...
Remember that Christian faith is grounded in Jesus Christ, not in the strength of our emotions.
Because Emmanuel isn't simply a beautiful Christmas name.
It's a declaration about who Jesus is.
God with us.
And that truth is worth remembering every day.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for the truth of Emmanuel. God with us. Lord, thank You for sending Jesus Christ into the world. Thank You for His birth. His sinless life. His sacrifice on the cross. And His resurrection. Father, I pray for the person who's feeling alone today. Give them encouragement and meaningful support. I pray for the person who's grieving. Surround them with comfort and care. I pray for the person who's facing uncertainty. Give them wisdom. And I pray for the person who's feeling spiritually discouraged. Help them remember the promises of Scripture. Lord, teach us to bring our questions before You honestly. Help us continue seeking You through prayer and Your Word. And may the truth of Jesus Christ remain the foundation of our hope. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY FOUR Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Eleven, Day Three!
And I hope today's lesson has reminded you of the beautiful truth of Emmanuel.
God with us.
Tomorrow, we're continuing our study of The Promise of Christmas — Hope, Peace, and Jesus. And our next lesson is called... The Joy of the Lord — Finding Joy When Life Isn't Perfect.
We'll explore what Scripture teaches about joy and why Christian joy is rooted in the goodness of God rather than perfect circumstances.
Until then, remember... Emmanuel.
God with us.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: The Joy of the Lord: Finding Joy When Life Isn't Perfect
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — WHEN JOY FEELS HARD TO FIND Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Eleven, Day Four. And we're continuing our study called... The Promise of Christmas — Hope, Peace, and Jesus.
On Day One, we talked about living hope. Hope rooted in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
On Day Two, we studied the Prince of Peace. And we learned that peace with God through Jesus Christ is deeper than simply having peaceful circumstances.
Yesterday, we talked about Emmanuel. God with us.
And we were reminded that our feelings about God's nearness can change, but the truth of who Jesus Christ is remains the same.
Now, today, we're talking about something that seems to be everywhere during the Christmas season. Joy.
We see the word written on Christmas decorations. We hear it in Christmas songs. We see it on greeting cards. And we hear people wishing one another a joyful Christmas.
But let me ask you something. What happens when Christmas doesn't feel joyful?
What happens when you're grieving someone you love?
What happens when you're facing financial difficulties?
What happens when family relationships are strained?
Or when you're simply exhausted from everything life has placed on your shoulders?
Now, I want to ask you something else. Have you ever felt guilty because you weren't happy during a season when everyone else seemed to be celebrating?
Maybe you looked around and saw people decorating their homes. Shopping for gifts. Planning family gatherings. And sharing beautiful pictures.
Meanwhile, you were simply trying to make it through another day.
Now, here's something I want you to understand. Christian joy is not the same as pretending everything is wonderful.
And it doesn't mean you have to smile through every difficult experience.
The joy Scripture describes is rooted in God. His character. His promises. And His saving work through Jesus Christ.
And that means joy and sorrow can sometimes exist in the same heart.
Now, that's what we're going to study today.
Our lesson is called... The Joy of the Lord — Finding Joy When Life Isn't Perfect.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for the gift of Jesus Christ. And thank You for the good news of His coming into the world. Lord, today we're studying joy. And You know that some people listening may be celebrating wonderful blessings. While others may be facing grief, disappointment, uncertainty, or exhaustion. Father, help us understand what Your Word teaches about joy. Remind us that we don't have to pretend our circumstances are perfect. Teach us to find our hope in Jesus Christ. Help us approach Scripture with open hearts. And give us compassion for those who are struggling during this season. May today's study encourage us and draw us closer to our Savior. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — LUKE 2:8–20 Now, let's turn to Luke chapter 2. We're going to read verses 8 through 20.
Before we begin, let's remember the setting. Jesus has been born in Bethlehem.
And Luke tells us about shepherds who were watching over their flocks at night.
Now, these shepherds are about to receive extraordinary news.
Not simply news of a child's birth.
But the announcement that the Savior has come.
Let's read Luke chapter 2, verses 8 through 20, from the King James Version. "And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid. And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord. And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying, Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men. And it came to pass, as the angels were gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds said one to another, Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see this thing which is come to pass, which the Lord hath made known unto us. And they came with haste, and found Mary, and Joseph, and the babe lying in a manger. And when they had seen it, they made known abroad the saying which was told them concerning this child. And all they that heard it wondered at those things which were told them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart. And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, as it was told unto them."
Now, I want you to hear verse 10 again. "Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people."
Good tidings.
Great joy.
And the announcement of a Savior.
Now, here's something important. The angel didn't announce that every difficulty in the world had disappeared.
The angel announced that Jesus Christ had been born.
And that is why the news was joyful.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH The greatest source of Christian joy is not the perfection of our circumstances, but the good news of Jesus Christ and the salvation He brings.
Now, I want you to hold on to that truth today.
PART ONE — WHY WAS THE ANGEL'S MESSAGE JOYFUL? Now, let's return to the shepherds.
Imagine being out in the fields at night.
You're watching over the sheep.
You're carrying out an ordinary responsibility.
And suddenly, an angel appears.
Luke tells us the shepherds were afraid.
But the angel tells them not to fear.
And then comes the announcement.
A Savior has been born.
Christ the Lord.
Now, that's the reason for the joy.
Not because the shepherds were promised wealth.
Not because they were promised an easy life.
And not because every difficulty they faced would immediately disappear.
But because the promised Savior had come.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The joy of Christmas begins with the good news of who Jesus is.
PART TWO — THE SHEPHERDS RESPONDED TO THE GOOD NEWS Now, let's look at what the shepherds did.
After the angels departed, the shepherds went to Bethlehem.
They found Mary.
Joseph.
And the baby Jesus.
And after seeing Him, they shared what they had been told.
Now, I want you to notice something. The shepherds didn't keep the news to themselves.
They told others.
And when they returned, Luke says they were glorifying and praising God.
Now, that's a beautiful response.
They heard the good news.
They responded.
And they praised God.
Now, here's something I want you to think about. When was the last time you paused to thank God for the gift of Jesus Christ?
Not for something you received.
Not for a circumstance that improved.
But simply for the Savior.
For His birth.
His life.
His sacrifice.
And His resurrection.
Now, that's a meaningful reason for gratitude.
PART THREE — THE JOY OF THE LORD IS YOUR STRENGTH Now, let's turn to Nehemiah chapter 8. We're going to read verse 10. The King James Version says: "Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength."
Now, I want you to focus on those final words. "For the joy of the LORD is your strength."
Now, this verse is often quoted when people are going through difficult times.
But let's understand its original setting.
In Nehemiah chapter 8, the people have gathered to hear the Law of God.
And as they hear it explained, they begin to weep.
They recognize the seriousness of God's Word.
But the leaders encourage them to celebrate the holy day.
To eat.
To drink.
And to share with those who have nothing prepared.
Now, isn't that interesting?
Their joy wasn't disconnected from God's Word.
It was connected to worship, understanding, and the Lord's goodness.
And notice something else. They were told to share with those who had nothing prepared.
Now, that reminds us that joyful worship can also lead to generosity.
We don't simply celebrate God's goodness for ourselves.
We look for opportunities to care for others.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The joy of the Lord is rooted in Him, and that joy can strengthen us to worship, obey, and serve.
PART FOUR — JOY IS NOT THE SAME AS HAPPINESS Now, let's talk about something important.
Because we often use the words joy and happiness as though they mean exactly the same thing.
And sometimes they overlap.
But when Scripture speaks about joy in the Lord, it points us toward something deeper than pleasant circumstances.
Now, happiness often describes how we feel when something enjoyable happens.
Maybe we receive good news.
Maybe we spend time with someone we love.
Maybe something we've been hoping for finally happens.
And we feel happy.
Now, there's nothing wrong with that.
Those moments can be wonderful gifts.
But what happens when circumstances change?
What happens when the good news doesn't come?
When plans fall apart?
Or when we experience loss?
Now, Christian joy is rooted in the Lord and His saving work.
That means we can have a reason to rejoice in Christ even when we are also experiencing sorrow.
Now, that doesn't mean we're always going to feel cheerful.
And it doesn't mean every difficult emotion disappears.
But it means our reasons for gratitude and hope extend beyond our immediate circumstances.
PART FIVE — WHEN JOY AND GRIEF EXIST TOGETHER Now, I want to spend a few minutes talking to someone who's grieving.
Because the Christmas season can be especially difficult when someone you love is no longer here.
Maybe you're remembering Christmas mornings from years ago.
Maybe you're thinking about someone who always made the holidays special.
Maybe there's a familiar recipe.
A favorite decoration.
Or a song that brings back memories.
And suddenly, you're reminded of how much you miss them.
Now, I want you to hear something. It's okay to grieve.
It's okay to cry.
And it's okay if Christmas feels different this year.
You don't have to force yourself to feel happy.
And you don't have to pretend that your loss doesn't hurt.
Now, here's something important. Christian joy and grief are not necessarily opposites.
A person can be thankful for the hope of Jesus Christ and still deeply miss someone they love.
A person can worship God and still have questions.
And a person can hold on to the promises of Scripture while experiencing sorrow.
Now, let's turn to Psalm chapter 30, verse 5. The King James Version says: "For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning."
Now, this is a poetic expression of praise for God's deliverance.
It isn't a promise that every period of grief will end after one night.
And it doesn't mean we can predict when someone will feel better.
But it does remind us of the hope of God's mercy and restoration.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to deny your sorrow to remember the goodness of God.
PART SIX — JOY WHEN CIRCUMSTANCES DON'T CHANGE Now, let's turn to Habakkuk chapter 3. We're going to read verses 17 through 19.
This is a powerful passage.
Because Habakkuk describes circumstances of severe loss and uncertainty.
Let's read from the King James Version. "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments."
Now, I want you to hear verse 18 again. "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation."
Now, think about that. The prophet describes circumstances in which crops have failed.
Food supplies are threatened.
And livestock are gone.
Yet he declares that he will rejoice in the Lord.
Now, here's something important. Habakkuk isn't pretending those circumstances are good.
He's not celebrating the loss itself.
He's expressing trust in the God of his salvation.
Now, that's meaningful.
Because sometimes our circumstances don't change immediately.
Sometimes we're still waiting.
Still grieving.
Still working through difficult decisions.
And still facing uncertainty.
But the character of God remains worthy of our trust.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Joy in the Lord is not the same as being happy about hardship. It is rejoicing in who God is, even when hardship remains.
PART SEVEN — THE JOY JESUS GIVES Now, let's turn to John chapter 15. We're going to read verses 9 through 11. The King James Version says: "As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you: continue ye in my love. If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love; even as I have kept my Father's commandments, and abide in his love. These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full."
Now, I want you to focus on those final words. "That my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full."
Now, Jesus is speaking to His disciples.
And He's teaching them about abiding in His love.
Obedience.
And the joy connected to life in Him.
Now, here's something I want you to think about. Sometimes we search for joy in things that cannot provide lasting spiritual hope.
We look for it in accomplishments.
In possessions.
In approval from other people.
Or in circumstances going exactly the way we planned.
Now, those things may bring temporary happiness.
But they cannot replace the joy rooted in Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The joy Jesus gives is connected to abiding in His love and following His Word.
PART EIGHT — JOY DOESN'T REQUIRE A PERFECT CHRISTMAS Now, let's bring this back to the Christmas season.
Because sometimes we place enormous expectations on ourselves.
We want the decorations to look beautiful.
We want the gifts to be perfect.
We want everyone to get along.
And we want the day to feel magical.
Now, there's nothing wrong with wanting to create meaningful memories.
But here's something I want you to remember. Christmas doesn't have to be perfect to be meaningful.
Maybe you can't afford expensive gifts.
Maybe your family gathering looks different this year.
Maybe you're celebrating with fewer people.
Or maybe you're carrying grief that makes the season difficult.
Now, none of those circumstances changes the truth of the Christmas story.
Jesus Christ has come.
The promised Savior.
The One through whom salvation is found.
And that's the foundation of Christian joy.
PART NINE — THE JOY OF GIVING AND SERVING Now, let's return to Nehemiah chapter 8.
Remember that the people were told to share portions with those who had nothing prepared.
Now, I think that's a beautiful reminder.
Because joy isn't always expressed through receiving something.
Sometimes it is expressed through generosity.
Through compassion.
And through serving others.
Now, I want you to think about something. Is there someone in your life who may be facing a difficult Christmas season?
Maybe someone who's grieving.
Maybe someone who's struggling financially.
Maybe someone who's lonely.
Or someone who simply needs encouragement.
Now, you may not be able to solve every problem.
And that's okay.
But perhaps you can do something meaningful.
You might prepare a meal.
Make a phone call.
Send a thoughtful message.
Or offer practical assistance.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Sharing God's love through generosity and compassion can be a meaningful expression of Christian joy.
PART TEN — WHEN YOU DON'T FEEL JOYFUL Now, I want to talk about something important.
Because sometimes we hear lessons about joy and immediately begin evaluating our emotions.
We ask ourselves... Why don't I feel happier?
Why am I still struggling?
Why can't I just be joyful?
Now, I want you to hear something. The Bible's teaching about joy isn't an invitation to shame ourselves for experiencing difficult emotions.
And it isn't a reason to ignore depression, anxiety, or other emotional struggles.
Sometimes we need rest.
Sometimes we need support from people we trust.
And sometimes we need professional care.
Now, those things are not enemies of faith.
We can seek help while continuing to trust the Lord.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to pretend to feel joyful every moment in order to grow in your relationship with Jesus Christ.
PART ELEVEN — JOY THROUGH TRIALS Now, let's turn to James chapter 1. We're going to read verses 2 through 4. The King James Version says: "My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience. But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing."
Now, I want you to notice something. James is speaking about trials.
And he encourages believers to consider how perseverance can develop through the testing of faith.
Now, here's something important. James isn't telling us to enjoy suffering.
And he isn't saying that every painful experience is good.
Instead, he's encouraging believers to recognize that trials can become occasions for perseverance and spiritual maturity.
Now, that doesn't mean we should seek out hardship.
Or ignore injustice.
But it does mean that our faith can continue growing even through difficult circumstances.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Christian joy isn't rooted in the suffering itself. It's rooted in God and the hope we have through Him.
PART TWELVE — THE GOD OF HOPE FILLS US WITH JOY Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 15. We're going to read verse 13. The King James Version says: "Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost."
Now, I love that verse.
Because it brings together three things we've been studying this week.
Hope.
Joy.
And peace.
Now, notice that Paul connects these things to believing and the power of the Holy Spirit.
He's pointing believers toward God.
Not simply toward better circumstances.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Our hope, peace, and joy are rooted in the saving work of Jesus Christ and the faithfulness of God.
PAUSE AND PRAY — LORD, HELP ME REMEMBER YOUR GOODNESS Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about one thing you're grateful for today.
It doesn't have to be something extraordinary.
Maybe it's someone who encouraged you.
Maybe it's an opportunity to rest.
Maybe it's a meaningful memory.
Or maybe it's simply the opportunity to open your Bible and study God's Word.
Now, take a moment to thank the Lord. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your goodness. Thank You for the gift of Jesus Christ. And thank You for the joy we have through the gospel. Lord, You know that not every season is easy. Some people are celebrating. While others are grieving. Some are facing uncertainty. And others are simply exhausted. Father, help us remember Your faithfulness. Teach us to rejoice in the salvation we have through Jesus Christ. Give us compassion for those who are struggling. And help us recognize opportunities to encourage and serve others. Lord, may our joy be rooted in You. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
PART THIRTEEN — THE JOY OF REMEMBERING Now, I want us to think about something.
Sometimes we become so focused on what is missing that we forget to remember what God has done.
Now, that doesn't mean we should ignore our needs.
Or pretend that our problems don't matter.
But it can be meaningful to pause and remember God's goodness.
Maybe you remember a time when Scripture encouraged you.
Maybe you remember someone who supported you during a difficult season.
Maybe you remember a prayer that helped you seek wisdom.
Or maybe you remember how your understanding of Jesus Christ has grown.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Gratitude doesn't require a perfect life. It involves recognizing God's goodness while honestly acknowledging our circumstances.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... When I think about joy, do I usually connect it to my circumstances or to my relationship with Jesus Christ? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... What does the announcement of great joy in Luke chapter 2 teach me about Jesus Christ?
Think about His identity.
His coming into the world.
And His mission to save. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... Is there an area of my life where I need to remember God's goodness while also acknowledging a difficult reality? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... Who could I encourage or serve during this Christmas season?
Maybe someone who's grieving.
Someone who's lonely.
Or someone who needs practical assistance. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — THE SOURCE OF OUR JOY Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because He's the reason the angel announced great joy.
The eternal Son of God became flesh.
He entered human history.
He lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn salvation by being cheerful.
We don't earn it by pretending we're happy.
And we don't earn it by having perfect circumstances.
Salvation is God's gracious gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
And that's the greatest reason for Christian joy.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. The joy of the Lord isn't dependent on a perfect Christmas or a trouble-free life. Our deepest reason for joy is the Savior who came into the world and accomplished our salvation.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because circumstances change.
Emotions change.
And seasons of life change.
But the truth of Jesus Christ remains the same.
