If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... What does it mean to me personally that Jesus Christ is the Light of the World? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... How can my words, actions, and attitudes better reflect the character of Jesus Christ? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... Is there an area of my life where I need to grow in obedience, humility, or compassion? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... What is one meaningful way I can carry the message of Christmas into everyday life? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — THE TRUE LIGHT Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because He is the true Light.
The eternal Son of God became flesh.
He entered human history.
He lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn salvation by doing enough good works.
We don't earn it by serving enough people.
And we don't earn it by appearing spiritually impressive.
Salvation is God's gracious gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
And our good works should flow from the grace we've received.
Now, that's the heart of the gospel.
And that's why Jesus Christ must remain the center of our lives.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. Jesus Christ is the Light of the World. As His followers, we're called to reflect His truth and love through faithful living, so that others may glorify our Father in heaven.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because Christmas is a season.
But following Jesus Christ is a daily calling.
LIVING IT OUT — CARRYING THE LIGHT Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... Carrying the Light of Christ Into Everyday Life.
Now, beneath that heading, write down four things.
First... One truth about Jesus Christ that you want to remember.
Second... One area of your character where you want to grow.
Third... One person you can encourage or serve this week.
And fourth... One practical way you can make Scripture and prayer part of your daily routine.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Ask God for wisdom.
Thank Him for the gift of Jesus Christ.
And seek opportunities to reflect His love.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, the truth that Jesus Christ is the Light of the World reminds me that...
Our second prompt is... One area where I need to grow as a reflection of Christ is...
And our third prompt is... Help me carry the light of Christ into everyday life by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. Jesus Christ is the Light of the World. Through faith in Him, I will seek to live with truth, humility, compassion, and obedience so that my life brings glory to God.
Now, say that again. Jesus Christ is the Light of the World. Through faith in Him, I will seek to live with truth, humility, compassion, and obedience so that my life brings glory to God.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize Matthew chapter 5, verse 16. "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven."
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about how your life can point others toward Jesus Christ.
Maybe you'll encourage someone who's struggling.
Maybe you'll demonstrate patience in a difficult situation.
Maybe you'll serve someone who needs practical assistance.
Or maybe you'll spend meaningful time studying God's Word.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHAT WILL YOU CARRY FORWARD? Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire one more time.
The evening is quiet.
The flames are beginning to settle.
And we're reflecting on everything we've studied this week.
Now, I want to ask you something. What truth from this week's Christmas study has encouraged you most?
Was it living hope?
The peace of Christ?
Emmanuel?
The joy of the Lord?
Or the love of God? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. How can you carry that truth into your life after Christmas is over?
Maybe it's through prayer.
Maybe it's through Scripture.
Maybe it's through serving others.
Or maybe it's through making a conscious effort to reflect the character of Christ. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's something I want you to remember. The light of Christmas isn't ultimately found in decorations.
It's found in Jesus Christ.
The Light of the World.
And as His followers, we're called to live in ways that bring glory to God.
CLOSING REFLECTION — KEEP THE LIGHT SHINING Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Christmas will come and go.
The decorations will eventually be packed away.
The lights will come down.
And our schedules will return to their usual routines.
But the truth of Jesus Christ remains the same.
He is the promised Savior.
The Word made flesh.
The Light of the World.
The One who died for our sins.
And the One who rose again.
Now, that's the foundation of our faith.
So as we finish this week...
Remember the hope we have through His resurrection.
Remember the peace we have with God through His saving work.
Remember the truth of Emmanuel.
Remember the joy of the gospel.
And remember the love God demonstrated through His Son.
Then carry those truths into everyday life.
Through your words.
Your actions.
Your relationships.
And your willingness to serve others.
Because the message of Christmas was never meant to remain in December.
It's meant to point us toward Jesus Christ every day.
And that's how we carry the light.
Not by drawing attention to ourselves.
But by living in ways that glorify our Father in heaven.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for carrying us through another week of Bible study. Thank You for the gift of Jesus Christ. The Light of the World. Lord, help us remember everything we've studied this week. The living hope we have through His resurrection. The peace we have with You through His saving work. The truth of Emmanuel. The joy of the gospel. And the love You've demonstrated through Your Son. Father, help us carry these truths into everyday life. Teach us to live with humility. Patience. Kindness. Compassion. And obedience. Help us recognize opportunities to serve others. Give us wisdom in difficult situations. And remind us that our good works should bring glory to You. Lord, may our lives reflect the truth and love of Jesus Christ. And may we continue growing in faith through Your Word. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — WEEK ELEVEN COMPLETE Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Eleven!
And what a meaningful week it's been.
We've studied hope. Peace. Emmanuel. Joy. Love. And the calling to reflect the light of Jesus Christ.
Now, next week, we're beginning our final week of this twelve-week journey.
And our theme is... Leaving the Old Behind — Preparing for a New Year.
We'll talk about reflecting on the past. Learning from difficult seasons. Letting go of what we cannot change. And preparing to walk forward in faith.
Our first lesson will be called... A New Thing — Trusting God With What Comes Next.
And we'll begin in Isaiah chapter 43.
Now, until then, remember... Jesus Christ is the Light of the World.
And our lives should point others toward Him.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you next week!

weeks.title: Leaving the Old Behind — Preparing for a New Year

lessons.title: A New Thing: Trusting God With What Comes Next
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — STANDING AT THE EDGE OF SOMETHING NEW Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Twelve, Day One. And can you believe it? We've made it to the final week of our twelve-week Bible study journey.
Now, before we go any further, I want to take a moment to recognize something. We've spent eleven weeks opening God's Word together. We've talked about faith. We've talked about trusting God when we can't see the way. We've talked about waiting. We've talked about grief, healing, and learning to walk forward. We've studied the joy of the Lord. We've talked about hope. Peace. And the love of Jesus Christ.
And now we're standing at the beginning of our final week.
Our theme is... Leaving the Old Behind — Preparing for a New Year.
Now, let me ask you something. Have you ever reached the end of a year and thought... I really didn't expect my life to look like this?
Maybe some things went better than you imagined. Maybe doors opened that you never expected. Maybe you experienced blessings that reminded you of God's goodness.
But maybe other things were difficult. Maybe you lost someone you loved. Maybe a relationship changed. Maybe you faced financial struggles. Maybe your health became a concern. Or maybe you spent much of the year trying to recover from something you never saw coming.
And now, as you look toward a new year, you find yourself wondering... What's next?
Will things get better?
Will I finally see an answer to the prayers I've been praying?
Will I find the courage to take the next step?
And perhaps the biggest question of all... Can I trust God with a future I cannot see?
Now, I want you to hear something today. You do not have to know everything the future holds in order to trust the God who holds your future.
But I also want us to understand something important. Trusting God doesn't mean every plan we make will succeed. It doesn't mean every difficult circumstance will disappear. And it doesn't mean every new year will be easier than the last.
It means we recognize that God is faithful, sovereign, and worthy of our trust. Even when we don't know what comes next.
Today, we're studying a passage from Isaiah that reminds God's people of His power to make a way where no way seems possible.
Our lesson is called... A New Thing — Trusting God With What Comes Next.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for allowing us to begin the final week of this Bible study. Lord, as we reflect on the past and look toward the future, help us approach both with wisdom. You know everything we've experienced. Every blessing. Every disappointment. Every difficult decision. Every answered prayer. And every situation we're still waiting to understand. Father, help us remember Your faithfulness. Teach us to trust You with what comes next. Give us wisdom to make responsible decisions. Courage to follow Your Word. And humility to recognize that our plans are always subject to Your will. May today's study strengthen our faith and draw us closer to Jesus Christ. In His precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — ISAIAH 43:18–19 Now, let's turn to Isaiah chapter 43. We're going to read verses 18 and 19.
But before we read, I want to give you a little background. Isaiah chapter 43 contains words of reassurance to God's covenant people, Israel.
God reminds them that He is their Creator and Redeemer. He recalls His power and faithfulness. And He announces that He will act on their behalf.
Now, the chapter also uses imagery connected to God's deliverance of His people from Egypt.
And then it looks ahead to a new act of deliverance.
Let's read Isaiah chapter 43, verses 18 and 19, from the King James Version. "Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert."
Now, I want you to hear verse 19 again. "Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it?"
Now, those are powerful words. But I want us to understand them carefully.
God was speaking to Israel about His redemptive purposes and His promised deliverance.
This passage is not a blanket promise that every believer will receive a new job, a new relationship, or financial prosperity in the coming year.
But it does reveal something important about God's character.
He is not limited by the circumstances that seem impossible to us.
He is faithful to His purposes.
And His people can trust Him.
Now, that's the truth I want us to carry into today's lesson.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH We can trust God with an uncertain future because His character is faithful, His wisdom is greater than ours, and His saving purposes are fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
Now, let's walk through this together.
PART ONE — GOD REMINDS HIS PEOPLE WHO HE IS Before we focus on the new thing God promises, I want us to look at the beginning of Isaiah chapter 43.
Let's read verse 1. The King James Version says: "But now thus saith the LORD that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine."
Now, notice how God begins. He reminds Israel of their relationship to Him.
He is their Creator. Their Redeemer. And the One who has called them.
Now, that's important. Because before God tells His people about what He will do, He reminds them of who He is.
And I think there's a meaningful lesson for us. Sometimes we become so focused on what God might do next that we forget to remember what Scripture has already revealed about Him.
We want answers. We want direction. We want reassurance.
But the foundation of our faith isn't our ability to predict the future.
It's the character of God.
Now, let me ask you something. When you're facing uncertainty, what do you usually focus on first?
The problem? The possibilities? The things you cannot control?
Or the truths Scripture teaches about God?
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Before we try to understand what comes next, we should remember who God is.
PART TWO — REMEMBERING THE PAST WITHOUT LIVING IN IT Now, let's return to Isaiah chapter 43, verse 18.
"Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old."
Now, at first, that might sound like God is telling His people to forget everything that happened in the past.
But that's not the point.
Throughout Scripture, God's people are repeatedly instructed to remember His mighty works.
So here, the command is not to erase history.
Rather, God is directing their attention toward the new deliverance He is announcing.
They should not assume that His future work must look exactly like His past work.
Now, that gives us something meaningful to think about as we approach a new year.
Sometimes we become so focused on what happened yesterday that we struggle to make wise decisions today.
Maybe we're still replaying a mistake.
Maybe we're holding on to disappointment.
Maybe we're comparing every new opportunity to something that happened years ago.
Or maybe we're afraid to try again because something didn't work out the first time.
Now, here's something important. Learning from the past is wise.
Acknowledging harm is necessary.
And sometimes healing requires time, support, and accountability.
But we don't have to allow every painful experience to define every future decision.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. We can learn from the past without allowing it to become the only lens through which we see the future.
PART THREE — WHAT ARE YOU STILL CARRYING? Now, I want us to make this personal.
As you think about the year behind you, what are you still carrying?
Maybe it's regret.
Maybe it's disappointment.
Maybe it's anger.
Maybe it's a dream that didn't happen.
Or maybe it's grief that still feels just as real today as it did months ago.
Now, I want to make something clear. Leaving the old behind doesn't mean pretending that painful experiences never happened.
It doesn't mean forgetting someone you love.
It doesn't mean excusing wrongdoing.
And it doesn't mean rushing through grief because the calendar is changing.
Some things require ongoing healing. Some circumstances require practical action. And some memories will always be meaningful.
But we can ask God to help us carry those realities with wisdom.
We can seek forgiveness where we have sinned.
We can make amends where appropriate.
We can establish healthy boundaries.
And we can receive support when we need it.
Now, let me ask you something. Is there something you've been carrying that needs your attention rather than your avoidance?
Maybe an apology.
A difficult conversation.
A decision you've been postponing.
Or a burden you need help carrying.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Moving forward faithfully sometimes means addressing the past honestly, not simply trying to forget it.
PART FOUR — GOD CAN MAKE A WAY IN THE WILDERNESS Now, let's return to Isaiah chapter 43, verse 19.
God says: "I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert."
Now, I want you to picture that. A wilderness.
A dry and difficult place.
A place where travel can be dangerous.
And where water may be difficult to find.
Now, God uses this imagery to describe His power to provide a way for His people.
In its original setting, this is part of His promise of deliverance.
Now, here's something important. We shouldn't turn every wilderness image in Scripture into a promise that our personal problems will disappear.
But we can recognize what this passage reveals about God.
He is powerful.
He is faithful.
And His purposes are not defeated by circumstances that seem impossible to human beings.
Now, I want you to think about something. Have you ever faced a situation where you couldn't see a clear way forward?
Maybe you didn't know what decision to make.
Maybe your plans fell apart.
Maybe you had to begin again after a major disappointment.
And perhaps you found yourself asking... Lord, what do I do now?
Now, in moments like those, we can seek God's wisdom through Scripture.
We can pray.
We can listen to wise counsel.
And we can take the next responsible step available to us.
Even when we cannot see the entire path.
PART FIVE — NEW DOESN'T ALWAYS MEAN EASY Now, let's talk about something important.
Because sometimes when we hear the phrase "a new thing," we immediately imagine something exciting.
A new opportunity. A new beginning. A new relationship. Or a wonderful change in circumstances.
And sometimes new beginnings really are exciting.
But new doesn't always mean easy.
Sometimes a new season requires courage.
Sometimes it involves responsibility.
Sometimes it requires learning skills we don't yet have.
And sometimes it means walking through unfamiliar circumstances.
Now, think about the people we read about in Scripture.
When God called Abraham, Abraham had to leave what was familiar.
When Moses was called to lead Israel, he faced enormous responsibilities.
When the disciples followed Jesus, they entered a life that included sacrifice and opposition.
Now, none of those stories teaches us that following God always leads to comfort.
But they remind us that faithfulness sometimes requires walking into the unfamiliar.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. A new season may bring opportunities, responsibilities, or challenges. Our calling is to remain faithful to God through whatever comes.
PART SIX — YOU DON'T HAVE TO KNOW THE WHOLE PLAN Now, let's turn to Proverbs chapter 3. We're going to read verses 5 and 6. The King James Version says: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart..."
Now, trusting God doesn't mean we stop thinking.
It doesn't mean we stop planning.
And it doesn't mean we ignore wise advice.
Instead, it means we recognize that our understanding is limited.
We seek God's wisdom.
We submit our plans to His will.
And we strive to live according to His Word.
Now, let me ask you something. Have you ever wanted God to show you the entire future before you were willing to take the next step?
Maybe you wanted to know exactly how something would turn out.
Maybe you wanted a guarantee that you wouldn't make a mistake.
Or maybe you wanted to know that every challenge would be removed.
Now, I understand why that kind of certainty would feel comforting.
But Scripture doesn't promise that we'll know everything in advance.
Instead, we're called to trust God.
To seek wisdom.
And to walk faithfully according to what He has revealed.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't need complete knowledge of tomorrow to make a faithful decision today.
PART SEVEN — WHEN YOUR PLANS CHANGE Now, let's turn to James chapter 4. We're going to read verses 13 through 15. The King James Version says: "Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain: Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that."
Now, that's a powerful reminder.
James isn't saying that planning is wrong.
He's warning against arrogant confidence in our ability to control the future.
Now, I want you to think about something. We make plans every day.
We schedule appointments.
We make financial decisions.
We plan family gatherings.
We set goals.
And we prepare for the future.
Now, those things can be wise and responsible.
But James reminds us that our lives remain dependent on God.
We don't control tomorrow.
And our plans are always subject to His will.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Faithful planning involves responsibility, humility, and a willingness to acknowledge God's sovereignty.
PART EIGHT — WHEN THE NEW YEAR BRINGS FEAR Now, I want to speak to someone who may be feeling anxious about the future.
Maybe you're facing a major decision.
Maybe you're concerned about your health.
Maybe you're worried about finances.
Or maybe you've experienced so much change that the thought of another new season feels overwhelming.
Now, I want you to hear something. It's possible to trust God and still experience fear.
Faith doesn't mean our emotions become perfectly steady.
And experiencing anxiety doesn't automatically mean we're failing spiritually.
But we can bring those concerns before God.
We can seek wisdom.
We can receive support.
And we can take practical steps toward the responsibilities in front of us.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Trusting God doesn't require pretending we're never afraid. It involves continuing to seek Him even when the future feels uncertain.
PART NINE — HIS MERCIES ARE NEW EVERY MORNING Now, let's turn to Lamentations chapter 3. We're going to read verses 21 through 23. The King James Version says: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."
Now, I love those words. "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."
Now, let's understand the setting. Lamentations is a book filled with sorrow over the destruction of Jerusalem.
The writer is not describing an easy season.
He's reflecting on suffering and devastation.
And in the middle of that sorrow, he remembers God's mercy.
Now, that's meaningful.
Because the hope in this passage isn't based on pretending that everything is fine.
It's based on the faithfulness of God.
Now, I want you to think about something. A new year can feel like an opportunity to begin again.
But God's mercy isn't limited to January first.
His faithfulness doesn't depend on a new calendar.
And we don't have to wait until a new year to repent, seek wisdom, or take a faithful step forward.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Every day is an opportunity to remember God's faithfulness and respond to His Word.
PART TEN — PRESSING TOWARD WHAT LIES AHEAD Now, let's turn to Philippians chapter 3. We're going to read verses 12 through 14. The King James Version says: "Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus. Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus."
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul acknowledges that he has not yet reached perfection.
But he continues pressing forward.
Now, in this passage, Paul is describing his pursuit of Christ and the goal of his heavenly calling.
He's not simply giving advice about New Year's resolutions.
But his example teaches us something important about Christian perseverance.
We are called to continue growing.
To pursue Christ.
And to remain faithful.
Now, let me ask you something. Is there an area of your spiritual life where you've stopped growing because you're discouraged by past mistakes?
Maybe you've struggled to maintain a prayer routine.
Maybe you've been inconsistent in studying Scripture.
Maybe you've been holding on to guilt over something you've already confessed.
Or maybe you've become discouraged because progress has been slower than you expected.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Christian growth is a continuing pursuit of Christ, not a demand that we have already become perfect.
PART ELEVEN — A NEW CREATION IN CHRIST Now, let's turn to 2 Corinthians chapter 5. We're going to read verse 17. The King James Version says: "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
Now, that's a beautiful verse.
But let's understand what Paul is teaching.
He's speaking about the new life and identity that come through union with Jesus Christ.
This is not simply a promise that a new calendar year will change our circumstances.
It's about the transforming work of God through Christ.
Now, here's something important. When someone places their faith in Jesus Christ, their relationship to God is changed.
They belong to Christ.
And they're called to live according to that new identity.
Now, that doesn't mean every struggle immediately disappears.
It doesn't mean temptation vanishes.
And it doesn't mean spiritual growth happens without effort or difficulty.
But it does mean that salvation through Christ brings genuine newness of life.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. The greatest new beginning is not a new year. It is the new life we receive through Jesus Christ.
PART TWELVE — GOD DIRECTS THE STEPS OF HIS PEOPLE Now, let's turn to Psalm chapter 37. We're going to read verses 23 and 24. The King James Version says: "The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD: and he delighteth in his way. Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down..."
Now, this Psalm encourages trust in the Lord rather than envy of those who prosper through wrongdoing.
It reminds God's people of His care and faithfulness.
Now, here's something I want you to think about. Sometimes we become so afraid of making mistakes that we hesitate to move forward at all.
We worry about choosing the wrong path.
Making the wrong decision.
Or experiencing another disappointment.
Now, wisdom matters.
Planning matters.
And seeking counsel matters.
But we also need to recognize that we are limited human beings.
We won't always know everything.
And we won't always make perfect decisions.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Our confidence should rest in God's faithfulness, not in the idea that we'll never make mistakes.
PART THIRTEEN — WHAT DOES FAITHFUL PREPARATION LOOK LIKE? Now, let's talk about something practical.
Because preparing for a new year can involve more than making a list of resolutions.
We can reflect on what we've learned.
We can identify responsibilities that need attention.
We can set realistic goals.
And we can seek God's wisdom about our priorities.
Now, I want you to think about four areas.
First, your relationship with God.
Are you making meaningful time for Scripture and prayer?
Second, your relationships with others.
Are there opportunities to demonstrate greater patience, honesty, or compassion?
Third, your responsibilities.
Are there practical decisions you've been postponing?
And fourth, your personal growth.
Is there something you need to learn?
A habit you need to change?
Or a responsibility you need to approach differently?
Now, here's something important. We shouldn't treat goal-setting as a way to guarantee success.
But thoughtful preparation can be an expression of wise stewardship.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. We can prepare responsibly for the future while remaining humble before God's will.
PART FOURTEEN — YOU DON'T HAVE TO BECOME SOMEONE ELSE Now, I want to speak to someone who may be feeling pressure as the new year approaches.
Maybe you're seeing messages everywhere about becoming a completely different person.
New year. New goals. New habits. New everything.
And sometimes that pressure can become overwhelming.
Now, there's nothing wrong with wanting to grow.
There's nothing wrong with making meaningful changes.
But here's something I want you to remember. Your value isn't determined by how many goals you accomplish.
And your standing before God isn't earned through a perfect list of resolutions.
For believers, our identity is rooted in Jesus Christ.
And our growth should flow from our relationship with Him.
Now, perhaps this coming year will include significant changes.
Or perhaps it will involve faithful perseverance in ordinary responsibilities.
Either way, we can seek to honor God.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Faithfulness isn't always dramatic. Sometimes it looks like continuing to do what is right, one day at a time.
PAUSE AND PRAY — TRUSTING GOD WITH WHAT COMES NEXT Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about one thing you're uncertain about as you look toward the future.
Maybe it's a decision.
A relationship.
A financial concern.
A health situation.
Or simply the unknown.
Now, take a moment to bring that concern before the Lord. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your faithfulness. Thank You for Your Word. And thank You for the hope we have through Jesus Christ. Lord, You know what lies ahead. You know the decisions we'll face. The responsibilities we'll carry. And the circumstances we cannot yet see. Father, give us wisdom. Help us make responsible decisions. Teach us to trust You without demanding that we understand everything in advance. Help us learn from the past. Repent where repentance is needed. Seek forgiveness where appropriate. And continue growing in faith. Lord, may our plans be submitted to Your will. And may our lives bring glory to You. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
PART FIFTEEN — THE NEXT FAITHFUL STEP Now, before we move into our reflection questions, I want us to consider something.
Sometimes the future feels overwhelming because we're trying to solve everything at once.
We're thinking about the entire year.
Every responsibility.
Every possible challenge.
And every decision that might need to be made.
But here's something I want you to think about. What is one faithful step you can take today?
Not next month.
Not next year.
Today.
Maybe it's opening your Bible.
Maybe it's making an appointment you've been postponing.
Maybe it's having an honest conversation.
Maybe it's organizing an important responsibility.
Or maybe it's simply taking time to pray before making a decision.
Now, here's something important. Not every next step will be exciting.
Some steps are ordinary.
Some require patience.
And some involve responsibilities we'd rather avoid.
But faithful living is often built through ordinary obedience.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to solve the entire future today. You can seek God's wisdom for the responsibilities in front of you.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... What experiences from this past year have shaped the way I think about the future?
Consider both the blessings and the difficult moments. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... Is there something from the past that I need to address, learn from, or release rather than continuing to carry it in the same way? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... How does remembering God's faithfulness help me approach an uncertain future? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... What is one faithful and responsible step I can take as I prepare for the year ahead? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — THE GREATEST NEW BEGINNING Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because He's the center of our faith.
The eternal Son of God became flesh.
He entered human history.
He lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, we have forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
Now, here's something important. We don't receive salvation by making enough New Year's resolutions.
We don't earn it by improving ourselves.
And we don't earn it by accomplishing everything on a list.
Salvation is God's gracious gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
And through Him, we receive new life.
Now, that's the greatest new beginning of all.
Not a new calendar.
Not a new set of circumstances.
But a new life in Jesus Christ.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. You may not know what the coming year holds, but you can trust the faithful God revealed in Scripture. Learn from the past, seek His wisdom for today, and continue walking forward in Christ.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because the future may be uncertain.
But God's character remains faithful.
LIVING IT OUT — PREPARING FOR WHAT COMES NEXT Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... Preparing for What Comes Next.
Now, beneath that heading, write down four things.
First... One lesson from the past year that I want to remember.
Second... One burden or unresolved responsibility that needs my attention.
Third... One area where I want to grow in faith and obedience.
And fourth... One practical step I can take this week.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Thank God for His faithfulness.
Ask Him for wisdom.
And commit your plans to His will.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, as I reflect on the past year, one thing I've learned is...
Our second prompt is... One concern I need to trust You with as I look toward the future is...
And our third prompt is... Help me take the next faithful step by...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. I do not know everything the future holds, but I can trust God's faithfulness. I will seek His wisdom, submit my plans to His will, and continue walking forward in Jesus Christ.
Now, say that again. I do not know everything the future holds, but I can trust God's faithfulness. I will seek His wisdom, submit my plans to His will, and continue walking forward in Jesus Christ.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize Proverbs chapter 3, verses 5 and 6. "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths."
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about what it means to trust God with your plans.
Maybe you'll spend time praying over a decision.
Maybe you'll seek wise counsel.
Or maybe you'll take one practical step toward a responsibility you've been postponing.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHAT ARE YOU TAKING INTO THE NEW YEAR? Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
The evening is quiet.
The fire is burning.
And we're reflecting on everything we've studied today.
Now, I want to ask you something. What are you carrying into the new year?
Maybe it's gratitude.
Maybe it's hope.
Maybe it's uncertainty.
Or maybe it's something painful that you're still working through. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. What would it look like to approach the future with faith rather than trying to control every outcome?
Maybe it would mean seeking wisdom before making decisions.
Maybe it would mean accepting that some things are outside your control.
Maybe it would mean asking for help.
Or maybe it would mean continuing to trust God's character even when the future remains uncertain. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to remember something. The new year doesn't require you to have every answer.
And it doesn't require you to become perfect overnight.
But it does give you an opportunity to reflect.
To seek wisdom.
And to continue growing in your relationship with Jesus Christ.
CLOSING REFLECTION — BEHOLD, I WILL DO A NEW THING Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
God spoke through Isaiah and said... "Behold, I will do a new thing..."
Now, in its original setting, that promise was part of God's message of deliverance to Israel.
And it reminds us of His faithfulness and power.
Now, as we prepare for a new year, we don't need to pretend we know exactly what God will do in our individual circumstances.
We don't need to make predictions.
And we don't need to claim promises that Scripture hasn't given us.
But we can remember what Scripture clearly reveals.
God is faithful.
His wisdom is perfect.
His mercy is great.
And His saving purposes are fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
So as you look toward the future...
Remember what you've learned.
Acknowledge what still needs attention.
Seek wisdom for the decisions ahead.
And continue growing in faith.
Because the greatest new beginning isn't found in a date on the calendar.
It's found in Jesus Christ.
And through Him, we have the hope of eternal life.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for Your faithfulness. And thank You for the hope we have through Jesus Christ. Lord, as we prepare for a new year, help us approach the future with wisdom and humility. Teach us to learn from the past. To acknowledge our responsibilities. And to trust You with the things we cannot control. Father, give us courage to make faithful decisions. Patience when circumstances are difficult. And wisdom when the path ahead is unclear. Help us remember that our plans are subject to Your will. And remind us that our greatest hope is found in Jesus Christ. Thank You for His birth. His sinless life. His sacrifice on the cross. And His resurrection. May our lives bring glory to You in the year ahead. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY TWO Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Twelve, Day One!
And we're now walking through the final week of our twelve-week Bible study journey.
Tomorrow, we're continuing our study called... Leaving the Old Behind — Preparing for a New Year.
And our next lesson is called... Letting Go of Yesterday — Learning to Walk Forward in Grace.
We'll explore what Scripture teaches about repentance, forgiveness, and moving forward without allowing past mistakes to define our identity in Christ.
Until then, remember... You don't have to know everything the future holds to trust the faithful God who holds your future.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: Letting Go of Yesterday: Learning to Walk Forward in Grace
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — WHEN YESTERDAY FOLLOWS YOU INTO TODAY Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Twelve, Day Two. And we're continuing our final week together. Our theme is... Leaving the Old Behind — Preparing for a New Year.
Yesterday, we studied Isaiah chapter 43. We talked about trusting God with what comes next. We learned that we don't have to know everything the future holds in order to trust the faithful God revealed in Scripture.
But today, I want to talk about something that can make moving forward especially difficult. The past.
Because sometimes the hardest part of beginning a new chapter isn't the uncertainty of what's ahead. It's what we're still carrying from behind us.
Maybe it's a mistake you made. Maybe it's something you said that you wish you could take back. Maybe it's a decision you regret. Maybe it's a relationship that ended. Or maybe it's something painful that happened to you.
And even though time has passed, you still find yourself thinking about it.
Replaying conversations. Wondering what you could have done differently. Questioning your decisions. And sometimes even questioning your worth.
Now, let me ask you something. Have you ever forgiven someone, or believed you had been forgiven, but still struggled with the memories?
Have you ever found yourself returning to a moment you cannot change?
Maybe you've said... If only I had known.
If only I had made a different decision.
If only I had spoken up.
Or maybe... If only that hadn't happened to me.
Now, I want you to hear something important. Moving forward doesn't require pretending the past never happened.
And receiving God's grace doesn't mean avoiding responsibility for our actions.
But Scripture does teach us that repentance, forgiveness, and new life in Jesus Christ are real.
And that means our past does not have to become the final definition of who we are.
Today, we're studying what it means to acknowledge yesterday honestly while continuing to walk forward in God's grace.
Our lesson is called... Letting Go of Yesterday — Learning to Walk Forward in Grace.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for Your mercy. Your patience. And Your grace. Lord, today we're talking about the past. And You know that some people listening are carrying regret. Some are struggling with guilt. Some are grieving things they cannot change. And others are trying to heal from experiences that were never their fault. Father, help us approach these things with truth and wisdom. Teach us the difference between conviction and condemnation. Help us understand genuine repentance. And remind us of the forgiveness available through Jesus Christ. Give us courage to take responsibility where we need to. Compassion for those who are hurting. And wisdom to continue moving forward. May Your Word guide our hearts today. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S SCRIPTURE — PHILIPPIANS 3:12–14 Now, let's turn to Philippians chapter 3. We're going to read verses 12 through 14.
Before we begin, let's understand the setting. The apostle Paul is writing to believers in Philippi. And in this chapter, he reflects on his former confidence in religious achievements.
He explains that knowing Jesus Christ is of far greater value than anything he once considered a source of righteousness.
Paul recognizes that he has not yet reached the fullness of his goal. But he continues pursuing Christ.
Let's read Philippians chapter 3, verses 12 through 14, from the King James Version. "Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus. Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus."
Now, I want you to hear verse 13 again. "Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before,"
Now, notice something. Paul doesn't claim to be perfect. He doesn't say that he has already arrived. And he doesn't say that his spiritual growth is complete.
Instead, he continues pursuing Christ.
Now, when Paul speaks about forgetting what is behind, he isn't teaching that we should erase every memory. He's describing a determined focus on his calling in Christ rather than resting in former accomplishments or being held back by what lies behind.
And that gives us a meaningful lesson. We can acknowledge the past without allowing it to replace our present calling to follow Jesus Christ.
OUR SECOND MAIN SCRIPTURE — 1 JOHN 1:8–9 Now, let's turn to 1 John chapter 1. We're going to read verses 8 and 9. The King James Version says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Now, I want you to notice the contrast. John warns against denying sin. But he also points us toward confession and God's faithfulness to forgive.
Now, that's important. Because sometimes we think moving forward means pretending we never did anything wrong.
But that's not biblical repentance.
And sometimes we believe that because we've sinned, we must spend the rest of our lives punishing ourselves.
But that's not the gospel either.
Scripture calls us to acknowledge sin honestly and turn toward the mercy of God through Jesus Christ.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH God's grace does not erase our responsibility for the past, but through Jesus Christ we can receive forgiveness, grow through repentance, and continue walking forward in faith.
Now, let's explore what that means.
PART ONE — YOU CANNOT CHANGE YESTERDAY Let's begin with a simple truth.
We cannot go backward in time.
We cannot unsay words we've spoken.
We cannot undo every decision.
And we cannot change every circumstance we've experienced.
Now, that's something most of us understand intellectually. But emotionally, it can be much harder to accept.
Sometimes we replay a moment so many times that we almost convince ourselves we can change the ending.
We imagine a different conversation. A different decision. A different response.
And sometimes that reflection can help us learn.
But other times it becomes a cycle of regret.
We keep returning to the same painful memory without moving toward understanding, accountability, or healing.
Now, here's something important. There is a difference between learning from the past and continually punishing yourself with it.
Learning asks... What happened? What can I take responsibility for? What can I do differently?
But destructive rumination keeps asking questions that have no new answers.
And it can leave us feeling trapped.
Now, I want you to remember something. You cannot change yesterday, but you can make faithful decisions about how you respond today.
PART TWO — NOT EVERYTHING THAT HAPPENED WAS YOUR FAULT Now, I want to make an important distinction.
Because not everyone listening is carrying regret over something they did.
Some people are carrying pain over something that was done to them.
Maybe someone betrayed your trust.
Maybe someone mistreated you.
Maybe you experienced abuse.
Or maybe someone else's choices caused lasting harm.
Now, I want you to hear this clearly. You are not responsible for another person's decision to abuse or mistreat you.
And moving forward doesn't require taking responsibility for someone else's wrongdoing.
Sometimes healing involves recognizing that distinction.
It may involve establishing boundaries. Seeking appropriate support. Allowing yourself to grieve. Or working with someone qualified to help you process painful experiences.
Now, Scripture calls us to truth.
And truth means acknowledging what actually happened.
Not minimizing harm. Not inventing blame. And not pretending that serious wrongdoing doesn't matter.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Healing and repentance are not the same thing. We repent of our own sin; we seek healing and justice when others have harmed us.
PART THREE — CONVICTION IS NOT THE SAME AS CONDEMNATION Now, let's talk about something that can be confusing.
The difference between conviction and condemnation.
Sometimes we feel sorrow because we've done something wrong.
And that sorrow can lead us toward repentance.
But sometimes we become trapped in a belief that we are permanently beyond God's mercy.
Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 8. We're going to read verse 1. The King James Version says: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit."
Now, that's a powerful statement.
Paul is speaking about the freedom from condemnation that belongs to those who are in Christ Jesus.
This isn't a declaration that sin no longer matters.
And it doesn't mean believers are never accountable for their actions.
But it does mean that our standing before God rests in Jesus Christ rather than in our ability to make ourselves righteous.
Now, here's a helpful way to think about it. Conviction leads us to acknowledge wrongdoing and turn toward God.
But hopeless self-condemnation can keep us focused on our failures without moving toward repentance or faith.
Now, I want you to remember something. The gospel calls us to repentance and faith, not endless self-punishment.
PART FOUR — WHAT DOES REAL REPENTANCE LOOK LIKE? Now, let's turn to 2 Corinthians chapter 7. We're going to read verses 9 and 10. The King James Version says: "Now I rejoice, not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance: for ye were made sorry after a godly manner, that ye might receive damage by us in nothing. For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death."
Now, I want you to notice something. Paul distinguishes between sorrow that leads to repentance and sorrow that produces destructive results.
Now, repentance is more than simply feeling bad.
It's more than saying we're sorry because we got caught.
And it's more than wishing the consequences would disappear.
Genuine repentance involves acknowledging sin and turning away from it toward God.
And when we've harmed another person, repentance may also involve making appropriate efforts to repair what we've damaged.
That might mean an honest apology.
Returning something that doesn't belong to us.
Correcting a false statement.
Or changing a harmful pattern of behavior.
Now, those actions don't purchase God's forgiveness.
But they can be appropriate expressions of repentance.
Now, here's something important. We cannot always undo the consequences of our actions.
But we can seek to respond faithfully to the truth.
PART FIVE — DAVID'S PRAYER OF REPENTANCE Now, let's turn to Psalm chapter 51.
This Psalm is traditionally connected to David's repentance after his sin involving Bathsheba.
Now, David's actions were serious. They involved adultery, abuse of royal power, and the death of Uriah.
And the Psalm does not invite us to minimize that wrongdoing.
Instead, it gives us a picture of confession before God.
Let's read Psalm 51, verses 1 through 4, from the King James Version. "Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions. Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me. Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest."
Now, notice something. David doesn't begin by making excuses.
He acknowledges his sin.
He appeals to God's mercy.
And he recognizes that his wrongdoing is evil in God's sight.
Now, David had also harmed other people. So when he speaks of sinning against God, we shouldn't interpret that as denying the harm done to Bathsheba and Uriah.
His sin was against God and involved grievous harm to others.
Now, let's read verse 10. "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me."
Now, that's a prayer worth remembering.
David isn't simply asking to escape consequences.
He's asking God to work within him.
To cleanse him. And renew him.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Repentance is not about pretending we were never wrong. It is about acknowledging sin and turning toward the mercy and transforming work of God.
PART SIX — WHEN YOU KEEP REPLAYING YOUR MISTAKES Now, let's make this personal.
Maybe you've confessed something to God.
Maybe you've apologized to someone you hurt.
Maybe you've taken responsibility and worked to change your behavior.
But you still find yourself replaying what happened.
And every time the memory returns, you feel the same shame.
Now, here's something important. Remembering a mistake doesn't necessarily mean God hasn't forgiven you.
Our memories don't disappear simply because we've repented.
And emotional healing doesn't always happen immediately.
Sometimes it takes time to learn how to respond differently when those memories return.
Now, I want you to think about something. When you remember a past mistake, what do you do next?
Do you return to God's promises?
Do you acknowledge what you've learned?
Do you consider whether any responsibility still needs attention?
Or do you begin telling yourself that you can never be anything more than your worst decision?
Now, here's something I want you to remember. A past failure can become part of your testimony without becoming your entire identity.
PART SEVEN — FORGIVENESS DOESN'T ALWAYS REMOVE CONSEQUENCES Now, I want us to talk about something important.
Because sometimes people hear messages about God's forgiveness and assume that forgiveness means every consequence will disappear.
But that's not what Scripture teaches.
God's forgiveness is real.
But earthly consequences may remain.
Relationships may need rebuilding.
Trust may take time to restore.
And some responsibilities must still be addressed.
Now, here's something important. Forgiveness doesn't mean accountability is unnecessary.
And repentance doesn't mean we can demand that other people immediately trust us again.
Sometimes we must allow others the time and space they need.
Sometimes reconciliation isn't possible.
And sometimes the wisest course is to respect appropriate boundaries.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. God's grace gives us hope for transformation, but it doesn't remove the importance of truth, responsibility, and wise action.
PART EIGHT — LEARNING TO FORGIVE OTHERS Now, let's turn to Ephesians chapter 4. We're going to read verses 31 and 32. The King James Version says: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you."
Now, I want you to think about those words. "Forgiving one another..."
Now, forgiveness can be difficult. Especially when the hurt is deep.
And I want to make something clear. Forgiveness doesn't mean calling evil good.
It doesn't mean pretending harm never happened.
And it doesn't mean remaining in an unsafe relationship.
Sometimes forgiveness is part of a long process.
And it may involve seeking God's help as we work through anger, grief, and the desire for revenge.
Now, here's something important. Forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical.
Reconciliation generally requires truth, accountability, and appropriate willingness from the people involved.
And trust should be rebuilt through trustworthy behavior, not demanded.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. We can seek to forgive while still maintaining necessary boundaries and pursuing justice.
PART NINE — THE PRODIGAL SON AND THE FATHER'S MERCY Now, let's turn to Luke chapter 15.
We're going to look at the parable commonly called the Prodigal Son.
Jesus tells the story of a younger son who asks for his inheritance.
He leaves home.
And he wastes what he has received.
Eventually, he finds himself in desperate circumstances.
And he decides to return to his father.
Now, let's read Luke chapter 15, verses 18 through 20. The King James Version says: "I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants. And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him."
Now, what a powerful picture.
The son acknowledges his wrongdoing.
He returns.
And his father receives him with compassion.
Now, Jesus tells this parable in a context where religious leaders are criticizing Him for welcoming sinners.
And the story reveals the joy associated with repentance and restoration.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. God's mercy is not earned by pretending we have never sinned. The gospel calls sinners to turn to Him in repentance and faith.
PART TEN — WHEN THE PAST IS PART OF YOUR TESTIMONY Now, I want to talk about something meaningful.
Sometimes we wish we could remove certain chapters from our lives.
We wish we could erase the pain.
The mistakes.
The disappointments.
Or the seasons when we felt completely lost.
But sometimes those experiences become part of what we share with others.
Not because every painful experience was good.
And not because God approves of everything that happened.
But because we can testify to His mercy and faithfulness even after difficult circumstances.
Now, I want you to think about something. Your testimony doesn't have to be a perfect story.
It can include mistakes.
It can include repentance.
It can include grief.
And it can include lessons you're still learning.
Now, here's something important. You also don't have to share every painful detail publicly.
Wisdom and privacy matter.
And some parts of your story may be better shared only with trusted people.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Your testimony can point others toward God's grace without requiring you to reveal every chapter of your life.
PART ELEVEN — LAYING ASIDE WHAT HINDERS US Now, let's turn to Hebrews chapter 12. We're going to read verses 1 and 2. The King James Version says: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God."
Now, I want you to focus on two things. "Lay aside every weight..."
And... "Looking unto Jesus..."
Now, Hebrews is encouraging believers to persevere in faith.
And it points them toward Jesus Christ.
Now, here's something important. Not every weight we carry is the same.
Some things are sinful habits that require repentance.
Some are unnecessary distractions.
Some are responsibilities we need to manage differently.
And some are painful experiences that require care and healing rather than blame.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. We need wisdom to recognize what must be repented of, what can be released, and what requires patient attention.
PART TWELVE — GOD'S MERCIES ARE NEW EVERY MORNING Now, let's turn to Lamentations chapter 3. We're going to read verses 22 and 23. The King James Version says: "It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."
Now, those words are especially meaningful as we prepare for a new year.
Because sometimes we think we have to wait until January first to begin making changes.
But God's mercy isn't limited to a new calendar year.
We can turn toward Him today.
We can confess our sins today.
We can seek wisdom today.
And we can begin making faithful decisions today.
Now, here's something important. A new year may provide a meaningful opportunity for reflection.
But the Christian life is lived one day at a time.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. You don't have to wait for a new year to take a faithful step toward God.
PART THIRTEEN — MOVING FORWARD DOESN'T MEAN RUSHING Now, I want to speak to someone who may feel pressure to move on.
Maybe people have told you that enough time has passed.
Maybe someone has said you should be over it by now.
Or maybe you've been telling yourself that you need to stop feeling the way you do.
Now, I want you to hear something. Healing doesn't always follow a predictable timeline.
And grief isn't something we can simply turn off.
Sometimes moving forward involves taking very small steps.
Sometimes it means seeking help.
Sometimes it means learning to live with a loss that will always matter.
And sometimes it means accepting that progress may not look the way we expected.
Now, here's something important. Christian faith doesn't require us to rush through sorrow.
We can grieve honestly while continuing to seek God's wisdom and comfort.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Moving forward in grace is not a race to prove that the past no longer hurts.
PART FOURTEEN — THE NEXT RIGHT STEP Now, let's make this practical.
Because sometimes we hear messages about moving forward and immediately think we need to change everything.
But perhaps the most meaningful thing you can do is identify one responsible next step.
Maybe you need to confess something to God.
Maybe you need to apologize to someone you've hurt.
Maybe you need to establish a boundary.
Maybe you need to seek counseling or other support.
Or maybe you need to stop revisiting a decision that you've already addressed as faithfully as you can.
Now, here's something important. Not every situation requires the same response.
And we shouldn't assume that every painful memory is something we can simply choose to forget.
But we can seek wisdom about what is within our responsibility today.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Grace doesn't mean doing nothing. It gives us reason to respond faithfully to the truth.
PAUSE AND PRAY — LORD, HELP ME WALK FORWARD Now, let's take a moment to pause.
I want you to think about something from your past that still weighs on your heart.
Maybe it's a regret.
Maybe it's a painful memory.
Maybe it's an unresolved responsibility.
Or maybe it's something you've been struggling to understand.
Now, you don't have to force yourself to revisit details that feel overwhelming.
Simply consider what kind of help, wisdom, or support you may need. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Let's pray. Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your mercy and grace. Thank You for the forgiveness available through Jesus Christ. Lord, You know the things we're carrying from the past. You know our mistakes. Our regrets. Our grief. And the experiences that have caused us pain. Father, help us acknowledge our own sins honestly. Give us courage to repent. Wisdom to make things right where possible. And humility to accept responsibility. For those who have been harmed by others, I pray for comfort, protection, justice, and meaningful support. Lord, help us understand the difference between repentance and shame. Teach us to trust Your Word. And help us continue growing in faith. May we walk forward with truth, wisdom, and grace. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
PART FIFTEEN — YOUR PAST IS NOT YOUR ENTIRE IDENTITY Now, before we move into our reflection questions, I want us to consider something.
Sometimes we begin describing ourselves according to our worst experiences.
We say... I'm the person who failed.
I'm the person who made that mistake.
I'm the person whose relationship ended.
Or I'm the person who went through that terrible experience.
Now, those events may be part of our history.
But they don't have to become our entire identity.
For those who belong to Jesus Christ, Scripture teaches that our identity is rooted in Him.
We are called to grow in faith.
To pursue righteousness.
And to live according to the grace we've received.
Now, here's something important. We don't need to deny the past to recognize that God calls us to continued growth.
And we don't need to pretend we've already reached perfection.
Remember what Paul said. "I press toward the mark..."
Now, that's the picture I want you to remember. Continuing forward in the pursuit of Christ.
Not because we've already become perfect.
But because He is worthy of our faith and obedience.
LET'S REFLECT TOGETHER Now, let's work through today's reflection questions.
If you have your journal nearby, take a moment to write down your answers.
Our first question is... Is there something from my past that I'm allowing to define how I see myself today? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our second question is... Do I need to acknowledge a mistake, seek forgiveness, make amends, or address an unresolved responsibility? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our third question is... Am I carrying guilt for something I did, or blame for something that was done to me?
And how might recognizing that difference help me respond wisely? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Our fourth question is... What is one faithful step I can take toward repentance, healing, or spiritual growth? [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS]
CHRIST CONNECTION — GRACE THAT MAKES FORGIVENESS POSSIBLE Now, let's bring everything back to Jesus.
Because the forgiveness we're studying today is made possible through Him.
The eternal Son of God became flesh.
He lived a sinless life.
He died on the cross for our sins.
And He rose again.
Through Him, sinners can receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
Now, here's something important. We don't earn salvation by punishing ourselves for past mistakes.
We don't earn it by making enough apologies.
And we don't earn it by becoming perfect.
Salvation is God's gracious gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
And genuine faith calls us toward repentance and a transformed life.
Now, that's the heart of the gospel.
Not denial of sin.
Not endless condemnation.
But forgiveness and new life through Jesus Christ.
GRACE NOTE Now, here's today's Grace Note. You cannot rewrite yesterday, but through Jesus Christ you can receive forgiveness, respond to the past with truth, and continue walking forward in God's grace.
Now, I want you to remember that.
Because your past may have shaped you.
But it doesn't have to determine every step you take from this moment forward.
LIVING IT OUT — A GRACE-FILLED REFLECTION Now, let's make today's lesson practical.
I want you to take a page in your journal.
And write down the words... Walking Forward in Grace.
Now, beneath that heading, write down four things.
First... One experience from the past that still affects me.
Second... What this experience has taught me, or what I still need help understanding.
Third... Whether my next step involves repentance, making amends, setting a boundary, seeking support, or simply allowing myself time to heal.
And fourth... One faithful action I can take this week.
Now, after you've written those things down, take a moment to pray.
Ask God for wisdom.
Thank Him for His mercy.
And seek His guidance for the next step.
PRAYER JOURNAL Our first journal prompt is... Lord, one part of my past that I need Your wisdom to address is...
Our second prompt is... Help me understand the difference between responsibility, repentance, and unnecessary shame by...
And our third prompt is... As I continue walking forward, help me grow in...
Now, take time to pray over those answers.
FAITH BUILDER Here's today's Faith Builder. Through Jesus Christ, I can receive forgiveness and grow in grace. I will acknowledge the past honestly, take responsibility for my actions, and continue pursuing Christ.
Now, say that again. Through Jesus Christ, I can receive forgiveness and grow in grace. I will acknowledge the past honestly, take responsibility for my actions, and continue pursuing Christ.
FAITH CHALLENGE Here's today's Faith Challenge. Memorize 1 John chapter 1, verse 9. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Now, throughout the day, return to those words.
And think about the faithfulness of God.
Maybe you'll spend time confessing something you've been avoiding.
Maybe you'll seek wisdom about an unresolved responsibility.
Maybe you'll take a step toward healing.
Or maybe you'll encourage someone who's struggling with regret.
AROUND THE FIRE — WHAT ARE YOU READY TO RELEASE? Now, let's imagine we're sitting together around the fire.
The evening is quiet.
The fire is burning.
And we're reflecting on everything we've studied today.
Now, I want to ask you something. What have you been carrying from yesterday that is affecting the way you live today?
Maybe it's regret.
Maybe it's shame.
Maybe it's anger.
Or maybe it's a painful memory that still needs care and attention. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, here's another question. What would it look like to respond to that experience with truth, wisdom, and grace?
Maybe it means repentance.
Maybe it means forgiveness.
Maybe it means establishing a boundary.
Maybe it means seeking help.
Or maybe it means accepting that you cannot change what happened, but you can make faithful decisions about what comes next. [PAUSE FOR 10 SECONDS] Now, I want you to remember something. You don't have to pretend the past never happened.
And you don't have to rush through healing.
But you can continue seeking Jesus Christ.
You can continue growing in faith.
And you can take the next faithful step.
CLOSING REFLECTION — KEEP PRESSING FORWARD Now, before we close, I want to leave you with one final thought.
Paul said... "I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus."
Now, think about those words. "I press toward the mark..."
Paul wasn't claiming to be perfect.
He wasn't pretending he had never made mistakes.
And he wasn't saying that the past no longer existed.
He was describing his continuing pursuit of Christ.
Now, that's what I want us to remember today.
We can acknowledge our mistakes.
We can repent.
We can seek forgiveness.
We can learn from difficult experiences.
And we can continue walking forward.
Not because we're perfect.
But because of the grace of God through Jesus Christ.
So as you prepare for the year ahead...
Don't allow shame to become your identity.
Don't confuse forgiveness with avoiding responsibility.
And don't assume that healing must happen according to someone else's timeline.
Instead, seek God's wisdom.
Walk in truth.
Take responsibility where needed.
And continue pursuing Jesus Christ.
Because yesterday is part of your story.
But through Christ, it doesn't have to be the end of your story.
CLOSING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for Your Word today. Thank You for Your mercy and grace. And thank You for the forgiveness available through Jesus Christ. Lord, help us approach the past with honesty. Give us courage to acknowledge our sins. Wisdom to take responsibility. And humility to seek forgiveness where appropriate. Father, I pray for those who have been hurt by others. Give them comfort. Protection. Justice. And meaningful support. I pray for those struggling with guilt and shame. Help them understand the truth of Your Word. And remind them of the forgiveness available through Jesus Christ. Lord, help us continue growing in faith. Teach us to walk in truth. To demonstrate compassion. And to pursue righteousness. May our lives reflect the grace we've received through our Savior. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
OUTRO — LOOKING AHEAD TO DAY THREE Thank you so much for joining me today on Walking Through the Word. We've officially completed Week Twelve, Day Two!
And I hope today's lesson has reminded you that moving forward doesn't require pretending yesterday never happened.
It means responding to the past with truth, wisdom, and grace.
Tomorrow, we're continuing our final week with a lesson called... A Heart Made New — Allowing God to Transform Us From Within.
We'll explore what Scripture teaches about spiritual renewal, a changed heart, and the transforming work of God through Jesus Christ.
Until then, remember... You cannot change yesterday. But through Jesus Christ, you can receive forgiveness and continue walking forward in grace.
Keep opening your Bible. Keep praying. And keep seeking the Lord.
And as always... You don't have to walk through the fire alone. Keep the faith. Keep walking. There is another side of the fire. God bless you, and I'll see you tomorrow!

lessons.title: A Heart Made New: Allowing God to Transform Us From Within
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION — WHEN CHANGING THE OUTSIDE ISN'T ENOUGH Hey, everyone! Welcome back to Walking Through the Word. I'm your host, Jessica Riles, and I'm so thankful you're joining me today.
Today is Week Twelve, Day Three. And we're continuing our final week of this twelve-week Bible study journey.
Our theme this week is... Leaving the Old Behind — Preparing for a New Year.
On Day One, we talked about trusting God with what comes next. Yesterday, we studied what it means to let go of yesterday and walk forward in grace. And today, we're talking about something that connects both of those lessons. Transformation.
Now, let me ask you something. Have you ever decided you were going to change something about your life?
Maybe you decided to become more patient. Maybe you wanted to stop worrying so much. Maybe you wanted to spend more time reading your Bible. Or maybe you wanted to change the way you responded when someone upset you.
And for a little while, everything seemed to be going well.
You were motivated. You were determined. You had a plan.
But then something happened.
Life became stressful. Someone hurt your feelings. Your schedule became overwhelming. Or you found yourself falling right back into an old habit.
And you started wondering... Why is it so hard to change?
Now, I want you to think about something. Sometimes we focus so much on changing our behavior that we forget to examine what's happening in our hearts.
We want different results. But we're still holding on to the same attitudes. The same fears. The same patterns of thinking. And sometimes the same sinful habits.
Now, here's something I want you to remember. Biblical transformation is deeper than changing our appearance, improving our schedule, or making a list of resolutions.
It involves the renewing work of God.
It involves repentance. Faith. And learning to live according to His Word.
Now, as we prepare for a new year, we may be thinking about things we want to accomplish. And there's nothing wrong with setting meaningful goals.
But I want to ask a different question today. Instead of only asking... What do I want to accomplish next year?
What if we also asked... Lord, how do You want me to grow in my relationship with You?
That's what we're studying today. Our lesson is called... A Heart Made New — Allowing God to Transform Us From Within.
Let's begin with prayer.
OPENING PRAYER Heavenly Father, Thank You for bringing us together for another day in Your Word. Thank You for Your mercy, patience, and grace. Lord, today we're studying what it means to experience genuine spiritual transformation. Help us understand that lasting spiritual renewal comes through Your saving work. Teach us to recognize the areas of our lives where we need to grow. Give us humility to acknowledge sin. Courage to repent. And wisdom to live according to Your Word. Father, I pray for anyone who feels discouraged by repeated struggles. Remind them that Christian growth is a process. Help us look to Jesus Christ rather than relying entirely on our own strength. May Your Word shape our thoughts, attitudes, and actions. In Jesus' precious name, Amen.
TODAY'S FIRST SCRIPTURE — EZEKIEL 36:25–27 Now, let's turn to Ezekiel chapter 36. We're going to read verses 25 through 27.
Before we begin, let's understand the setting. The prophet Ezekiel was speaking to God's covenant people during a time of judgment and exile.
Israel had repeatedly turned away from the Lord. And through Ezekiel, God announced both judgment and future restoration.
In chapter 36, God promises to restore His people and cleanse them from their uncleanness.
He also promises a new heart and a new spirit.
Now, these words are part of God's covenant promises to Israel. And they reveal the importance of God's work in spiritual renewal.
Let's read Ezekiel chapter 36, verses 25 through 27, from the King James Version. "Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them."
Now, I want you to hear verse 26 again. "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you..."
Now, that's a powerful promise.
Notice who is doing the work. God says... "I will give you..."
"I will put within you..."
And... "I will take away..."
Now, that's important. Because spiritual renewal isn't simply a matter of human determination.
It requires the work of God.
And as Christians, we understand the transforming work of the Holy Spirit through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
TODAY'S SECOND SCRIPTURE — ROMANS 12:1–2 Now, let's turn to Romans chapter 12. We're going to read verses 1 and 2.
In the earlier chapters of Romans, Paul explains the gospel and God's mercy.
Then, in chapter 12, he begins explaining how believers should respond to that mercy in everyday life.
Let's read Romans chapter 12, verses 1 and 2, from the King James Version. "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God."
Now, I want you to hear those words again. "Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind..."
Now, Paul isn't telling believers to become transformed simply through positive thinking.
He's calling them to live in response to God's mercy.
To resist conformity to sinful patterns.
And to have their thinking renewed according to God's truth.
Now, that brings us to today's key truth.
TODAY'S KEY TRUTH True spiritual transformation begins with God's saving grace and continues as the Holy Spirit renews our hearts and minds, teaching us to live according to His Word.
Now, let's walk through this together.
PART ONE — GOD IS CONCERNED WITH THE HEART Now, let's begin with something important.
When we think about change, we often think about outward behavior.
We want to stop doing certain things. Start doing other things. Develop better habits. And become more disciplined.
Now, those things can be valuable.
